bullets: The new AgentJudgeBench release tests whether large language models used as automated judges can grade tool-calling workflows represented as dependency graphs. Its 3,808 instances span six graph structures and three difficulty levels, and compare judging with and without ground-truth workflow information. This targets structured execution rather than open-ended text preferences. The separate scale-reversal probe in today’s feed also tests whether judges follow rubric meaning rather than numerical conventions. [E010, E060] Why it matters: If you use model-based graders for agent evaluations, ordinary agreement scores may not establish that the grader understands workflow dependencies or the rubric itself. These releases provide targeted checks that can inform whether to retain automated grading, supply execution ground truth, or add human review for complex workflows. [E010, E060] Evidence: E010, E060. Medium confidence.

The new TraceProbe benchmark runs agents in executable sandboxes, records normalized action traces, and replays tool actions to locate where safety risks entered and propagated. It scores both final outcomes and hidden rule violations, rather than treating an apparently acceptable endpoint as sufficient evidence of safe execution. [E008] Why it matters: If you evaluate agents that use files, tools, memory, retrieved content, or other agents, TraceProbe offers a way to distinguish a safe-looking result from an unsafe path to that result. That can change whether a security suite is selected for release gating, incident diagnosis, or comparison of safeguards. [E008] Evidence: E008. Medium confidence.

The new MESSIER corpus standardizes 957,611 evaluation records from 30 benchmarks, covering 745 agents, 11,891 tasks, and 74,263 verifiers, while adding runs on six underrepresented professional and scientific benchmarks. It maps otherwise heterogeneous tasks, agent scaffolds, scoring rules, and result records into a common schema. [E004] Why it matters: If you are choosing a suite for cross-benchmark agent comparison, MESSIER may reduce the need to rerun every system merely to obtain comparable records. Its common schema also makes verifier and scaffold differences visible, helping teams decide whether an apparent performance difference reflects the agent or the evaluation setup. [E004] Evidence: E004. Medium confidence.

The new MACRO benchmark evaluates how multi-agent systems handle underspecified travel requests. Its 107 fully annotated tasks include 703 process milestones, expected user clarifications, task-state requirements, and standardized interfaces between specialized agents, so scoring can examine how a system reached its result rather than only whether the trip plan succeeded. [E005] Why it matters: If your product must ask users for missing constraints before coordinating dependent subtasks, end-to-end success can hide failures such as guessing preferences or losing state. MACRO provides process-level checkpoints that can influence which orchestration design, clarification policy, or agent interface you choose. [E005] Evidence: E005. Medium confidence.

The new ConformWeb benchmark derives hidden interaction sequences from public behavioral contracts and executes them against generated web applications. Its protocol tests whether an application preserves specified behavior across dynamic workflows without requiring an undisclosed reference implementation. [E011] Why it matters: If you compare coding agents on web-application generation, screenshots or shallow functionality checks may reward plausible interfaces that fail under interaction. Contract-grounded hidden workflows offer a basis for selecting systems on behavioral conformance while keeping the expected public scope visible to the system being tested. [E011] Evidence: E011. Medium confidence.
bullets_zh: 新发布的 AgentJudgeBench 测试被用作自动化评审器的大语言模型能否对以依赖图表示的工具调用工作流进行评分。其 3,808 个实例涵盖六种图结构和三个难度级别，并比较了有无工作流真实信息时的评审结果。它针对的是结构化执行，而非开放式文本偏好。今日信息流中另一项独立的量表反转探测还测试评审器遵循的是评分标准的含义，还是数值惯例。[E010, E060] Why it matters: 如果你在智能体评估中使用基于模型的评分器，常规一致性分数可能不足以证明评分器理解工作流依赖关系或评分标准本身。这些发布提供了有针对性的检查，可为以下决策提供依据：是否继续使用自动化评分、提供执行过程的真实信息，或对复杂工作流增加人工审核。[E010, E060] Evidence: E010, E060. Medium confidence.

新发布的 TraceProbe 基准在可执行沙箱中运行智能体，记录规范化的动作轨迹，并重放工具操作，以定位安全风险在何处进入以及如何传播。它同时对最终结果和隐藏的规则违规进行评分，而不是将表面上可接受的终点视为安全执行的充分证据。[E008] Why it matters: 如果你评估的智能体会使用文件、工具、记忆、检索到的内容或其他智能体，TraceProbe 提供了一种方法，用于区分看似安全的结果与通向该结果的不安全路径。这可能改变安全测试套件是否被选用于发布门控、事件诊断或安全措施对比。[E008] Evidence: E008. Medium confidence.

新发布的 MESSIER 语料库对来自 30 个基准的 957,611 条评估记录进行了标准化，涵盖 745 个智能体、11,891 项任务和 74,263 个验证器，同时增加了在六个代表性不足的专业与科学基准上的运行记录。它将原本异构的任务、智能体脚手架、评分规则和结果记录映射到一个通用模式中。[E004] Why it matters: 如果你正在选择用于跨基准智能体比较的测试套件，MESSIER 可能会减少仅为获得可比记录而重新运行每个系统的需要。其通用模式还使验证器和脚手架之间的差异清晰可见，帮助团队判断表面上的性能差异究竟来自智能体，还是来自评估设置。[E004] Evidence: E004. Medium confidence.

新发布的 MACRO 基准评估多智能体系统如何处理信息不完整的旅行请求。其 107 项完整标注的任务包含 703 个流程里程碑、预期的用户澄清、任务状态要求，以及专业化智能体之间的标准化接口，因此评分不仅可以考察旅行计划是否成功，还可以考察系统如何得出结果。[E005] Why it matters: 如果你的产品必须先向用户询问缺失的约束条件，再协调相互依赖的子任务，端到端成功可能会掩盖猜测用户偏好或丢失状态等失败。MACRO 提供流程级检查点，可影响你对编排设计、澄清策略或智能体接口的选择。[E005] Evidence: E005. Medium confidence.

新发布的 ConformWeb 基准从公开的行为契约中推导隐藏的交互序列，并在生成的 Web 应用程序上执行这些序列。其协议测试应用程序能否在动态工作流中保持规定的行为，而无需一个未公开的参考实现。[E011] Why it matters: 如果你比较的是用于生成 Web 应用程序的编程智能体，截图或浅层功能检查可能会奖励那些界面看似合理、但在交互中失效的系统。以契约为依据的隐藏工作流为按照行为一致性选择系统提供了基础，同时让被测系统能够看到预期的公开范围。[E011] Evidence: E011. Medium confidence.
briefing.caveat: This is a keyword-filtered, non-representative feed. Only 165 of 626 corpus evidence records were supplied for analysis, although none of those selected records were dropped for size. Brave, OpenReview, and Semantic Scholar were unavailable, and several attention collectors had partial reads or stale carry-forwards. The findings describe source-authored releases in the captured evidence, not independently validated benchmark quality or field-wide prevalence.

evidence_items.summary: Embodied planning is dedicated to the goal of building agents capable of perceiving, reasoning, and executing long-horizon tasks in physical environments. However, existing embodied benchmarks predominantly focus on single-agent execution or restricted multi-agent settings, leaving long-horizon tasks that involve complex inter-agent dependencies largely underexplored despite their prevalence in real-world embodied scenarios. To address this gap, we introduce CoEmbod, the first realistic 3D simulated embodied benchmark for long-horizon multi-agent embodied cooperation with diverse inter-agent dependencies. CoEmbod contains 155 expert-curated tasks across 40 scenes and 10845 objects, covering three cooperation regimes: spatial distribution, parallel constraint, and failure recovery. These regimes cover a broad spectrum of cooperative requirements, ranging from distributed task allocation to synchronized execution and assisted failure recovery. CoEmbod further provides a process-level evaluation framework with Budgeted Cooperative Success (BCS), which jointly measures goal completion, cooperation fidelity, and execution efficiency. Experiments reveal that even the leading LMM powering a well-established agentic workflow achieves only 20.23% success, highlighting the difficulty of long-horizon multi-agent cooperation with diverse inter-agent dependencies in complex embodied environments.
evidence_items.title: CoEmbod: A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Multi-Agent Embodied Cooperation with Diverse Inter-Agent Dependencies
evidence_items.watchlist_note: Evaluations targeting extended multi-step agent execution.

organizations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential in medical AI through their natural language understanding and reasoning capabilities. However, real clinical practice involves multi-stage, dynamically evolving decision-making where physicians continuously adjust pathways based on updated examination results—far more complex than single-turn question answering. Existing medical benchmarks focus on static scenarios, failing to evaluate LLMs in realistic clinical environments. We present MMedAgentBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM-based medical agents in multi-stage clinical decision-making. Unlike previous benchmarks, MMedAgentBench captures the temporal complexity of clinical workflows by simulating authentic patient journeys across multiple diagnostic and treatment stages. The benchmark comprises a high-quality dataset of over 150 de-identified clinical cases from tertiary hospitals, encompassing 500+ clinical stages, with each case meticulously structured into sequential stages and annotated by board-certified physicians. Our evaluation framework simultaneously assesses diagnostic accuracy and resource efficiency, requiring agents to plan examinations and control costs while navigating progressive information disclosure. This enables systematic evaluation of medical agents across dynamic decision-making, cost control, and multi-stage reasoning dimensions, providing a realistic testbed for advancing medical AI toward clinical deployment.
evidence_items.title: MMedAgentBench: A Multi-Stage Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Medical Agents

organizations: Shaanxi University of Science and Technology
evidence_items.summary: Evaluating LLMs for crisis communication requires more than judging isolated responses, because public feedback and competitor actions can reshape trust over time. Existing benchmarks remain largely static and single-turn, offering limited evidence about long-horizon risk-sensitive communication. We introduce BrandEval, a two-track benchmark for product-crisis communication, focusing on public brand responses to product-related safety, quality, service, and trust incidents. BrandEval-Static evaluates stakeholder-aware strategic analysis, while BrandEval-Dynamic stress-tests response policies in BrandPolis, a controlled multi-agent sandbox with consumer feedback, competitor responses, and trust-risk trajectories. We also construct BrandSRD, a Chinese crisis-response dataset, and instantiate a reference Strategic Agent using Strategic Rationale (SR). Across proprietary and open-source models, we find that static strategic quality is informative but incomplete: it aligns with some end-state outcomes but does not reliably predict volatility and delayed recovery; dynamic stress tests further expose tail-risk failures under manipulative or weakly grounded policies. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/htgan-ai/BrandEval.
evidence_items.title: BrandEval: A Two-Track Multi-Agent Benchmark for Risk-Sensitive LLM Crisis Communication

evidence_items.summary: Despite rapid advances in Code LLMs, their training datasets are often opaque due to proprietary and competitive concerns. Since many evaluation benchmarks are open-source and widely available online, models may unintentionally train on them, leading to data contamination that compromises evaluation validity. Reliable techniques for detecting whether a code snippet appears in a model’s training data are therefore essential. Compared with natural language, code contamination detection presents two unique challenges. First, code tokens from different syntactic categories contribute unequally to contamination signals, making uniform token treatment ineffective. Second, models trained on semantically equivalent code variants can evade detectors based solely on text matching. To address these challenges, we propose a syntax-aware framework that explicitly models token-type contributions. With a lightweight supervised detector trained on few labels, it captures contamination signals efficiently. Experiments across 8 Code LLMs, 2 languages, and 4 code transformations show absolute AUC gains of 8–10% for pretraining data detection and 15–20% for fine-tuning data detection, with AUC exceeding 90% on most fine-tuned tasks. Our work demonstrates that syntax-aware modeling is essential for trustworthy Code LLM evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Syntax-Aware Detection of Training Data Contamination in Code LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Comprehensively evaluating AI agents across interactive environments is difficult due to fragmented tasks, scaffolds, verifiers, and scoring rules. Unfortunately, existing efforts to unify these evaluations are limited in scale and domain, making costly reruns necessary and leaving available data incomparable. We introduce MESSIER, a unified corpus of 957,611 records spanning 30 benchmarks, 745 agents, 11,891 tasks, and 74,263 verifiers. MESSIER combines public evaluation results with new runs on six underrepresented professional and scientific benchmarks, standardizing their heterogeneous components into a common schema. Using this corpus, we show that frontier progress is uneven across benchmark groups, with function-calling evaluations largely saturated, programming improving fastest, and enterprise workflows remaining most challenging. Counterfactual rescoring further shows that strict all-pass scoring in multi-verifier tasks can alter agent rankings. Finally, we derive capability scores from our corpus that correlate with Epoch's Evaluation Capability Index rankings at Spearman ρ = 0.84. The scores can also be estimated for subsets defined by domain, occupation, action space, or verifier type. In essence, MESSIER is a reusable resource for studying agent performance at scale, and a basis for designing better evaluations.
evidence_items.title: Messier: A High-Resolution Corpus for Cross-Benchmark Agent Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Clarification-aware multi-agent orchestration is challenging because systems must elicit missing information, maintain task state, and coordinate dependent subtasks. Existing benchmarks do not comprehensively evaluate such orchestration under underspecified user requests, focusing instead on end-to-end success or isolated abilities like tool use and dialogue. We introduce MACRO, a travel-domain benchmark designed to address these gaps by providing structured task tiers, process-level user-side and system-side milestone annotations that include expected user clarifications, and standardized sub-agent interfaces. MACRO-Full contains 107 fully annotated tasks with 703 milestones, and MACRO-Core provides a tractable 30-task subset with 164 milestones. We evaluate three representative orchestration frameworks and a reference decoupled planning–execution orchestrator (MACRO-DPE) using trace-level metrics and failure analysis. Results show that MACRO-DPE improves routing fidelity and execution efficiency while maintaining task completion, whereas staged planning ensures milestone coverage at higher cost. The dataset (https://huggingface.co/datasets/weier248/MACRO-bench) and code are publicly available at https://github.com/liuweie/MACRO-bench/.
evidence_items.title: MACRO: A Benchmark for Clarification-Aware Multi-Agent Orchestration

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.
evidence_items.title: AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System Development

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on coding and reasoning benchmarks; however, their ability to solve graph-structured machine learning problems remains largely unexplored. In particular, no benchmark currently evaluates whether LLMs can autonomously solve end-to-end Graph Neural Network (GNN) coding tasks under realistic competition settings. To address this gap, this paper introduces GNN-CB, the first competition-based benchmark for evaluating both humans and LLMs on GNN coding tasks. GNN-CB consists of 18 curated competitions spanning node-, edge-, and graph-level prediction across diverse graph categories, domains, and difficulty tiers. All submissions are evaluated through a unified automated pipeline with hidden test sets and standardized scoring. Human participants solve tasks under controlled competition constraints, while LLMs are evaluated using a frozen zero-shot prompting protocol based on a plan-then-code paradigm with bounded execute-and-repair loops. The benchmark additionally supports both non-agent and autonomous agent-based evaluation within the same protocol. Under our evaluated protocol, LLMs rarely match Human Top performance and show less stable performance across competitions. No single model dominates: a few competitions are won by LLMs, yet humans still hold the top score on most tasks. We release GNN-CB as a living benchmark with automated evaluation infrastructure, dynamic leaderboards, and reproducible execution pipelines. Beyond benchmarking, GNN-CB provides a practice-oriented resource for studying GNN implementation across progressively diverse graph-learning tasks. The benchmark and evaluation framework are publicly available at https://basiralab.github.io/GNN-CB/.
evidence_items.title: GNN-CB: A Graph Neural Network Competition Benchmark for Human and LLM Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act through files, tools, memory, retrieved content, and other agents, which can trigger safety failures during execution. Existing benchmarks mostly focus on endpoint outcome evaluation or model-assisted moderation of pre-constructed trajectories, leaving limited evidence about where risks enter and how they propagate. To address this issue, we introduce TraceProbe, an execution-based benchmark for agent safety diagnosis. TraceProbe places agents in executable sandbox scenarios, scores endpoint and latent rule violations based on normalized traces and structured evidence, and replays recorded tool actions for step-level risk localization. Our benchmark contains 155 scenarios across three risk-source categories: non-adversarial failures, internal authority compromise, and external attacks. Across 12 contemporary LLMs, the mean attack success rate (ASR) is 0.347, indicating substantial residual risk, especially under internal authority compromise. Our analysis also demonstrates that endpoint-safe runs can contain unsafe intermediate actions, and the actual execution paths of agents may differ from the intended hazards of the testing scenarios. The TraceProbe benchmark and our findings support a more actionable form of agent safety evaluation: beyond assessing ASR or final outcomes, evaluators can also ask what went wrong, where it occurred, and where an intervention could be placed.
evidence_items.title: TraceProbe: An Execution-Based Benchmark for Diagnosing Safety Failures in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both interactive worlds and the tasks agents must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation (WD). World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. Explicit states and tool-call traces support task validation and agent evaluation. We evaluate 22 models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 88.8% mean Pass@1. Construction experiments demonstrate token efficiency and expansion of task coverage. At the richest knowledge level, WD fully covers 22/23 properties, 19/29 functionalities, and 30/39 event requirements specified in a real RobotVacuum protocol. Furthermore, the 1,000 sampled tasks semantically cover 81.6% of the 854 reference instructions in the real-world corpus. SynthDCB connects an expanding space of real-to-sim executable capabilities to verifiable agent evaluation.
evidence_items.title: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking

evidence_items.summary: LLM-based agent systems increasingly adopt skill-based architectures to reduce repetitive reasoning costs and improve stable, efficient task execution. Recent studies propose self-evolving agents that autonomously generate, refine, and reuse skills from past experiences to enable continuous capability evolution. However, autonomous skill evolution introduces a new attack surface in which malicious capabilities are generated, stored, and reused as legitimate skills. In this paper, we define EvoSkill Injection as a threat model targeting the autonomous skill generation and evolution pipeline of self-evolving agents. We further propose SARGE (Red-teaming Autonomous Skill Generation and Evolution in self-evolving agents), a red-teaming framework for evaluating this threat model through iterative generation, escalation, and reinforcement interactions. To support our framework, we construct EvoSkillBench, a benchmark dataset of malicious interaction trajectories for inducing malicious skill formation in self-evolving agents, and introduce EvoSkillSafetyBench, a post-attack benchmark for evaluating whether injected malicious skills are subsequently retrieved and activated as harmful behaviors. Our evaluation shows that SARGE induces malicious skill formation and that injected skills are persistently stored and repeatedly activated, highlighting the risk of persistent capability corruption.
evidence_items.title: EvoSkill Injection: Red-Teaming Autonomous Skill Generation and Evolution in Self-Evolving Agents

evidence_items.summary: Current AI-driven game development has made substantial progress in asset generation, gameplay design, and web-based game coding, yet project-level code engineering on professional game engines remains largely unexplored due to the absence of large-scale datasets and deterministic evaluation methods. We present JamSet and JamBench, the first project-level game code framework dataset and benchmark built on a professional game engine. Our key insight is that Game Jam competitions, community events where developers build complete games under tight time constraints, yield thousands of open-source projects suitable for this purpose. Building on the Godot engine's text-based format and headless execution mode, we design a deterministic verification pipeline from file integrity to runtime behavior collection, distilling 8,133 verified projects from over 240,000 repositories. Of these, 300 manually verified projects form JamBench; the rest constitute JamSet. JamBench defines theme-driven generation and code completion tasks, evaluated through a pipeline combining compilation pass rates, Structural Completeness Score (SCS), and Behavioral Alignment Score (BAS). Evaluation of 9 frontier models reveals a capability cliff as project scale increases, with runtime pass rates dropping from 80.4% on small projects to 5.7% on large ones(Task2a). Code Agents improve compilation rates yet yield no gains in runtime behavioral quality, indicating that the bottleneck lies in architectural design rather than syntactic correctness. Experiments validate JamSet as effective training data. All data and code are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: JAMER: Project-Level Code Framework Dataset and Benchmark on Professional Game Engines

evidence_items.summary: LLM judges are widely used to evaluate agentic tool-calling systems, yet their reliability on structured, dependency-driven workflows remains largely unexamined. We present AgentJudgeBench, the first benchmark to systematically study LLM-as-a-judge reliability for agentic tool-calling over workflow DAGs, as distinct from the broader LLM-as-a-judge task of open-ended text or preference evaluation. The benchmark comprises 3,808 instances spanning six DAG topologies and three difficulty tiers, evaluated with five generators (3B-70B open-weight models and GPT-5.4) and six judges (20B to frontier scale) under paired with- and without-ground-truth conditions. Judge alignment degrades monotonically with task difficulty, 1.5x faster without ground truth, and on hard queries without ground truth all six judges converge to a narrow 77-82% band regardless of scale, revealing a structural ceiling driven primarily by task difficulty, though its height is partly prompt-dependent for weaker generators, that model capacity alone cannot overcome. Ground-truth exposure is not uniformly beneficial: it reduces alignment for GPT-5.4 (1.5 pp) and Gemini-2.5-Pro (3.9 pp), consistent with over-anchoring. Among mitigation strategies, chain-of-thought reasoning and judge temperature both have negligible effect, while structured evaluation rubrics improve alignment by up to 6.5 pp but do not generalize uniformly across judge-generator pairs. With ground truth, QwQ-32B best matches the programmatic reference, while a human validation study identifies GPT-OSS-120B as the most human-aligned judge; without it, frontier judges lead only marginally within the shared ceiling. These results expose fundamental limitations of current LLM judges and yield practical guidelines for reliable evaluation in agentic systems.
evidence_items.title: AgentJudgeBench: A Multi-Difficulty Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Judges on Agentic Tool-Calling

organizations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
evidence_items.summary: Large language models and coding agents can produce web applications that appear functional, yet surface plausibility is an unreliable proxy for behavioral conformance under interaction. We introduce ConformWeb, a contract-grounded protocol and benchmark that operationalizes public behavioral contracts to construct hidden interaction scenarios, evaluating whether agent-generated applications preserve strict conformance under dynamic execution. By decoupling hidden interaction sequences from the public behavioral scope, the protocol guarantees a fair held-out workflow evaluation without relying on undisclosed reference implementations. Evaluated across 24 validated instances scaling to 756 evaluation scenarios and 6,433 semantic steps, only 252 of the 2,160 total execution runs achieve full conformance, yielding a strict pass rate of 11.7%. While scenario-level conformance reaches 36.7% and step-level progress averages 49.4%, this quantitative gap demonstrates that generative systems frequently achieve substantial partial progress but fail to maintain the critical behavioral invariants required for end-to-end conformance. All code and data are released at https://github.com/deep-diver/ConformWeb.
evidence_items.title: Do LLM-Generated Web Apps Behave Correctly? A Contract-Grounded Benchmark for Behavioral Conformance

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well on standard reasoning and question-answering benchmarks, yet such evaluations often fail to capture their ability to handle long-tail, expertise-intensive knowledge in real-world professional scenarios. We introduce LPFQA, a long-tail knowledge benchmark derived from authentic professional forum discussions, covering 7 academic and industrial domains with 430 curated tasks grounded in practical expertise. LPFQA evaluates specialized reasoning, domain-specific terminology understanding, and contextual interpretation, and adopts a hierarchical difficulty structure to ensure semantic clarity and uniquely identifiable answers. Experiments on over multiple mainstream LLMs reveal substantial performance gaps, particularly on tasks requiring deep domain reasoning, exposing limitations overlooked by existing benchmarks. Overall, LPFQA provides an authentic and discriminative evaluation framework that complements prior benchmarks and informs future LLM development. Our data is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/m-a-p/LPFQA.
evidence_items.title: LPFQA: A Long-Tail Professional Forum-based Benchmark for LLM Evaluation

organizations: Hunyuan Team, Tencent; Georgia Institute of Technology
evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced Machine Translation (MT), yet they remain vulnerable by hallucinations. Most existing benchmarks, originally designed for neural MT models, do not effectively elicit hallucinations from multilingual LLMs, resulting in a low density of samples for LLM translation hallucination analysis. To address this, we create HalloMTBench, a human-verified hallucination benchmark derived from tens of millions of translations, for studying signals that trigger LLM translation hallucinations across 11 English-to-X directions. We curate 6,908 authentic hallucination instances through a rigorous process: frontier LLMs first translate a large source corpus, and their outputs are then validated by both an LLM-judge ensemble and human experts. Based on our analysis of these hallucination instances, we introduce a taxonomy for translation hallucination that distinguishes Instruction Detachment from Source Detachment. Our evaluation of 21 model variants on HalloMTBench reveals several observable vulnerability patterns, including model Characteristics, source length, language proximity, hallucination reproducibility, and model-dependent effects of reasoning-style decoding. HalloMTBench offers a forward-looking testbed for diagnosing LLM translation hallucination. All resources will be released.
evidence_items.title: HalloMTBench: A Large-Scale Human-Verified Benchmark for Diagnosing Hallucination Triggers in LLM Translation

organizations: Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technolog
evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on static benchmarks, even though natural language constantly evolves through newly emerging words and meanings. Existing Korean benchmarks are centered on established vocabulary and therefore provide limited coverage of such recent lexical change, and their English-oriented design makes it difficult to assess the typological properties of Korean, in which content words combine productively with functional morphemes. In this paper, we introduce KoNeoBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs' understanding of Korean neologisms. KoNeoBench is built on 1,785 Korean neologisms attested in online news since 2020 and curated through expert lexicographic review. Each entry provides usage examples, word-formation analyses, and dictionary-style definitions. Based on this resource, we define four tasks and report results on recent models, together with a human baseline. Our experiments show that current LLMs exhibit clear limitations in recovering source components, distinguishing semantic categories, and generating accurate definitions. These results reveal specific aspects of recent Korean lexical change that remain challenging for current LLMs. KoNeoBench is available at https://github.com/bcmilab/ko-neobench/ .
evidence_items.title: KoNeoBench: A Curated Evaluation Dataset for LLM Understanding of Korean Neologisms

evidence_items.summary: This archive provides independently auditable numerical output datasets for the finite-prime-to-zero inverse problem, investigated through a proprietary finite-prime spectral inversion operator. The archive contains six CSV datasets covering: 1. 10,000 consecutively indexed approximate Riemann zeta zero ordinates generated using the first two million primes (P = 2,000,000), without evaluating ζ(s) or consulting precomputed zero tables during spectral generation. 2. A separate 3,000-point forward ordinal-quantization experiment using the first 600,000 primes (P = 600,000) and known reference zero ordinates. 3. Classical Riemann–Siegel spectral unfolding and Dyson–Mehta spectral rigidity measurements (L = 1 to 40) with exact GUE sine-kernel and Poisson reference baselines. 4. Chebyshev explicit-formula ψ(x) reconstruction and reflection-symmetric off-critical-line pair sensitivity (δ = 0.00, 0.05, 0.15, 0.25). 5. Real-part exponent scans (σ ∈ [0.35, 0.65], step 0.01). 6. Finite-aperture resolution measurements for the first Lehmer close-zero pair (n = 6709, 6710) across five prime counts up to 4,000,000 primes. The reported numerical benchmarks include a 3,000/3,000 (100.00%) forward ordinal-locking rate, 253.50-fold mean-squared-error compression (+24.04 dB) relative to the classical smooth counting baseline, a coordinate MAE of 0.002495 over the first 3,000 generated ordinates (with 10,000th ordinate error 0.00077663, relative error 7.862×10⁻⁸), and finite-range spectral-rigidity plateau measurements (0.165791 ± 0.000785 over L = 15–40). File-level SHA-256 checksums are provided for integrity verification. The archived outputs support independent numerical auditing against standard mathematical benchmarks. The proprietary inversion operator is not included, and independent reproduction of the generation procedure is outside the scope of this dataset.
evidence_items.title: Finite-Prime-to-Zero Inversion: Numerical Benchmark Dataset for 10,000 Riemann Zeta Zero Ordinates

evidence_items.summary: ESG analysis requires complex language understanding across diverse sources, including corporate reports, news, and disclosures, for tasks such as ESG relevance detection, action interpretation, impact analysis, and question answering. However, existing ESG datasets are fragmented by task and source, with heterogeneous formats and annotation schemes, limiting their use for training general-purpose ESG LLMs and unified evaluation. In this work, we construct ESG-Instruct, a 30,000-instance ESG instruction dataset built from public ESG resources, and ESGU-Bench, an ESG understanding benchmark covering six representative ESG tasks. Based on these resources, we further develop ESGPT, an 8B ESG-specialized LLM, and evaluate it against diverse open-source and API-based LLMs. Experimental results show that general-purpose LLMs exhibit substantial performance variation across ESG tasks, while ESGPT, despite its relatively small scale, achieves the best performance on multiple ESG tasks. This work provides unified data and benchmark resources for training and evaluating ESG-specialized LLMs.
evidence_items.title: ESGPT: A Data-Centric ESG Language Model with Unified Instruction and Benchmark Resources

evidence_items.summary: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria are essential for evaluating corporate sustainability, yet professional ESG analysis is hindered by data fragmentation and complex multi-step workflows. Existing ESG benchmarks rely on LLM-generated questions that often suffer from semantic ambiguity, limiting their diagnostic reliability. We introduce ESGAgent, a hierarchical multi-agent system with a domain-oriented toolset for automating end-to-end ESG workflows, and a three-level benchmark derived from 310 corporate sustainability reports, featuring expert-sourced questions with verified, unambiguous answers at Levels 1-2 and full report generation at Level 3. Evaluations across 20 state-of-the-art closed-source LLMs show that ESGAgent achieves 84.15% accuracy on Levels 1-2, surpassing the strongest baseline by 3.26 points, and produces Level 3 reports with higher factual consistency and analytical depth than commercial deep research systems, validated by both multi-LLM judging and human expert evaluation, showing a robust alignment (Pearson r=0.551).
evidence_items.title: Advancing ESG Intelligence: An Expert-level Agent and Comprehensive Benchmark for Sustainable Finance

evidence_items.summary: Data contamination undermines the reliable evaluation of large language models (LLMs) on mathematical problem solving. While rewriting-based evaluation mitigates memorization, existing methods lack guarantees of problem validity and answer correctness. We propose Proof-Verified Benchmark Rewriting (RePro), the first framework to integrate Lean-oriented neural automated theorem provers (ATPs) into benchmark rewriting, which rewrites problems and regenerates answers with correctness ensured by Lean-verified proofs. Experiments on GSM8K and MATH show that RePro's retained rewritten instances achieve 100% well-definedness, feasibility, and answer correctness, while existing methods still produce invalid or incorrect instances. Moreover, several models exhibit accuracy drops on proof-verified rewritten benchmarks, suggesting that their performance is sensitive to surface-level and structural variations and may partly reflect memorization effects. Our source code and data are available at https://github.com/AI4Engi/RePro.
evidence_items.title: RePro: Proof-Verified Benchmark Rewriting for Reliable Evaluation of LLM Mathematical Problem Solving

organizations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
evidence_items.summary: Cross-market factor research studies whether firm-level signals from one or more markets can predict returns in a target market, but existing public benchmarks do not support cross-market disclosure-to-return evaluation. Building such a benchmark is challenging because filings differ across languages and regulatory systems, disclosure-derived similarity can be biased by common reporting components, and cross-market signals must be evaluated under feasible trading-time alignment. We introduce CrossAlpha, a public annual-report benchmark for cross-market factor research. CrossAlpha addresses these challenges through three corresponding components: Disclosure Distillation, which standardises heterogeneous filings into ten-category English business descriptions; Residual Schema Graph Construction, which builds PCA-whitened cross-market firm-pair scores from schema-level disclosures; and Timing-Aligned Evaluation, which pairs the graph with 11 years of daily OHLCV data to construct forward-return labels under feasible cross-market execution protocols. CrossAlpha covers 3,587 firms and about 10,700 firm-year reports from the United States, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea, and Hong Kong, and releases about 19M directed firm-pair scores. In experiments, disclosure-derived cross-market peers outperform domestic text, industry-code, and return-correlation peers in the US-to-Japan setting (ICIR 0.39 versus 0.07–0.18), and cross-market sources beat the domestic text baseline in most target markets. CrossAlpha offers a publicly released, reusable, return-grounded benchmark for cross-market financial NLP.
evidence_items.title: CrossAlpha: An Annual-Report Benchmark for Cross-Market Factor Research (with LLM Agents)

evidence_items.summary: External-eye photography captures clinically relevant periocular anatomy at low acquisition cost, yet no large-scale standardized resource exists for evaluating self-supervised external-eye representations. We introduce a 4.35-million-image Standardized External-Eye Corpus (SEEC) derived from fourteen heterogeneous public face datasets, together with a benchmark for external-eye representation learning. For evaluation, we provide held-out evaluation distributions, landmark-annotated anatomical probe sets, and clinical disease-classification experiments spanning ptosis, thyroid eye disease, and craniofacial syndromes. We evaluate representations at two complementary levels: (a) the representation level, by assessing embedding geometry across multiple data distributions, and (b) the functional level, by assessing anatomical recovery, out-of-distribution anatomical transfer, and disease classification. Our models include ResNet-101 and ViT-B encoders pretrained using InfoNCE, VICReg, and LeJEPA objectives and compared with DINOv2 and MAE. Our results indicate that representation-level and functional-level evaluations are dissociable: broader embedding-space utilization does not consistently correspond to anatomical transfer or disease-classification performance, and no single encoder is universally optimal. Domain-specific external-eye encoders outperform DINOv2 and MAE on cross-dataset anatomical transfer despite being pretrained at substantially smaller scale, while external-eye-pretrained ViT models match or outperform these general-purpose baselines on frozen disease-classification probes. We release benchmark code, evaluation scripts, and preprocessing pipelines to reproduce SEEC at https://monkeygobah.github.io/seec-project/
evidence_items.title: SEEC: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Self-Supervised External-Eye Representation Learning

evidence_items.summary: Generative adversarial networks and diffusion-based synthesis have made photo-realistic facial manipulation — commonly called deepfakes - inexpensive, fast and widely accessible. Such synthetic media is increasingly used for misinformation, impersonation, financial fraud and reputational attack, and human observers perform poorly at distinguishing it from authentic content. Detection methods reported in the literature achieve high accuracy when training and test manipulations originate from the same generator, but degrade sharply on unseen generation techniques, and most are released as research code rather than as usable end-to-end systems. This paper presents DeepGuard, an applied detection framework that couples MTCNN-based face detection and alignment, interval-based frame sampling for video input, and an ImageNet-pretrained XceptionNet backbone fine-tuned by two-stage transfer learning, into a single pipeline that classifies an uploaded image or video as real or deepfake and returns a confidence score. The contribution is not a new network topology but an engineered, reproducible pipeline together with a controlled comparison of convolutional backbones under one fixed preprocessing and video-disjoint splitting protocol. The system was evaluated on the Face Forensics++ (c23) corpus using a 70/15/15 split partitioned by source video, and achieved 92.40% accuracy, 93.10% precision, 91.80% recall, an F1-score of 0.9244 and a ROC-AUC of 0.9612 on the held-out test set. Limitations concerning cross-generator generalisation, compression robustness and audio-driven forgeries are analysed, and directions for extending the framework are outlined.
evidence_items.title: Resource-Efficient Deepfake Detection with Cross Dataset Evaluation and Web Deployment

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: https://github.com/sanjari-orb/appsci-bench.
evidence_items.title: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?

evidence_items.summary: As language-model agents are applied to increasingly extended tasks, their working context continuously accumulates interaction history, tool observations, intermediate decisions, and task progress. Context compaction offers a practical way to reduce this growing history while allowing execution to continue, yet the compaction ability of modern LLMs remains insufficiently understood. We introduce CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction through its downstream effect on agent task completion. Starting from successful agent trajectories, we insert compaction boundaries at different stages of execution, compress the preceding working context with the model under evaluation, and let the same executor continue the original task. To enable fair comparison across compactors, we evaluate them under controlled retention ratios using a lightweight iterative ratio-adjustment procedure. CompAct-Bench covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks through BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and an internal CompanyBench evaluation. Our experiments show that working-context compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models: Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, yet substantial degradation in downstream task accuracy persists under aggressive compaction. Further analysis reveals that failures are often caused not only by omitted information, but also by distorted task state, such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions or forgetting previously established results, which can lead to incorrect decisions or redundant execution. These findings highlight working-context compaction as a distinct and still challenging ability for LLMs operating in extended agent tasks.
evidence_items.title: CompAct-Bench: A Benchmark for Working-Context Compaction in Long-Horizon Agent Tasks

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) now help develop many models published as general solutions. Should generality instead reside in the agent that builds a model for each new task? We examine this question in prognostics and health management (PHM), where every model must work on unseen equipment. Our deployment-style benchmark, NextUnit-Bench, covers 24 public datasets split into 58 folds that hold out units or operating conditions; each agent has two hours to deliver an executable predictor, then run on the hidden units. First, frontier agents outperform AutoML, which reaches less than half the best agent's score, and faithful implementations of published methods on four datasets, of which only 6 of 30 beat the strongest agent's own design; published accuracies, where reproducible, rest on the papers' own conventions, and a single convention, capping the remaining life of test engines, can halve the reported error. Second, the agents' advantage is a design made on each machine's data; once made, a plain-text plan of a few hundred words carries most of the gap between two frontier agents, and given a weaker agent's plan, the strongest agent falls to that agent's level, often to identical predictions. Before touching the data, however, it matters little whose plan an agent carries out, and domain toolkits appear to help neither: what sets the strongest apart is how much it learns from the data. Third, such designs reach only implementers that can execute them: given the strongest agent's designs, a locally deployable open-weight model delivers half as often, even when they are lightened, and scores no higher than without them. Generality, we argue, is not disappearing but moving, from the model to the modeler.
evidence_items.title: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.
evidence_items.title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Design verification (DV) remains a major bottleneck in hardware development, with large-scale verification using the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) being highly labor-intensive. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems offer new opportunities for DV automation. However, existing benchmarks primarily construct mutually decoupled subtasks, which deviates from the real-world workflow. In this paper, we present DVBench, the first end-to-end benchmark for Real-World UVM design verification agents. DVBench comprises 95 tasks across 9 functional domains and 5 difficulty levels, covering diverse verification scenarios and design scales. Each task requires agents to independently complete the full verification workflow. DVBench evaluates final testbenches via compilation, coverage, and bug detection, while assessing intermediate artifacts including feature lists, test plans, and reference models. We evaluate frontier LLMs (e.g. Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra) and agent frameworks (e.g. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode). Experimental results show that the best LLM-based agent (Codex \& GPT-6 Astra) can only achieve an overall success rate of 21.05\%, revealing substantial room for improvement in complex verification tasks.
evidence_items.title: DVBench: End-to-End Benchmark for Real-World UVM Design Verification Agents

evidence_items.summary: Reproducible codebase, solver convergence audits, multi-seed experimental datasets (CSV/JSON), and figure/table generation scripts accompanying the manuscript: "Hybrid Surrogate–Numerical PDE Forecasting from Observation Prefixes: Error Decomposition, Posterior Collapse, and Differentiable Inference in 1D and 2D" (submitted to Mathematics and Computers in Simulation). Contents:- src/: 1D periodic pseudospectral RK4 solvers (Allen–Cahn, viscous Burgers, advection–diffusion plus exact spectral propagator), 2D periodic vectorized IFRK4 solvers (2D Allen–Cahn with Strang cross-check, 2D incompressible Navier–Stokes vorticity), FiLM-conditioned FNO and circular ResUNet surrogates trained with multi-step rollout curriculum, differentiable continuous prefix optimizer (A1-Diff), observation-space Fair Stochastic EnKF, disjoint seed registry, crossed-bootstrap metrics, and split-conformal coverage diagnostics.- experiments/ & scripts/: End-to-end experiment scripts (run 01–run 05), publication figure builder (make figures and tables.py), and crossed-bootstrap LaTeX table summary script (generate latex tables.py).- tests/: Automated pytest suite verifying solver accuracy, disjoint splits, posterior collapse, EnKF, and batched/sequential A1-Diff equivalence.- outputs/: Complete empirical datasets covering 72 trained 1D models and 18 trained 2D models, including convergence audits, N=512 (1D) and 128x128 (2D) refined-truth evaluations, CPU/GPU single-query timings, and 200-resplit conformal Beta-Binomial checks.
evidence_items.title: Hybrid Surrogate–Numerical PDE Forecasting from Observation Prefixes: Code and Benchmark Dataset (1D and 2D)

evidence_items.summary: Deepfake detectors often score well on benchmarks but degrade on videos from other datasets, manipulation methods and compression levels. This work studies deepfake video detection with emphasis on cross-dataset generalization, dataset integrity and reliable evaluation, using EfficientNet-B4 and Xception classifiers on FaceForensics++ (C23), Celeb-DF and additional collected videos. An audit of 17,407 video records (14,888 fake; 2,519 real) found zero byte-identical duplicate groups, but an earlier filename-derived split showed about 90.7% filename-token overlap between test and train/validation rows. We construct a revised split (V11) and a sensitivity-analysis candidate (V12) that groups seven candidate visual links within single partitions, with zero cross-split pairs among 76,263 existing visual-match rows. The V11 model reached 86.69% accuracy and 74.76% AUROC on the external Celeb-DF set (6,528 videos), but balanced accuracy was only 51.65% and real-class specificity 3.49%. V12 results reported are validation-only (best AUROC 0.981005 at epoch 2); V12 test and Celeb-DF evaluation are pending. The findings show that accuracy and fake-class recall alone are insufficient evidence of reliable detection.
evidence_items.title: Leakage-Aware Deepfake Video Detection and Explainable Verification: Dataset Auditing, Split Design and Cross-Dataset Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: KOLD (Korea Open-source Landslide Dataset) is a benchmark dataset for detecting rainfall-induced landslides in South Korea from Sentinel-2 imagery. It was built for developing and evaluating deep learning models under Korean conditions, where landslides are mostly small, shallow failures and debris flows on forested slopes that end close to farmland, roads and streams. Such landslides are hard to tell apart from other surface changes in 10 m imagery, and they are not covered by existing public benchmarks. The dataset contains 1,952 image patches from five landslide events between 2020 and 2025, each with pre- and post-event imagery, slope, elevation and a pixel-level landslide mask. Because every patch has an image from before the event, models can learn the change caused by the event rather than the appearance of bare ground. The three archives are the training, validation and test splits, and the test split is a separate event, so that results show how well a model transfers to a new event.
evidence_items.title: Korea Open-source Landslide Dataset (KOLD): A Bitemporal Sentinel-2 Benchmark for Mapping Rainfall-Induced Landslides in South Korea

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous heavy-duty trucks require high safety assurance across complex operational domains, necessitating comprehensive risk assessment of their intricate multi-subsystem interdependencies. Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) is a systematic risk assessment methodology widely employed across safety-critical industries, yet it relies heavily on manual, experience-dependent expert judgment and is difficult to apply consistently at scale. Large language models (LLMs) offer an opportunity to support this language-centered workflow. This study presents a framework that couples a fine-tuned LLM with an uncertainty-aware post-filter (UAPF) as a severity-scoring assistant and consistency checker within the human-led FMEA process. We employed quantized low-rank adaptation to adapt the Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct LLM to a comprehensive dataset of over 38,000 FMEA records of autonomous truck systems. UAPF refines the predicted severity according to the model’s predictive uncertainty, and rows whose uncertainty exceeds a validation-set threshold are escalated to expert review. On the held-out test set, the fine-tuned LLM reaches 97.75% accuracy, and UAPF raises it to 97.83% while improving calibration. With a 5% expert-review budget, the escalation rule intercepts 78.2% of the remaining model errors. Under a stricter evaluation in which entire subsystems are held out, accuracy is 94.15%, characterizing transfer to unseen functional domains. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this work is among the first to combine a fine-tuned LLM with uncertainty-aware post-processing for FMEA severity assessment of autonomous trucks.
evidence_items.title: Uncertainty-Aware Large Language Model Framework for Failure Mode and Effects Analysis Severity Prediction: A Case Study on Autonomous Truck Systems

evidence_items.summary: Joint recognition of speech and non-verbal vocalizations (NVVs) is hindered by scarce event-rich training data and inaccurate or missing event labels. We present Xing-Audio-NVVASR, an end-to-end recognizer trained through progressive data mining and iterative supervision refinement. Guided by unified acoustic criteria, two heterogeneous models cross-audit annotations, flagging disagreements for teacher reannotation. To uncover shared omissions that model agreement may conceal, complementary breath detectors screen the entire corpus for human review. Human-confirmed labels accumulate across rounds and are preserved during subsequent refinement. Over five rounds, we refine annotations for 170,000 utterances from public corpora and incorporate 630,000 mined utterances. The resulting corpus of approximately 800,000 utterances is used to train a single 1.7B-parameter model that transcribes speech with inline tags for six NVV classes. Across four human-annotated benchmarks, Xing-Audio-NVVASR ranks first among nine models in both composite score and six-class Macro-F1. It achieves a mean composite score of 64.46, surpassing the strongest comparison model, StepAudio 3 Chat Preview, by 6.03 points, and exceeds the annotation teacher's breathing F1 by 14.40 to 31.57 percentage points. We plan to release the model weights, inference code, four evaluation benchmarks, annotation guidelines, and evaluation code.
evidence_items.title: Xing-Audio-NVVASR: Scaling and Refining Supervision for Joint Recognition of Speech and Non-Verbal Vocalizations

evidence_items.summary: A new drug reaches patients only after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has reviewed its trial evidence, which every application carries as analysis datasets in the Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium (CDISC) Analysis Data Model (ADaM) format that programmers derive by hand from raw trial data, a statistical analysis plan (SAP) and dataset specifications. Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) could take over this work, and a slow-changing industry will adopt them only with evidence of what they get right and wrong. However, work on large language models (LLMs) for CDISC data stops short of evaluating a complete, conformant and reproducible package, and the standard validator checks structure rather than whether each value is derived correctly. We introduce ClinDataBench, built on the public CDISC pilot study: an agent receives 22 Study Data Tabulation Model (SDTM) domains, the statistical analysis plan (SAP) and specifications, and must deliver 13 Analysis Data Model (ADaM) datasets, Define-XML metadata and a program that rebuilds them offline. Agents run in containers whose only network route is their model API, restricting online access to published reference outputs during execution. A host-only evaluator scores conformance under the Pinnacle 21 Community (P21) validator, selected derivations, clean reconstruction and effort separately. We compare three settings: Base, which submits the agent's first package; Self-Refine, which revises it without external validation feedback; and CRITIC, which revises it with the agent's own validator report. In an exploratory pilot with six models, the three closed models and DeepSeek delivered all 13 datasets in every setting and eleven of their twelve packages rebuilt semantically, while two other open-weight models delivered no complete package. Validator findings ranged from 15 to 64 dataset-rule pairs.
evidence_items.title: ClinDataBench: Benchmarking Large Language Model Agents in Clinical Trial Analysis Dataset Construction

evidence_items.summary: Air-Ground Object Search (AGOS) in urban environments is a challenging embodied task, which requires an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) and an Unmanned Ground Vehicle (UGV) to jointly search for and verify a specified target vehicle from multi-view visual references. To study this underexplored problem, we introduce AGOS-Bench, the first dedicated benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can integrate aerial discoveries and ground-level verification through UAV-UGV cooperation. We further provide AGOS-Dataset as the companion resource of exemplary trajectories constructed by an automatic pipeline. It consists of 7.7k episodes for searching objects of diverse categories and attributes, spanning three difficulty levels. To address the AGOS task, we propose AGOS-Agent, a training-free and tool-augmented approach. The agentic method relieves VLMs from complex and dynamic coordination via a deliberate search-handoff-verify cooperation protocol, only demanding VLMs for scene understanding and decision-making. Extensive experiments on nine VLMs show that AGOS-Agent improves overall success rate for eight of the nine evaluated backbones while reducing decision steps for all nine. On the hard split, the SR and SPL of Gemini-3.6-Flash increase from 8.6% to 55.7% and from 7.6% to 44.0%, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Towards Embodied Air-Ground Cooperative Object Search: Benchmark, Dataset and Agentic Method

evidence_items.summary: AgroNexus-Bench v1.0.0 is a curated, provenance-aware leaf spectroscopy dataset designed to support reproducible research on leaf nitrogen estimation and the evaluation of spectral learning methods under biologically meaningful data partitions. The resource integrates three previously published datasets: citrus leaf VNIR reflectance and laboratory nitrogen measurements, the EcoSIS eight-crop leaf spectra and biochemical traits collection, and SensOFOREST holm oak leaf biochemical and spectral observations. The release contains 895 source-level observation records and 892 spectra, including 886 unique observations eligible for four source-specific nitrogen benchmark tasks: Citrus: 684 composite leaf samples, with 204 spectral bands (397.32–1003.58 nm), direct Dumas nitrogen measurements on a dry-mass basis, and orchard, cultivar, and collection-date metadata. EcoSIS: 187 biochemical trait records, 184 paired spectra across eight crop species, and 178 quality-eligible observations. It provides direct dry-mass nitrogen measurements and an explicitly derived area-based nitrogen variable. SensOFOREST: 24 leaf-age observations nested within 12 physical Quercus ilex trees, with 2,101 spectral bands (400–2500 nm) and direct area-based nitrogen measurements. AgroNexus-Bench preserves source-native spectral axes, original measurement units, biological sampling hierarchies, source identifiers, and transformation provenance. It provides structured metadata, quality and eligibility information, nitrogen target definitions, and fixed evaluation partitions for reproducible within-source analysis and group-aware assessment of distribution shifts. Dry-mass nitrogen concentration and area-based nitrogen are treated as distinct quantities. Derived measurements are explicitly identified, and biological dependencies are preserved to reduce the risk of invalid comparisons and data leakage.
evidence_items.title: AgroNexus-Bench: A Curated Leaf Nitrogen Spectral Dataset with Provenance and Reproducible Evaluation Splits

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. However, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modality and lack joint consideration of both visual content and text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image editing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that measures system-level safety awareness of advanced image editing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, covering safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1\% and 81.6\% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while only refusing 24.2\% and 22.4\% cases with both unsafe images and neutral instructions. At the category level, most risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g., GPT allows 70.4\% editing attempts of unsafe political content while Gemini only allows 34.8\%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings highlight the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.
evidence_items.title: Text-Aware, Vision-Blind: How Multimodal Image Editing Systems Handle Unsafe Inputs

evidence_items.summary: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) often answer questions from incomplete records. Missing information might be interpreted as unknown or false, depending on the completeness of the source. Current evaluations fail to distinguish these two aspects, as they are usually interwoven with other reasoning demands. We present ClosureBench, a benchmark that tests whether LLMs follow the stated rules for dealing with missing information. Every base scenario is tested under OWA, CWA, and LCWA, and only the treatment of missing information changes between variants. ClosureBench provides a verified base benchmark as well as agent extensions for action choice, source scope, and updates. A model is considered correct on a base scenario only if it provides correct answers in all of its closure variants. Across 960 instances, overall accuracy can mask substantial closure mistakes. Models achieve overall accuracy from 71.18% to 99.86% across replicated runs, but their core switch accuracy, measured on the scenarios whose gold label actually changes with the contract, varies between 18.23% and 99.31%. Large discrepancies emerge under LCWA. For example, some agents choose unknown despite the prompt indicating that missing information should be treated as false. Our findings demonstrate that evaluations of AI agents should not only measure whether agents can reason over existing facts but also whether they use the appropriate assumption when information is absent.
evidence_items.title: ClosureBench: A Benchmark for Reasoning under Closure Assumptions

evidence_items.summary: Current research agents are moving beyond academic search toward literature synthesis and experiment planning. These workflows increasingly rely on literature retrieval systems, which serve as standalone systems or as components of research agents. However, existing scientific literature retrieval benchmarks mainly evaluate these methods using topical relevance or citation links as supervision, which cannot capture which prior methods are used for empirical comparison. To address this gap, we introduce Lineage, a benchmark for empirical lineage retrieval in AI scientific literature. An empirical lineage relation links a prior paper to a source paper that explicitly uses its method as an empirical comparison baseline. These relations form lineage graphs whose multi-hop neighborhoods provide retrieval ground truth for structural evaluation. To construct these graphs at scale, we develop Lineage-Constructor, which converts heterogeneous paper records and full-paper empirical baseline evidence into calibrated lineage graphs. Built from 121,048 papers across 17 top AI venues from 2018 to 2025, Lineage contains 3,950 graph components, 67,502 paper nodes, 164,948 lineage edges, and 80,000 multi-facet retrieval queries. Experiments with 19 representative retrieval systems show that empirical lineage retrieval remains challenging. Performance drops sharply with lineage distance, while structural metrics reveal that isolated retrieval hits often fail to recover closely connected empirical comparison neighborhoods.
evidence_items.title: LINEAGE: A Benchmark for Empirical Lineage Retrieval in AI Scientific Literature

evidence_items.summary: Rare language model behaviors can be difficult to study because obtaining them through ordinary sampling can require a very large number of samples. This motivates the behavior posterior sampling problem: given a language model and a behavior of interest, is there an algorithm that efficiently samples from the model's distribution over transcripts that exhibit this behavior? We introduce PosteriorBench, a benchmark for comparing algorithms by their compute cost and by how close their samples are to the true posterior in forward and reverse KL divergence. PosteriorBench contains 21 tasks on Qwen3.5-0.8B with behavior probabilities from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-1}$, each with exact posterior samples from a corpus of one billion labeled responses. We find that no method we evaluate is both efficient and faithful: simple methods like prompting are cheap but plateau at a high KL divergence from the posterior, fine-tuning on posterior samples is often cost-prohibitive, and several training methods from prior work do not perform better. Building a posterior sampler that can cheaply approximate the true posterior remains an open problem, and we hope PosteriorBench can measure progress towards this objective. Code and data are available at https://github.com/TransluceAI/PosteriorBench.
evidence_items.title: PosteriorBench: Evaluating Behavior Posterior Sampling in Language Models

evidence_items.summary: We propose VC-VQA, a large-scale benchmark for vision-centric knowledge reasoning, aiming to systematically evaluate the capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition and complex multi-stage reasoning. Unlike existing benchmarks that primarily treat visual information as entity recognition and rely on text-based external knowledge, VC-VQA explicitly models the role of visual information by considering both its source (internal vs. external images) and stage of involvement (pre-retrieval vs. post-retrieval). Specifically, VC-VQA requires models to retrieve external visual evidence, identify visual clues before retrieval, and localize, verify, or match retrieved knowledge against the internal image. We further construct a controlled multimodal knowledge base with traceable textual and visual evidence for each sample. We evaluate 21 representative MLLMs under four settings: no external knowledge, with provided evidence, knowledge base retrieval, and open-web search. Experimental results lead to three key findings: current models still struggle with vision-centric knowledge reasoning; fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition remains the primary bottleneck; and agentic retrieval highlights the value of multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration. Overall, VC-VQA provides a more challenging benchmark for evaluating vision-centric knowledge reasoning in MLLMs. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/CASIA-IVA-Lab/VC-VQA.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Entity Recognition: Vision-Centric Knowledge Visual Question Answering

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly deployed for long-running tasks that execute arbitrary shell commands or programs. However, these actions can result in unauthorized network requests or persistent, malicious changes to the user's file system, processes, or privileges. Existing defense mechanisms rely on either LLM-based monitors, which lack provable safety guarantees, or stateless policy enforcement layers, which miss multi-step data flows and execution side-effects unmodeled by the policy language (e.g., network calls initiated inside a Python script). We introduce Tether, a framework for runtime enforcement of stateful security policies over the observed side-effects of an agent's actions. Tether executes each proposed action in an ephemeral, isolated sandbox, inferring abstract action semantics from observed system calls. Tether then enforces stateful policies over these inferred semantics, permitting actions to proceed only if they comply with the policy. Policies and action semantics are defined in an embedded DSL in Lean 4 capable of expressing diverse constraints, including information flow control (IFC), access control, and network security policies. Because actions can propagate labels from sources to destinations, a single rule can enforce fine-grained IFC policies across multi-step execution flows of arbitrary length. Expressing policies in Lean enables formal verification that they satisfy global security invariants (e.g., preventing network access after reading a sensitive file). We evaluate Tether on realistic coding-agent benchmarks across both benign and adversarial trajectories. With a single policy shared across all tasks, Tether blocks 100% of in-scope attacks while maintaining a benign false-positive rate under 5%.
evidence_items.title: Tether: Verified Stateful Policy Engine for System-Level Monitoring of Agents

evidence_items.summary: Banks continue to depend on handwritten signatures, yet a verifier that scores well on its own benchmark can act very differently once it meets documents it has never seen. This paper examines how a Siamese convolutional network for writer-independent offline signature verification carries over between datasets, scripts and scan conditions. We train on writer-disjoint splits of CEDAR (English) and BHSig260 (Hindi and Bengali), using contrastive and triplet loss, and then test on unseen writers, on the other datasets, and on images corrupted with noise, blur, ruling lines and stamp marks. The decision threshold is set once on validation data from the training dataset and is never adjusted afterwards. Under contrastive loss the equal error rate (EER) averages 7.8% within a dataset but 19.3% across datasets. The most telling case is a CEDAR-trained model that still ranks Hindi and Bengali pairs usefully (AUC 0.868 and 0.890) while accepting 98.6% and 97.7% of forged pairs at its fixed threshold. Accuracy quoted at a best-case threshold would conceal this failure. Degraded scans raise the EER to between 30.1% and 50.1%. All results are means over 3 random seeds. Training on degraded images lowers the average EER on degraded scans from 41.8% to 20.9% (one seed), at a small cost on clean images. We propose no new architecture. Instead, we offer a controlled and reproducible account of when such a verifier can be trusted on new data and when it needs recalibration.
evidence_items.title: CROSS-DATASET AND CROSS-SCRIPT EVALUATION OF SIAMESE NETWORKS FOR OFFLINE SIGNATURE VERIFICATION IN BANKING DOCUMENTS

evidence_items.summary: TITLE Data and code for: The water price of decentralisation – an agent-based model of Iran's potato, onion and tomato supply chains benchmarked against central planning under drought and export bans DESCRIPTION This dataset accompanies a manuscript submitted to Agricultural Water Management. It contains everything needed to reproduce the comparison between a decentralised and a centrally planned supply chain for irrigated potato, onion and tomato in Iran, at the resolution of 429 counties. The decentralised chain is represented by an agent-based model in NetLogo 6.4. The model has 429 county farmers, producer unions with cold stores, 30 provincial buyers and an exporter. The benchmark is a mixed-integer crop-planning program solved with HiGHS by a fully informed planner on the same data. Both models receive identical shocks: spatially correlated droughts generated through the Standardized Precipitation Index, and export bans drawn from a drought-linked stochastic policy process. The study compares irrigation water, cost and supply per tonne delivered, and reports the water price of decentralisation, defined as the extra irrigation water that each tonne delivered by the decentralised chain carries relative to the coordinated plan.
