evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong Helpfulness, Harmlessness, and Honesty (3H) alignment in English-centric settings, but these gains transfer poorly to low-resource languages due to cultural mismatches. Existing multilingual 3H benchmarks rely predominantly on automated translation or LLM based synthesis, propagating source-language biases while sacrificing local relevance. To address this gap, we introduce Pak3H1, the first human-validated, culturally contextualized Urdu benchmark suite for 3H alignment, comprising PakAlpaca (helpfulness), PakBeaverTails (harmlessness), and PakTruthfulQA (honesty). Our multi-stage pipeline integrates manual cultural adaptation and dictionary-guided post editing to prioritize native speaker judgment, ensuring both semantic fidelity and contextual authenticity. Zero-shot evaluations across multiple open and proprietary LLM architectures reveal systematic cross-lingual alignment gaps: helpfulness win rates decline under localized contexts, harmlessness guardrails break down against regional safety risks, and composite honesty metrics degrade substantially due to localized factual constraints. These findings expose structural limitations in current alignment approaches, underscoring the necessity of human-guided localization for equitable multilingual evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Pak3H: Evaluating the Cost of Cultural Mismatch in LLM Alignment with a Human-Contextualized Urdu Benchmark

organizations: College of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, Fudan University
evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to explain numerical time series, but fluent explanations can misstate when a change occurs, overstate a trend, or introduce unsupported patterns. Existing evaluations often score forecasts, answers, or whole explanations, leaving claim-level temporal grounding undermeasured. We introduce TimeClaimBench, a benchmark that parses explanations into atomic temporal claims and verifies them against a deterministic extracted event graph. Across five LLMs on controlled synthetic series, event-grounded prompting raises the strict graph-supported rate by 18.3 points and reduces graph-unsupported claims by 27.9 points under this fixed operational criterion. Calibration analyses show the boundary of that result. The extractor recovers the designed primary event in 394 of 400 series, but this does not estimate the precision of additional extracted events. A blinded two-annotator comparison on one model and 40 series reverses the automatic ordering: holistic ratings favor Direct and chain-of-thought outputs over event-grounded outputs. TimeClaimBench therefore distinguishes four axes that should not be conflated: designed-event recovery, the unresolved precision of additional events, claim-to-graph consistency, and whole-explanation human judgment. Code: https://github.com/lunaaa95/TimeClaimBench
evidence_items.title: TimeClaimBench: A Claim-Level Benchmark for Grounded LLM Explanations of Time Series

evidence_items.summary: Glyph-level obfuscation can leave harmful Chinese content readable to humans while degrading automated moderation. We introduce SinoGlyphBench, a diagnostic benchmark that identifies label-critical semantic anchors and creates matched original and glyph-obfuscated inputs in text and image modalities. By perturbing anchors, background context, or both, this design distinguishes corruption of moderation-relevant evidence from general surface variation. Across 176,916 paired evaluations of 12 LLMs and MLLMs, obfuscation increases harmful false-negative and false-positive rates by 6.1 and 4.7 percentage points, respectively, and reduces four-way accuracy by 5.0 points. Models retain 75.7% of the decisions that were correct on the matched original inputs. Full-scope perturbations cause the largest degradation, anchor-only perturbations are more damaging than background-only perturbations, and cross-script substitution is particularly difficult in the text modality. Analysis of structured outputs identifies observable mismatches in visible-form reading, intended-message recovery, and final safety judgment. The evaluated models, therefore, remain brittle to Chinese content written with non-canonical glyphs. Resources are available at https://github.com/fengshun124/SinoGlyphBench.
evidence_items.title: SinoGlyphBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Chinese Glyph-Level Obfuscation in Language-Model Moderation

evidence_items.summary: Hallucination research in low-resource languages fragments easily: each newly named failure mode prompts its own dataset, spending scarce annotators on incomparable resources. We argue for consolidation and test it at community scale. Alikbachan is a Bengali hallucination-detection benchmark stratified along three crossed axes: a human-validated cultural-distance band, six task types, and a five-family, 32-mode hallucination taxonomy. It comprises a harvested 2,516-item test set (Phase 1) and a quota-constructed, gold-labeled 5,000-item set (Phase 2). The stratification is diagnostic. Four zero-shot LLM judges vary by over 30 macro-F1 points across strata, and the item-level predictions of 99 Phase-1 and 32 Phase-2 competition systems reproduce the profile: discourse-level omission defeats judges and most teams alike, whereas only a minority over-flag negative controls. The judges' verdict probabilities rank items well (ROC-AUC 0.74-0.95) but are overconfident (ECE 0.04-0.29). An open competition on Alikbachan drew 222 teams and 3,566 submissions, and a single-prompt 32B judge reaches the 57th percentile. Of the 25 teams in both phases, 24 regress on Phase 2 (mean $-17.6$ points) while every zero-shot judge improves, and Phase-1 rank barely predicts Phase-2 rank (Spearman $ρ=0.35$), so a Phase-1 leaderboard alone would have crowned a different winner.
evidence_items.title: One Framework to Diagnose Them All: A Stratified Benchmark for Bengali LLM Hallucination

evidence_items.summary: Air traffic control (ATC) requires structured, safety-critical decision making whose effects unfold through aircraft trajectories, so text-level correctness alone is insufficient for evaluating large language models (LLMs) in this domain. We introduce ATC-Bench, a simulation-grounded benchmark for ATC instruction generation with Chinese-facing scenario descriptions and controller-style instruction fields. Given a structured Chinese traffic situation, a model generates a JSON control plan that is translated into BlueSky commands and evaluated through closed-loop simulation against separation, no-fly-zone (NFZ) avoidance, and route-recovery constraints. The benchmark spans four task families that form a controlled complexity gradient: single-aircraft NFZ avoidance, pairwise conflict resolution, joint conflict-airspace constraints, and multi-aircraft conflict graphs. Experiments with 11 representative LLM endpoints show that while most models produce format-valid instructions, task success varies widely across models and task families: the highest-scoring endpoint under our fixed protocol achieves 63.5% macro-average task success rate (TSR), while the two lowest endpoints fall below 25%, with the largest gaps appearing under joint constraints and multi-aircraft coordination. These results expose a persistent execution gap between static validity and simulation-passing behavior, motivating simulation-in-the-loop evaluation for LLM-based decision making in safety-critical aviation settings.
evidence_items.title: ATC-Bench: A Simulation-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-Generated Air Traffic Control Instructions

evidence_items.summary: Research-evaluation indicators are increasingly produced by large language models rather than human coders, yet the repeatability of machine annotation and the effect of rater disagreement on scores and rankings are rarely quantified. This paper examines both in two separate studies. In Study 1, a single LLM annotator coded 92 papers from three AI venues on the eleven rubric indicators of the 23-indicator Artificial Intelligence Meta-Science Index (AIMSI), producing 1,012 evidence-linked decisions that have not been verified by human coders. Same-model repeat coding of 15 papers gave pooled ordinal Krippendorff's alpha = .87 but drifted upward by 0.115 scale points; this measures consistency, not accuracy. Treating structurally inapplicable indicators as zero inflated the paper-type effect from epsilon-squared = .054 to .227, and the AIMSI–citation association fell from rho = .303 to .047 once venue and paper type were controlled. Study 2 is an external benchmark, not a validation of AIMSI: in a public dataset of 150 STEM-tutoring responses rated by three experts and judged by six LLM families, six-model consensus tracked the expert factuality ordering (Spearman rho = .748) but binary error agreement was moderate (Cohen's kappa = .386), against expert–expert kappa of .23–.83; 71.9% of items kept their tercile while the median item moved nine rank positions. Two lessons follow for composite indicators: score construct-inapplicable indicators as missing rather than zero, and report rank intervals, benchmarking judge–human agreement against measured expert–expert agreement. The suggestion that machine judges suit triage rather than exact ranking rests on Study 2 alone and remains a hypothesis for research evaluation until same-task human validation is done.
evidence_items.title: Machine-Assisted AI Research Evaluation Under Uncertainty: Study 2 external human–LLM agreement benchmark (analysis code and results)

evidence_items.summary: Accurately extracting and mapping road surface elements is crucial for applications such as high-definition maps, road asset management, and intelligent transportation systems. This study first provides a comprehensive review of the benchmark datasets for extracting and mapping road elements, encompassing overhead-to-perspective data, large-to-local scales, and coarse-to-fine details. Subsequently, we thoroughly review the relevant approaches for extracting road surface elements. However, we argue that existing datasets still require enhancements in semantic richness, data modality diversity, and scenario complexity. To bridge these gaps, this paper presents WHU-Road3D, a large-scale multimodal dataset for fine-grained road surface mapping to address these shortcomings. WHU-Road3D provides approximately 100 km of diverse Chinese highways and urban streets. It features a rich combination of MLS point clouds, associated panoramic images, vehicle trajectories, detailed vectorized annotations, and pointwise instance annotations for road surface elements. The dataset carefully annotates 15 distinct categories of road elements, including common markings like road boundaries, zebra crossings, lane dividers, stop lines, as well as 10 types of direction symbols. To our knowledge, WHU-Road3D stands as the first multimodal dataset for mapping such a comprehensive range of road surface elements, designed to facilitate cutting-edge research in instance segmentation, full-element extraction and mapping on road surfaces. Beyond these immediate applications, WHU-Road3D also provides a valuable source for hierarchical road topology reasoning, map updating, and street scene generation. The dataset, along with the code for our benchmark methods, will be made publicly available at \href{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}.
evidence_items.title: WHU-Road3D: A dataset and benchmark towards fine-grained road surface mapping

evidence_items.summary: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp
evidence_items.title: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming

evidence_items.summary: Abstract This document describes the KnowAir-V2 dataset, a high-quality, large-scale data resource first introduced in our paper, "PCDCNet: A Surrogate Model for Air Quality Forecasting with Physical-Chemical Dynamics and Constraints"(arXiv:2505.19842). This dataset is specifically designed to serve as a benchmark for the development and validation of deep learning surrogate models that incorporate physical-chemical principles. Given that traditional numerical models are computationally expensive and pure data-driven models often lack physical consistency, this dataset aims to bridge that gap. The data has been preprocessed, including the imputation of missing values, and has been utilized in operational online forecasting systems. It serves as a robust foundation for building and evaluating interpretable, physically-consistent AI models for environmental science. Dataset Description Geographic and Temporal Coverage Regions: The dataset covers two major, densely populated regions in China: The Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei and Surrounding Areas (BTHSA), with data from 228 monitoring stations. The Yangtze River Delta (YRD), with data from 127 monitoring stations. Temporal Span: The data spans from January 1, 2016, to December 31, 2023, providing an extensive timeline for training and evaluation. A continuously updated extension continues the same stations from January 1, 2024 onward (currently to October 31, 2026); see Extension from 2024 below. All times are UTC.
evidence_items.title: KnowAir-V2: A Benchmark Dataset for Air Quality Forecasting with PCDCNet

evidence_items.summary: Particle swarm optimisation (PSO) can train small neural networks for engineering prediction, but reported accuracies are usually in-sample. This study applies a nested leave-one-out (LOO) protocol to internal corrosion-rate prediction on one dataset of 40 pipeline samples with nine measured predictors. Hyperparameters are selected in an inner loop that never sees the held-out sample, and twelve models are evaluated on identical folds. Four findings follow, and they apply to this dataset only. First, Bayesian ridge regression ranks first on all four accuracy metrics (LOO coefficient of determination R² = 0.45, root-mean-square error RMSE = 0.0313 mm/yr), and a small validated multilayer perceptron (MLP) ranks second (R² = 0.42). Second, a fixed 45-weight network with weight decay reaches R² = 0.43, so small regularised models are competitive. Third, a 233-weight PSO-trained network reaches an in-sample R² of 0.70 (0.95 after gradient refinement), and its LOO R² across ten PSO seeds (median −17.9) shows why out-of-sample validation is needed when the parameter count approaches the sample size. Fourth, defect depth (Spearman ρ = 0.89 with corrosion rate) leaks the target and was excluded, which keeps the benchmark clean. The contribution is a reproducible protocol, a benchmark on a small corrosion dataset, and clear guidance on sizing PSO-trained networks to the data
evidence_items.title: Particle Swarm Optimization of Neural Networks for Corrosion-Rate Prediction in Crude Oil Production Pipelines: A Nested Validation Study

evidence_items.summary: Systems for Natural Language to Visualization (NL2VIS) allow non-expert users to automatically perform exploratory visual analytics over complex multi-table databases. However, current Large Language Model (LLM) single-turn architectures have limitations including visual hallucinations, suboptimal perceptual channel selection, and failures on ambiguous or multi-table join queries. In this paper, we propose AgentViz, an autonomous multi-agent collaborative framework for hallucination-reduced, perceptually optimized data visualization. The architecture decomposes the visualization pipeline into four cooperating agents: (1) a Data Profiler Agent that extracts statistical moments, semantic column data types, and correlation topologies; (2) a Semantic Disambiguation and Hypothesis Agent that identifies analytical hypotheses and resolves semantic constraints; (3) a Perceptual Visual Design Agent that leverages Cleveland-McGill graphical perception rankings to generate declarative Vega-Lite specifications; and (4) a Quality Critic and Verification Agent that performs closed-loop verification to identify field hallucinations and visual distortions. Evaluated on 25,750 natural language queries across 105 domains in the nvBench 2.0 benchmark, AgentViz reports an overall Visualization Exact Match Accuracy of 93.65%, a 10-fold reduction in visual hallucinations (1.15% versus 11.80%), and 89.20% accuracy on ambiguous multi-table queries, with an inference latency of 1.14 seconds per visualization. The framework aims to provide a verifiable approach to automated visual analytics and AI-assisted data visualization.
evidence_items.title: AgentViz: An Autonomous Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework for Hallucination-Free Natural Language Data Visualization on the nvBench Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Machine learning can forecast supply chain disruptions, but black-box models limit transparency, and the reliability of post-hoc explanations is rarely evaluated. We provide a leakage-checked, reproducible comparative benchmark for shipment-level risk classification on a public synthetic dataset of 5000 shipments, comparing XGBoost alone with a hybrid XGBoost–neural model (XAI-SC-RiskNet), both explained with SHAP and LIME. The hybrid (71.60% accuracy, ROC-AUC 0.819) is statistically indistinguishable from XGBoost (72.60%, 0.819; McNemar’s test p=0.123), as repeated cross-validation and a chronological hold-out confirm. On 500 test shipments, the Local Explanation Consensus Index (LECI; top-6 overlap of local SHAP and LIME features) and LIME stability are lower for the hybrid (0.57 versus 0.68; 0.80 versus 0.88), so the hypothesis that hybridization stabilizes explanations is not supported. LECI was modestly associated with misclassification (AUC 0.61) but added no significant information to predictive uncertainty (AUC 0.77); it is therefore a descriptive measure of explanation agreement, which does not establish explanation correctness or better decisions, and not a validated quality-control mechanism. These findings are specific to one synthetic benchmark with a concentrated weather signal and do not show that hybrid architectures are generally inferior.

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for empiric antibiotic decision support, but it remains unclear whether contemporary systems behave similarly under the same clinical and stewardship constraints. We compared four LLM configurations on real internal medicine admissions using a common, auditable stewardship benchmark. Methods: This single-center, retrospective, paired, non-interventional shadow-mode study included 486 admissions from a previously published 493-admission internal medicine cohort. For each admission, the clinician-prescribed empiric regimen was compared with recommendations from OpenAI GPT-5.5, Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7, Google Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Mistral Large 2512; OpenAI GPT-5.2 was analyzed separately as a supplementary legacy bridge. All LLMs received identical clinical content, local epidemiology context, antibiotic ontology, and three-field output schema. The primary endpoint was any contextually unsupported broad-spectrum escalation, defined by the study’s prespecified guardrail rules; the key secondary endpoint was a weighted contextual escalation penalty. Results: Clinician regimens met the primary endpoint in 16.7% of admissions. Rates were 13.0% for GPT-5.5 (paired risk difference [RD] −3.7 percentage points; Holm-adjusted p = 0.216), 15.0% for Gemini 2.5 Pro (RD −1.6; Holm-adjusted p = 0.509), 29.8% for Claude Opus 4.7 (RD +13.2; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), and 31.9% for Mistral Large 2512 (RD +15.2; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Mean weighted contextual escalation penalty was 0.288 for clinician prescribing, 0.173 for GPT-5.5, 0.165 for Gemini, 0.510 for Claude, and 0.348 for Mistral. Global heterogeneity across contemporary LLMs was significant for both endpoints (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Contemporary LLM configurations were not interchangeable under the same stewardship benchmark.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models Are Not Interchangeable for Empiric Antibiotic Recommendations Under a Stewardship Benchmark: A Paired Retrospective Multi-Model Study

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as reasoning and decision support components in intelligent systems, yet aggregate benchmark scores provide limited evidence about whether they can reliably access primitive operations, combine them compositionally, adapt to reformulated contexts, and preserve successful behavior under perturbation. We introduce PPC-Bench, a controlled behavioral benchmark comprising 5000 deterministic samples across mathematical computation, Python code execution, and rule-based reasoning. Nine open-source models are evaluated along five dimensions: Direct Accessibility, Compositional Utilization, Prompt Elicitation, Contextual Adaptation, and Robustness Consistency. To distinguish inaccessible primitive capability from failed composition, we further construct a separate paired set of 1800 samples organized into 240 matched task families. Each family aligns atomic probes with composition, prompted, contextual, and perturbed variants of the same task. Qwen3.5-27B correctly answers 839 of 840 atomic probes but successfully composes only 74 of 239 atom-accessible families. In contrast, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct correctly composes 132 of 164 atom-accessible families despite lower atomic accuracy. Gemma-3-1B-IT exhibits limitations in both atomic accessibility and compositional utilization. Step-by-step prompting recovers approximately half of the accessible-but-uncomposed families for Qwen3.5-27B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, while successful composition is preserved under perturbation in more than 91% of eligible families for both models. These results provide condition-specific behavioral profiles that distinguish initial composition success, recovery of composition failures, and correctness preservation within successful subsets. PPC-Bench combines broad model-level evaluation with matched-family conditional analysis, providing a basis for investigating model and prompt choices without inferring internal mechanisms from task accuracy.
evidence_items.title: A Controlled Behavioral Benchmark for Diagnosing Atomic Accessibility and Compositional Utilization in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have become a cornerstone of modern generative artificial intelligence, demonstrating remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, including machine translation, question answering, and dialogue generation. However, most existing reviews primarily emphasize theoretical foundations and training methodologies, and offer limited insights into real-world application performance and domain-specific deployment patterns. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review following PRISMA guidelines, synthesizing the application of LLMs across diverse vertical domains. The review examines system architectures, technical approaches, and performance benchmarks reported in the literature. In addition, it analyzes core challenges associated with LLM deployment, such as hallucinations, explainability, value alignment, and data quality, along with targeted solutions. Finally, it identifies emerging research opportunities and future directions, contributing to a more coherent, application-oriented understanding of LLM development and impact.
evidence_items.title: Vertical Domain Large Language Models: Applications, Challenges, Future Prospects

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Reaction monitoring is central to chemical process development, but systematic evaluation of machine-learning models is limited by the scarcity and heterogeneity of experimental monitoring data. ReactionFormer provides a controlled and reproducible framework for evaluating machine-learning-based reaction-state inference from simulated infrared mixture spectra and molecular reaction context. The benchmark pairs reaction context with simulated spectral snapshots generated from computed and experiment-derived pure-component infrared spectra. The reaction-monitoring trajectories are not experimentally measured; they are simulated from pure-component spectra and represented as serialized sequences combining reactant and product simplified molecular-input line-entry system (SMILES) strings with discretized infrared mixture spectra. ReactionFormer supports reaction-progress regression, practical-completion classification, spectrum-only ablation, cross-source transfer, and low-data adaptation under matched reaction-level splits. The results show that infrared snapshots contain substantial reaction-state information, molecular context provides additional gains, and masked-language-model pretraining improves cross-source transfer and adaptation when only a limited number of labeled examples from the experiment-derived spectral variant are available. Beyond predictive performance, the study quantifies how molecular context, spectral-source variation, and self-supervised pretraining affect the robustness and transferability of learned spectroscopic representations.

Spectral Reaction Monitoring

evidence_items.summary: Background Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) disease integrates metabolic, renal, and cardiovascular systems. Learning in probability samples is challenged by rare outcomes, unequal sampling, clustered dependence, and miscalibration. This study aimed to develop a design-consistent, calibration-first framework for concurrent CKM multimorbidity classification in complex surveys and quantify the consequences of ignoring survey design. Methods We analyzed the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2017–March 2020 data for U.S. women aged 20–44 years. CKM multimorbidity was defined as the coexistence of at least two of the following: hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and clinical cardiovascular disease. Five learners were compared using 20×5 whole-PSU design-aware cross-validation, fold-contained preprocessing, survey-weighted loss functions, and cross-fitted sigmoid recalibration. The evaluation used design-based and survey-bootstrap procedures across key performance metrics. A 6,000-replicate survey-plasmode benchmark was used to evaluate bias, RMSE, and 95% coverage against finite-population truth. Results Among 1,743 classifiable women, 44 unweighted cases yielded a survey-weighted prevalence of 1.97% (95% CI, 1.30%–2.65%). The elastic net minimized the calibrated weighted log loss (0.089) and achieved a ROC AUC of 0.797 (95% CI, 0.765–0.830), PR AUC of 0.062 (0.023–0.100), and calibration slope of 0.90. Naive random cross-validation yielded an absolute log-loss bias of 0.0539 and 30.2% coverage; weighted design-aware cross-validation with recalibration achieved 95.0% coverage. Conclusion For rare CKM outcomes in complex surveys, valid population-level performance estimation requires survey-aware resampling, proper scoring rules, cross-fitted calibration, and design-consistent uncertainties. The framework distinguishes investigator-defined multimorbidity from guideline-aligned CKM staging.
evidence_items.title: Design-consistent statistical learning for rare survey outcomes: a cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic multimorbidity plasmode benchmark in women

evidence_items.summary: Typed decision models (TDMs) return structured decisions instead of generating free-text responses, enabling fast and cheap decisions in real-world applications. Recent support for image inputs extends Jev, a representative TDM, to visual decision-making. We refer to this setting as Visual Jev. However, red teaming of Visual Jev leaves two gaps: a systematic evaluation of direct image manipulations is lacking, and universal visual attacks remain underexplored. To address these gaps, we introduce VisualJevBench, a benchmark for evaluating the adversarial robustness of Visual Jev. It comprises 800 images and 3,200 questions across eight scenarios and four visual attack surfaces: typographic manipulation, visual evidence spoofing, target selection interference, and geometric transformation. We also introduce Adaptive Black-Box Parameter Search (ABPS), a lightweight framework that uses typed-output feedback to find effective image manipulations. ABPS supports both image-specific attacks and universal attacks that transfer to unseen images and tasks in new scenarios without further optimization. Extensive experiments on jev-1.14.0 show that image-specific attacks achieve an attack success rate (ASR) of up to 69.6%, while universal attacks achieve an average ASR of 33.15% on unseen images. Geometric transformations achieve an average ASR of 40.09% in cross-scenario transfer.

evidence_items.summary: Background: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a morbid but underrecognized disease diagnosed by right heart catheterization (RHC). Automated extraction of RHC data from electronic health systems is likely to expedite PH diagnosis. However, RHC outputs are typically unstructured, free-text reports and current large language models (LLM) that extract patient-level RHC data are imprecise and derived from small datasets. Methods and Results: We established an iterative development and validation framework using the LLM GPT-4-0125-preview to extract patient-level data from RHC reports. The extraction accuracy was assessed against manual expert-curated ground truth using micro-averaged precision, recall, and F1 metrics across all extracted variables. Evaluation on an independent test set of 100 previously unseen reports yielded a precision of 99.8%, a recall of 99.5%, an F1 score of 99.8%, and a hallucination rate of 0.09%. Next, we deployed the LLM to all n = 17,151 RHC reports captured in the Electronic Health Record of the University of Maryland Medical System (UMMS; ~2.3 million patients across 12 hospitals) from 1 January 2016 to 31 December 2024. Manual validation on 200 random reports demonstrated a precision of 99.7%, a recall of 99.2%, an F1 score of 99.5%, and a hallucination rate of 0.17% (all realistic and physiologically plausible). To further explore reproducibility across deployment settings, we deployed the LLM to a targeted sample of 3000 randomly selected RHC reports that included previously identified error cases. Validation of 200 random reports demonstrated a hallucination rate of 0.33% (precision 99.4%, recall 99.9%, F1 99.6%). Notably, four of the seven observed hallucinations in the large-scale deployment were absent when processed in a smaller deployment cohort. Conclusions: We demonstrate high precision for LLMs when deployed on a scale to RHC reports from a large, diverse multi-hospital EHR.
evidence_items.title: Large-Scale Deployment of Large Language Models to Extract Hemodynamic Variables from Cardiac Catheterization

evidence_items.summary: Group Emotion Analysis (GEA) is moving from closed-set group emotion recognition toward open-world understanding of multi-person social affect. Large Language Models (LLMs), and multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) in particular, are driving this shift because they return more than a label or a score: rationales, role claims, profiles, pseudo-labels, and tool-grounded reports. Existing GEA surveys organize the field by architecture or modality, which cannot capture the fact that a single model may perform multiple functions within a single pipeline. We therefore organize LLM use in GEA by functional role. Following a PRISMA-guided, evidence-layered protocol, we reviewed 105 studies from January 2020 to May 2026, separating 45 core GEA studies from 38 adjacent transferable and 22 reliability-supporting studies, so that validated group-level findings are not confused with results transferable only by analogy. We derive a taxonomy of five functional roles: Predictor, Perceiver, Generator, Data-Engine, and Hybrid. We strictly define Hybrid as tool-augmented reasoning over structured intermediate evidence rather than ordinary preprocessing. We map each role to its GEA tasks, modalities, emotion representations, datasets, and evaluation requirements. Synthesizing reported results, we find that on closed-set accuracy zero-shot systems trail trained baselines and that apparent gains often reflect permissive metrics. The value these models promise lies in their wider output space, which current benchmarks cannot yet score, so the field faces an evaluation gap rather than demonstrated parity. Because each role carries its own evidence, metrics, reliability checks, and governance concerns, we close with a role-specific research agenda.
evidence_items.title: A Role-Based Taxonomy of Large Language Models for Group Emotion Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background : Patient-level clinico-transcriptomic cohorts are used for biomarker discovery, patient stratification, validation and model training. However, most transcriptomic data remains siloed in hospitals, biopharma, and consortia because expression profiles and linked clinical metadata carry re-identification risk. Synthetic RNA-seq cohorts that capture population structure without retaining individual records could be shared in their place, but only if they accurately reproduce the results of standard translational analyses on the real data. We test this with dbTwin, a proprietary generator, on three public cohorts, so that every synthetic result can be checked against its real source, and release the synthetic cohorts with the benchmark used to evaluate them. Results: Synthetic versions of TCGA lung adenocarcinoma (510 samples; 19,719 genes), whole-blood sepsis (152; 27,097), and pediatric inflammatory bowel disease (322; 43,790) recovered most of the differential-expression (DE) signals tested. Across five contrasts on clinical variables declared to dbTwin as anchor columns, synthetic effect sizes kept their real magnitude (log2 fold-change slope 0.92–1.01), and 71.9–90.8% of real DE genes were recovered (81.7–97.2% at a relaxed screening threshold). For STK11 mutation (non-anchor column), effect sizes shrank (slope 0.70) but 96.8% of DE genes kept their direction. In five-fold cross-validation, classifiers trained on synthetic data were within 0.002 ROC-AUC of real-trained ones on held-out real patients and relied on largely the same driver genes (SHAP Pearson r = 0.808–0.975). Synthetic cohorts also retained gene–gene co-expression (Spearman ρ = 0.940–0.996), and 0 of 22 clinical comparisons exceeded sampling noise.
evidence_items.title: Biomarker discovery on synthetic patient transcriptomes: three public cohorts and a benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present MitoEM 2.0, a difficulty-aware extension of the original MitoEM benchmark for training and evaluating three-dimensional (3D) mitochondria instance segmentation in volume electron microscopy. The collection assembles multiscale vEM datasets (FIB-SEM, SBF-SEM, ssSEM) spanning diverse tissues and species, with expert-verified instance labels emphasizing biologically difficult scenarios, including dense mitochondrial packing, hyperfused networks, and thin filamentous connections with ambiguous boundaries. All releases include native-resolution volumes and standardized processed versions, per-volume metadata (voxel size, modality, tissue, splits), and official train/validation/test partitions to enable reproducible benchmarking. Annotations follow a consistent protocol with quality checks and instance reindexing. Data are provided in NIfTI with nnU-Net–compatible layout and OME-Zarr for cloud-aware workflows, alongside machine-readable split files and checksums. Baseline scripts support common training pipelines and size-stratified evaluation. By consolidating challenging volumes and harmonized labels, MitoEM 2.0 facilitates robust model development and fair comparison across methods while supporting reuse in bioimage analysis, algorithm benchmarking, and teaching.
evidence_items.title: MitoEM 2.0: A Benchmark for Challenging 3D Mitochondria Instance Segmentation from EM Images

evidence_items.summary: Collaborative learning scripts are usually fixed, and collaboration dashboards do not necessarily prompt teachers to intervene. We present a hybrid intelligent decision-support architecture that diagnoses five group dysfunctions, explains each alert and proposes one script adaptation from a closed catalogue, with an open simulation benchmark providing planted dysfunctions and a per-group oracle. It combines fuzzy inference, a lexical content classifier, calibrated gradient-boosting detectors with SHAP explanations, expected-benefit operator selection and NSGA-II regrouping. All evidence comes from controlled simulations; no teacher used the system, and learning outcomes were not evaluated. Over 20 development datasets, the detectors reached a macro-F1 of 0.591, and the fuzzy indicators were practically equivalent to their absence in accuracy. Because development data, including test windows of one seed, were inspected while the system was built, these results are not an independent confirmation; a pre-specified evaluation of the frozen system on 20 new datasets replicated 14 of 15 endpoints (macro-F1 0.590), but the defect rate of filtered explanations doubled (0.029 to 0.059). Performance did not survive distribution shift: macro-F1 fell from 0.586 to 0.297 under a changed generating mechanism, the full model fell below the interaction-only model on a held-out topic, and misconception F1 on unseen paraphrases (0.146) was no better than flagging every window. A training-selected operating point achieved 0.399 of the oracle’s simulated harm reduction with 18.7% unneeded interventions, and detector-triggered regrouping increased simulated harm. The benchmark serves as a pre-deployment stress test; the scores are upper bounds, not evidence of teaching benefit.
evidence_items.title: Hybrid Intelligent Decision-Support Architecture for Explainable Adaptation of Collaborative Learning Scripts: A Simulation Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract While spatial transcriptomics technologies are increasingly accessible, spatial proteomics remains constrained by high costs and limited throughput. Furthermore, poor mRNA-protein correlation, driven by post-transcriptional regulation, necessitates multi-omics integration for complementary biological insights. Current RNA-to-protein prediction models, primarily trained on bulk or single-cell data, often overlook critical spatial context. Consequently, it remains unclear which model architecture, spatial representation, or histopathological features best facilitate spatial protein abundance inference. To address these gaps, we defined the STP (Spatial Transcriptome-to-Proteome) task and launched the STP Open Challenge, a competition for predicting spatial proteomics from spatial transcriptomics of adjacent tissue sections. Utilizing a curated paired spatial dataset and a standardized evaluation framework, the challenge attracted 101 teams and yielded 896 valid submissions. Top-performing methods achieved strong predictive performance while preserving spatial organization. The landscape of submitted models revealed diverse modeling strategies and motivated us to develop a consensus-based ensemble framework that leverages various participant methods to enhance prediction robustness. Extended evaluation on unseen datasets demonstrated that the top-performing models outperformed existing baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of the community effort for this task. By formally defining the STP task and providing a standardized benchmarking platform, this work establishes a foundation for scalable, cost-effective spatial proteomics prediction and future multi-omics integration.
evidence_items.title: The STP Open Challenge: A Community Effort to Define and Benchmark Spatial Transcriptome-to-Proteome Prediction

It contains a race simulator for 2024 Formula 1 Grands Prix calibrated on 2021-2023 data (simulator v10eGQ), five deep reinforcement learning agents (Double DQN, A2C, TRPO, PPO, Recurrent PPO, agents v10g and v10gsm), a quadratic mixed-integer programming benchmark, and the look-ahead decision-support analysis of the paper. Files f1-pit-stop-drl-v2.0.0-code.zip: source code, data and documentation (see the README). f1-pit-stop-drl-v2.0.0-models.tar.gz: simulators and selected agents (88 agents, with a manifest of the seed and SHA-256 of each). evidence_items.summary: Advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have improved remote sensing image analysis and supported geospatial decision-making. However, fine-grained understanding of remote sensing imagery remains challenging for VLMs. Large variations in object scale, complex geospatial relations among instances, and limited visual detail hinder precise instance localization, visible attribute identification, and spatial relation understanding, potentially leading to descriptions that lack visual grounding. Existing datasets and benchmarks insufficiently assess end-to-end instance localization and captioning without target-specific textual cues. To support this evaluation, we introduce RICapBench, a dataset and benchmark that unifies instance localization and fine-grained captioning in remote sensing. RICapBench contains 245,466 instance-level annotations and 498,005 spatial relation tuples spanning general remote sensing, UAV remote sensing, and dense small-object scenarios. Each annotation pairs an object's oriented bounding box with a natural language description of its visible attributes and spatial relations to surrounding instances and environmental elements. To evaluate the accuracy and completeness of spatial relation captioning, we propose a remote sensing spatial relation parser and the RelCap-F1 metric. We combine RelCap-F1 with instance localization and attribute captioning metrics into a composite metric, RICScore. Our evaluation of 15 advanced open-source and closed-source VLMs identifies instance localization as a major bottleneck for these models. LocateAnything achieves the highest RICScore of 31.68, but scores lower on spatial relation captioning than other task-fine-tuned open-source VLMs. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Xldln/RICapBench.
evidence_items.title: RICapBench: A Fine-Grained Visual Understanding Benchmark Dataset for Vision-Language Models in Remote Sensing

evidence_items.summary: Wildfires represent a critical ecological and socio-economic challenge in Canada, where vast boreal forests and a warming climate have amplified the frequency and severity of extreme fire seasons. Predicting next-day wildfire spread can support fire management, but requires capturing complex interactions among weather, fuels, and terrain. Deep learning has emerged as a promising approach to learning these relationships from heterogeneous environmental data, yet its development and evaluation depend on representative datasets. Existing deep learning research on wildfire spread relies predominantly on US-focused datasets, leaving Canadian fire environments underrepresented. To address this gap, we present DailyWildfireCAN, a multi-modal, multi-temporal dataset and benchmark for predicting next-day wildfire spread across Canada. The dataset tracks continuous fire progression over multi-day events at a high spatial and temporal resolution of 90-m and 24-hour, respectively. This resolution preserves fine-scale information relevant to fire-edge geometry, local fuel variations, and terrain effects, supporting research toward improved daily wildfire spread forecasting. DailyWildfireCAN covers 2,440 wildfire events across eight fire seasons 2017-2024 and integrates 33 features across diverse modalities, including topography, meteorology, land cover, vegetation and forest structure, human influence indices, and satellite imagery. We establish a comprehensive benchmark comparing mono-temporal and multi-temporal prediction models, accompanied by a multi-dimensional evaluation framework assessing robustness across wildfire characteristics, geographic regions, and temporal conditions, spatial prediction quality, and sensitivity to reference label variations.
evidence_items.title: DailyWildfireCAN: A Dataset and Benchmark for Next-Day Wildfire Spread Prediction in Canada

evidence_items.summary: We introduce DF26, a novel benchmark for detecting AI-generated videos containing fully synthetic clips produced by recent text-to-video and image-to-video models. The videos capture single-person public-speaking scenarios, spanning direct-to-camera recordings, official statements, and studio interviews - 271 real and 2,420 synthetic videos generated by seven modern video models. The study on DF26 shows that human accuracy in detecting AI-generated videos is 52.6% while recognizing 76.0% of real ones, and that state-of-the-art deepfake detectors, using the current evaluation setup, perform close to random chance. Our results highlight the limitations of current evaluation protocols and motivate the need for benchmarks that explicitly measure robustness to modern generative model distribution shifts. DF26 can be accessed at https://huggingface.co/datasets/DF26/DF26
evidence_items.title: DF26: We Cannot Tell Fake From Real Anymore

evidence_items.summary: Political bias in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly significant, but difficult to measure reproducibly across political and linguistic contexts. We introduce Polar, a 4,026-instance multiple-choice benchmark that measures political bias through option-level likelihoods rather than prompt-based generation. Polar covers two ideological axes and eight issue categories derived from the Manifesto Project, and evaluates models in parallel across U.S. and South Korean political contexts. Across 38 LLMs, measured bias varies systematically with political context, issue category, model group, and presentation language. All models lean left-progressive on U.S. political content, but show more centered and mixed patterns on South Korean content. Translation experiments further show that presentation language alone can shift measured bias. These findings highlight the need for multilingual and cross-contextual evaluation of political bias in LLMs. The code and dataset are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/mcrl/Polar) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/thunder-research-group/Polar).
evidence_items.title: Polar: A Benchmark for Evaluating Political Bias in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Super-resolution (SR) techniques have made major advances in reconstructing high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs. The increased resolution provides visual enhancement and utility for monitoring tasks. In particular, SR has been increasingly developed for satellite-based Earth observation, with applications in urban planning, agriculture, ecology, and disaster response. However, existing SR studies and benchmarks typically use fidelity metrics such as PSNR or SSIM, whereas the true utility of super-resolved images lies in supporting downstream tasks such as land cover classification, biomass estimation, and change detection. To bridge this gap, we introduce GeoSR-Bench, a downstream task-integrated SR benchmark dataset to evaluate SR models beyond fidelity metrics. GeoSR-Bench comprises spatially co-located, temporally aligned, and quality-controlled image pairs from about 36,000 locations across diverse land covers, spanning resolutions from 500m to 0.6m. To the best of our knowledge, GeoSR-Bench is the first SR benchmark that directly connects improved image resolution from SR models with downstream Earth monitoring tasks, including land cover segmentation, infrastructure mapping, and biophysical variable estimation. Using GeoSR-Bench, we benchmark GAN, transformer, neural operator, and diffusion-based SR models on perceptual quality and downstream task performance. We conduct experiments with 270 settings, covering 2 cross-platform SR tasks, 9 SR models, 3 downstream task models, and 5 downstream tasks for each SR task. The results show that improvements in traditional SR metrics often do not correlate with gains in task performance, and the correlations can be negative, indicating that these metrics provide limited guidance for selecting superior models for downstream tasks. This reveals the need to integrate downstream tasks into SR model development and evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Visual Fidelity: Benchmarking Super-Resolution Models for Large-Scale Remote Sensing Imagery via Downstream Task Integration

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Agent^2 RL-Bench, a compact diagnostic benchmark for evaluating agentic RL post-training, which tests whether LLM agents can autonomously design, implement, debug, and execute post-training pipelines that improve foundation models. RL post-training increasingly drives model alignment and specialization, yet existing benchmarks are largely static, rewarding supervised fine-tuning or script generation without assessing an agent's ability to close an interactive RL loop. Agent^2 RL-Bench provides a unified agent-facing interface: each run starts from an isolated workspace containing a base model, task data, instructions, and a grading API, and agents must iterate within a fixed budget by training models and submitting artifacts for evaluation. The benchmark spans six tasks across three levels, from static rule-based training to judge-based optimization and closed-loop online RL with trajectory collection. Two diagnostic skills, namely runtime recording and post-hoc summarization, enable structured analysis of agent behavior, facilitating smooth and effective iteration of the benchmark's evaluation framework. Across five agent systems and six driver LLMs, agents show intelligent behavior but clear limitations: one RL-oriented run improves ALFWorld from 4.85 to 93.28 via SFT warm-up and GRPO with online rollouts, yet DeepSearchQA remains difficult, most successful routes rely on supervised pipelines, and interactive outcomes show large differences across agent stacks. Overall, Agent2 RL-Bench shows that current agents can sometimes engineer online RL, but stable agent-driven RL post-training remains rare under fixed budgets. It also demonstrates that our benchmark provides a strong and effective evaluation framework for future research in this direction. Code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/RD-Agent.
evidence_items.title: Agent^2 RL-Bench: Can LLM Agents Engineer Agentic RL Post-Training?

evidence_items.summary: Beam is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 501.3B total parameters and 23.4B active parameters, specifically built and optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam delivers frontier level reasoning, while requiring 3-4x less inference compute than many models of its class. Pretrained on 23.8T diverse, curated, high-quality tokens, Beam features a 1M-token context window achieved through a novel two-stage midtraining phase, built on verifiable, correctness-anchored data. Post-training leveraged a large-scale, fully asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) campaign across 10.5K GB300 GPUs, generating over 100M rollouts over 4 weeks of training. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date. Across our evaluation suite, capabilities continued to improve as we increased RL compute, with no sign of a plateau. Supported by deep hardware-model co-design, FP8/NVFP4 quantization, and a 1.93B-parameter speculative decoding drafter (DFlash 2), Beam maximizes serving throughput with efficient, flexible deployment. Averaged across conversation turns and harm categories, Beam refuses or pivots on 88.9% of harmful requests while complying with 81.5% of harmless requests, achieving the highest refusal/pivot rate on harmful requests among open-weight models on the Pareto frontier.
evidence_items.title: Beam Model Technical Report

evidence_items.summary: Numerical simulation is important in ocean engineering, but model construction requires expert knowledge. Large language models support automated modelling, but code syntax and successful execution alone do not establish whether generated models and results meet engineering requirements. We present OceanCoder, a Qwen3-8B-based large language model for automated simulation modelling in ocean engineering. To address specialised programming requirements and scarce training data, we develop an extensible data construction pipeline producing 12,000 verified supervised fine-tuning (SFT) examples across 12 engineering task categories. A three-layer verification framework checks model inputs against engineering parameters and task constraints, verifies completion of required simulation analyses, and assesses the engineering plausibility of computed outputs. Its outcomes provide graded rewards for group relative policy optimisation (GRPO), guiding the model towards engineering task completion. We also construct the first benchmark for automated modelling in ocean engineering, covering out-of-distribution tasks and real-world engineering cases. Experiments and ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the data pipeline, verification framework and reward design. OceanCoder outperforms both base models and the closed-source comparison, with Pass@1 increasing from 0% for the base model to 46.77% after SFT and 51.43% after GRPO. These results support engineering verification as a training signal for automated simulation modelling.
evidence_items.title: OceanCoder: A Verification-Guided Large Language Model for Automated Simulation Modelling in Ocean Engineering

evidence_items.summary: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success-latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sofilyzia/Fast-JEPA.
evidence_items.title: Fast-JEPA: Advancing the Success-Latency Frontier for Latent World Models

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents increasingly carry out long-horizon development tasks, autonomously planning and executing multi-step actions that span files, tools, and sessions. Because developers rarely follow each action, and agents resuming the work depend on records of what was done, the agent's work report often becomes the primary account of what was changed and established. When the report contains false or unsupported claims, it gives recipients false assurance: incomplete work may be accepted without verification, incorrect assumptions about the current state can propagate to later steps and agents, and evaluators that credit stated success may reward the report rather than the work. Yet little is known about what unfaithful reporting looks like in real development work, or how developers and agents handle it once it surfaces. Starting from real developer--agent conversations in SWE-chat, we conduct a systematic mixed-methods analysis of self-admitted unfaithful reports. We identify eleven subtypes in four categories: misreported observations, misattributed evidence, overstated task success, and faulty technical explanations, with overstated task success the most common. Handling these problems involves on average 4.3 further user turns and 12.71 minutes of recorded response and execution time, and users express dissatisfaction more often. Among 435 work reports that we separately sample and annotate, \NaturalPositiveShare{}\% contain at least one unfaithful claim. We also develop FaithDetector, a detector for unfaithful reporting informed by the observed patterns. On naturally sampled reports, FaithDetector attains \NaturalDetectorMacro{}\% macro-F1, about 13 percentage points above the baseline. Together, our findings and FaithDetector provide empirical evidence and an automated method for checking reporting faithfulness, informing agent evaluation and training feedback.
evidence_items.title: Characterizing and Detecting Unfaithful Work Reports by Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: Recent benchmark evaluations increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) as automatic judges. This paradigm assumes LLMs evaluate based on the rubric's semantic meaning rather than its numeric scale. We question this assumption by introducing semantic faithfulness: the principle that semantically equivalent rubrics must yield consistent scores. To quantify this, we propose a scale-reversal probe that inverts score anchors without altering evaluation criteria. Furthermore, we introduce floor normalization to calibrate reversal disagreement against intrinsic model variability, enabling fair cross-model comparisons. Experiments across five meta-evaluation benchmarks with seven diverse LLM judges spanning open-weight and proprietary models reveal widespread violations of semantic faithfulness, showing that raw reversal agreement alone is misleading. Finally, we demonstrate that bidirectional anchor averaging reduces dependence on any single anchor direction without compromising alignment with human judgments. Our findings emphasize that trustworthy LLM judges must reliably follow rubric semantics, not just correlate with human ratings.
evidence_items.title: Rubric Semantics or Numerical Priors? Auditing Scale-Direction Bias in LLM Judges

evidence_items.summary: Recent work reports strong pragmatic performance by large language models (LLMs) in English, yet whether this performance generalises across languages and evaluation settings remains unclear. This question is increasingly important as LLMs are deployed across languages, cultures, and conversational contexts. In this paper, we first introduce PILAPS, a bilingual English/Mandarin Chinese benchmark covering eight pragmatic phenomena across purpose-written and dialogue-derived items, with both culturally adapted and independently sourced data. We then evaluate eight LLMs from four families across a range of model sizes and prompting strategies. Our results reveal substantial variation across models and pragmatic phenomena: open-source models continue to struggle particularly with humour, while cross-linguistic performance varies with model origin. Our error analysis shows that, compared with human participants, models are more prone to literal interpretations in conversational contexts. Theory-of-Mind prompting lowers the literal share of errors, whereas Chain-of-Thought prompting slightly raises it. Together, these findings demonstrate that strong pragmatic performance in one evaluation setting does not necessarily generalise across languages or conversational contexts.
evidence_items.title: PILAPS: A Bilingual Benchmark for Evaluating Pragmatic Inference across Phenomena and Settings

evidence_items.summary: Understanding an egocentric environment requires reasoning about how surrounding entities affect the observer's actions. Existing evaluations of multimodal foundation models (MFMs) examine observer localization, motion trajectories, and action feasibility, but leave the discovery and interpretation of evolving observer-entity interactions insufficiently assessed. We introduce EgoPass-Bench, a benchmark for observer-relative interaction understanding in real-world egocentric video. EgoPass-Bench comprises 284 manually reviewed evaluation clips recorded using Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2) smart glasses and 2,201 distinct questions across five tasks assessing motion perception, interaction judgments about specified entities, and relevant-entity discovery without target cues. Our evaluation of eight frame-based and six native-video configurations reveals a pronounced discrepancy between motion perception and interaction understanding. The strongest evaluated model, GPT-6 Astra, correctly recognizes object motion in 91.37% of 394 comparisons involving the same targets, but correctly identifies changes in passage constraints in only 66.50%. Across all 574 entity-discovery questions, it trails the two-person human baseline by $23.65 \pm 7.45$ percentage points (paired 95% CI), while exceeding the always-empty baseline (36.76%) by at least 18.9 percentage points. Further analysis reveals frequent inclusion of entities that neither pose a plausible physical conflict nor constrain passage, showing that accurate motion recognition does not ensure reliable relevant-entity discovery.
evidence_items.title: EgoPass-Bench: Identifying Objects That May Affect the Wearer's Passage in Egocentric Video

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents are often evaluated by reducing execution traces to labels such as final-answer correctness, tool verification, and fault propagation. These labels are measurements produced by parsers, behavioral detectors, and harness rules, yet evaluations rarely report whether a measurement actually fits the trace it describes. We study what happens when those measurements do not fully capture the trace's behavior. Agents solve GSM8K problems with a calculator whose outputs are occasionally corrupted, which gives ground truth for what the tool returned, what the model later used, and what the detectors reported; a chemistry task with search and retrieval tests the case where the model cannot recompute the tool's output. Across eight models and up to 1,000 traces per model, final correctness, visible re-verification, and fault propagation disagree in systematic ways. The most common gap is the silent tool-output override: the model replaces a corrupted value without calling the tool again, so the error stops propagating while a verification detector records no re-check. Human review finds verification labels the least reliable (\k{appa} =0.29), and checking depends on the task: the same calculator that several models re-checked on arithmetic was never re-checked on chemistry. Execution limits and serving failures also change what is measured. These findings motivate measurement transparency: an automated label should be reported with its evidence, whether the detector's question applied, whether the run was censored, and any human corrections. Our trace viewer makes this information inspectable alongside the reported results.
evidence_items.title: What the Trace Shows and What the Label Says: Auditing Behavioral Detectors in Agent Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: (Internal code: C000000) This study establishes the symbolic conventions, mathematical terminology, and notation used throughout the author's studies on integer sequences, polynomial integer sequences, and the arithmetic structure of composite numbers. Its purpose is to provide a consistent reference for mathematical expressions, definitions, figures, tables, and terminology across the series. For polynomial integer sequences, the study adopts the representation x=Y d [y], where x denotes the polynomial value and y the integer index. The real number line is placed along the horizontal X-axis, while the index is represented along the vertical Y-axis. Polynomial evaluation is written with square brackets, and explicit conventions distinguish derivatives, integer index shifts, and algebraic operations. The study defines the Taylor integer shift and Pascal orbit, introduces the symmetry coordinate and canonical offset, and establishes the terminology for the three types of polynomial integer sequences. It also specifies the notation for differences between consecutive terms, the direction and sign of sequences, and operations such as union, interleaving, joining, and set difference. A separate part distinguishes factors from divisors and standardizes terminology related to prime and composite numbers. Additional conventions cover important numerical families, including square, oblong, and golden ratio numbers, together with their associated representations. The study also provides a standardized color system for mathematical figures and tables, distinguishing numerical categories, polynomial curves, divisor relationships, and structural classifications. An extensive glossary collects the mathematical symbols, abbreviations, and specialized terms used throughout the series.
evidence_items.title: Symbolic Conventions and Lexicon

evidence_items.summary: Agents increasingly operate software and even write it, yet they are almost always told what to achieve: given a goal, a mock-up, or a demonstration. We ask whether an agent can instead understand an unfamiliar product by using it, and then rebuild it. The agent sees only rendered pixels and acts through pointer and keyboard, without access to the DOM, source, logs, or back-end. Within this interface, it explores, generates a replica, and checks its own work before evaluation. We present SWE-Recreation, a benchmark of 54 real applications (28 websites and 26 Android apps) with 1,446 hidden requirements describing multistep, stateful workflows and explicit exclusions for behavior outside the reconstruction scope. A fixed judge grades workflows with pixel evidence; a separate post-hoc judge estimates exploration coverage. Across 54 evaluated applications, five frontier systems reach at most 0.530 weighted fidelity and 22.9% fully reproduced requirements under application-equal averaging. These descriptive results expose both exploration-evidence gaps and implementation shortfalls. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nologistic/recreateanything.
evidence_items.title: SWE-Recreation: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Software Recreation

evidence_items.summary: AI agents are increasingly expected to act as AI scientists, which requires three increasingly open abilities: carrying out a given computational workflow correctly, choosing the next measurements from a given design space, and designing their own experiments. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate the first two abilities, in a terminal or in a closed loop that selects from predefined candidates. Evaluating the third ability requires reliably executing an experiment that an agent designs, with readings grounded in a real laboratory. We introduce TwinLab-Bench, which evaluates AI scientists on self-designed experiments in 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, the life sciences, and engineering. The benchmark supports more than 100 experimental action types, and the agent's report is scored by comparison with a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records. Each task has its own TwinLab agent, an agent that serves as the environment and executes the experiments that the tested agent designs, reading the raw materials of the laboratory and calling calculators that are built from its records. Compared with a language model that sees only the task description, the TwinLab agent almost eliminates readings that deviate from the real records and inconsistent answers to a repeated request, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory. We find that these tasks remain hard for frontier models: the strongest, Claude Fable 5.2, averages a score of only 45.0, and we conduct an empirical study of where it fails.
evidence_items.title: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs

evidence_items.summary: This research repository contains data, source code, analysis results, and figures supporting an astronomy-inspired colour–colour diagram (CCD) approach for river turbidity assessment and indirect arsenic contamination screening in the Kok and Sai Rivers, Thailand. The approach adapts established principles of astronomical photometry and optical physics to Sentinel-2 multispectral surface reflectance observations. The repository includes 300 ground-based arsenic observations from 22 monitoring rounds conducted between March 2025 and August 2026, of which 296 were paired with turbidity measurements, and 45 exploratory satellite–ground observations from the Kok River. The accompanying materials include Google Earth Engine scripts, Python analysis scripts, spatial and temporal matching procedures, colour indices, cross-validation results, bootstrap confidence intervals, sensitivity analyses, and reproducible manuscript figures. The results provide preliminary insights into the potential of astronomical photometric techniques for environmental monitoring but do not establish reliable satellite-based arsenic screening. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2025–2026. OpenStreetMap data and other third-party datasets retain their original attribution and applicable licensing conditions. This repository supports reproducible research and future interdisciplinary investigations integrating astronomy, optical physics, and environmental remote sensing.

evidence_items.summary: v0.6 restructures the registry: a claim is now a general proposition that several papers can support or contradict, and each study’s own result is stored as its finding (R-CLM-19). Up to v0.5.2, 87% of claims had a single source and read like a paper’s abstract. In v0.6 a claim has at most 25 words and one idea, contains no numbers and never describes a study, and is worded no more strongly than its evidence licenses. The study-specific result (numbers, population, verbatim quote, verification, risk of bias) sits on the evidence row under the proposition. A proposition’s GRADE follows a fixed rule from its findings. Dataset: 42 versioned questions; 215 active claims (general propositions) under 288 question–claim links; 168 rest on more than one primary study and 40 are shared across questions (46 duplicates merged). 837 study-level findings (823 verified, 6 disputed, 8 unverified), 356 distinct DOIs. The 514 single-paper claims of v0.5.2 are kept as superseded (490) or retired (24), never deleted. All answers were recompiled. Method: per question, a consolidator model proposed the propositions. Deterministic code checked every proposal. An independent verifier with a fresh context reviewed each proposition and the whole set, and questions with major problems got a repair round. All 42 ended with no major problem left. Both models are from the same vendor (Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet, run as Claude Code subagents), so verification is less independent than a cross-vendor check. All per-question results, verifier reports and tools are included. One wrong reference DOI was corrected (SCR-LIP-000121, now 10.1111/iwj.12949). It registers; it does not arbitrate.
evidence_items.title: Scientific Claim Registry (SCR): A Versioned Memory of How Scientific Answers Evolve — Framework v0.6: General Propositions Backed by Study-Level Findings

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) now underpins FinTech services that support digital financial inclusion and sustainable economic growth, yet AI-enabled fraud threatens users' trust in this innovation. Some users intend to discontinue AI-enabled FinTech services even when they are satisfied and habituated, a pattern that traditional continuance explanations do not explain. This study examines a Dual Evaluation Mechanism in which discontinuance intention forms through an internal path (confirmation, satisfaction, and habit) and an external path (vicarious exposure to AI fraud and perceived AI fraud risk), and tests whether perceived AI fraud risk moderates the relationship between habit and discontinuance intention. The study employs cross-sectional survey data from 507 Indian users of AI-enabled FinTech services, analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling and complemented by predictive, importance-performance, endogeneity, and necessary condition analyses. The results show that confirmation raises satisfaction (β = 0.648), satisfaction raises habit (β = 0.578), and habit lowers discontinuance intention (β = −0.330). Vicarious AI fraud exposure raises perceived AI fraud risk (β = 0.588), which raises discontinuance intention (β = 0.507), and the interaction between risk and habit is positive (β = 0.174); all paths are significant at p < 0.001. The model explains 39.9% of the variance in discontinuance intention and outperforms the indicator-average benchmark in out-of-sample prediction. The findings suggest that all six hypotheses are supported, that perceived AI fraud risk is the most important predictor of discontinuance intention (0.507) and weakens the protective effect of habit, and that no construct is a strong necessary condition for discontinuance (d ≤ 0.163). JEL Classification Codes: D91, G21, G23, G41, O33.

evidence_items.summary: This repository provides the complete Python implementation and verified experimental results associated with the research article entitled “AI-Based Bearing Fault Classification Using Vibration Sensor Data: Effects of Signal Representations and Decision Thresholds.” The study investigates the effects of dimensionless vibration features, signal representations, physical-time dynamics, and source-derived decision thresholds on artificial intelligence-based bearing fault classification. Experiments were conducted using 59 source recordings from the MCC5–THU three-phase asynchronous motor dataset and 32 target recordings from the University of Ottawa Electric Motor Dataset. Five predefined feature and temporal configurations, 11 classification models, and four decision rules were evaluated. The models include physical-time spiking neural networks, a memoryless SNN counterpart, conventional machine learning classifiers, and ensemble methods. Model training, calibration, and decision threshold selection were performed exclusively on source data using nested stratified group cross-validation with three outer folds and two inner folds. The trained models were evaluated on the Ottawa recordings without target-side parameter updates. The Ottawa analyses include exploratory comparisons at the recording level. The archive contains: The complete Python source code and software dependencies. Publication Figures 5–10 in PNG and SVG formats. Publication Tables 5–8 in CSV format. Source cross-validation results and record-level predictions. Ottawa classification scores, calibration results, and decision thresholds. Group-based bootstrap results and supporting feature statistics. Experimental protocol, raw-data checksums, software environment information, and reproducibility verification reports. Numerical results were checked against the manuscript at the reported precision.

evidence_items.summary: Existing LLM reasoning benchmarks are largely static, single-turn, English-centric, and reliant on biased LLM-as-a-judge scoring. We present MTGBench, a bilingual (English/Russian) suite of seven multi-turn puzzle games—Wordle, Word Chain, Situation Puzzles, 20 Questions, Wheel of Fortune, 20 Features, and Alias—spanning deductive, semantic, lateral, consistency, and knowledge-retrieval reasoning. Four games use algorithmic checkers; the remaining three use a constrained LLM-as-a-rule-enforcer validated against human annotators, and episodes are regenerated natively per language rather than translated. Across 16 frontier models and a human baseline comprising 476 sessions we find that (i) rankings are highly task-dependent, (ii) chain-of-thought is near-essential for letter-level games but uneven on knowledge-driven ones, and (iii) the strongest reasoning-enabled LLMs match or exceed our collected Russian human baseline across the entire suite. Game scores align most consistently with cognitive batteries probing Causal Reasoning, Pragmatics, Planning, and Common-sense Reasoning, though these associations are game-specific rather than a single executive-function signal. Code and data are available in MTGBench github.

evidence_items.summary: Cell tracking in time-lapse microscopy is essential for studying dynamic biological processes such as migration, proliferation, and lineage formation. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on high-framerate imaging, where short temporal intervals simplify correspondence between cells across consecutive frames. We present the Low Frame-rate Cell Tracking dataset (LFCT), a benchmark dataset designed specifically for evaluating cell tracking methods under low-frame-rate conditions. The dataset contains multi-day live-cell microscopy sequences from four human cell lines (MCF10A, MDA-MB-231, HEK293T, and U87), acquired at 10× and 20× magnifications using phase-contrast and fluorescence imaging (nucleus). Ground-truth annotations include cell identifications, temporal linking, lineage relationships, and mitosis events. To generate reliable annotations, automated segmentation and tracking were combined with extensive manual curation. LFCT provides a comprehensive resource for developing and benchmarking robust cell tracking algorithms capable of handling sparse temporal sampling and large inter-frame motion in long-term live-cell imaging experiments.
evidence_items.title: LFCT: A Benchmark Dataset for Low-Frame-Rate Cell Tracking in Long-Term Live-Cell Microscopy.
