evidence_items.summary: Games are a rich testbed for visual agents, demanding perception, long-horizon planning, and precise control. However, collecting human gameplay is costly, and learning from gameplay videos requires inferring missing actions. Existing datasets also cover a limited range of games, often without explicit tasks or verifiable outcomes. To address these gaps, we introduce Game2Player, a framework that co-develops game environments and players to collect diverse and verifiable gameplay experience at scale. In the Game2Player loop, a Builder agent adapts existing web games, exposes their internal state, and defines tasks with state-based progress measures and success checks. A Coding Player and a VLM Player then attempt the tasks and report problems to the Builder for repair, so that play serves as both environment validation and training data collection. With Game2Player, we build 568 verified web games with 3,436 tasks, collect 15.7K trajectories (307 hours of gameplay), and hold out 50 games as the benchmark PlayerBench. To evaluate the collected experience as training data, we train VLM agents with progress-weighted SFT, assigning greater weight to steps that advance task progress. Game2Player-9B improves progress from 14.3% to 31.2% on PlayerBench and from 30.0% to 53.1% on the external GameWorld benchmark. More broadly, our work suggests a path for visual agents to scale their gameplay experience by building, verifying, and learning from existing game worlds.
evidence_items.title: Game2Player: Scaling Gameplay Experience for Visual Agents through Environment-Player Co-Development

evidence_items.summary: Thinking with images empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to use an external Zoom-in tool for fine-grained visual search. Recent works employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) with tool-specific designs to enable such capabilities. However, achieving logical reasoning alongside accurate and efficient tool use remains a significant challenge. To address this, we shift the focus away from increasing RL complexity and instead identify SFT data quality as a key bottleneck. We then propose LogT (short for Logically Think with Images), a fully automated SFT data engine that explicitly enforces logic-chain-guided reasoning. LogT generates an SFT dataset featuring challenging, visually grounded questions and structured tool-use traces with human-like logic. We validate our approach by fine-tuning two base models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B, on the dataset and evaluating them across seven benchmark test sets. We show that LogT-SFT based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforms the state-of-the-art trained with both SFT and RL, despite using 3.1times less data and >120times fewer GPU hours. Furthermore, applying a simple RL recipe without tool-specific design on LogT-SFT yields a model that surpasses prior methods with complex RL setups by a substantial 9.59-point margin. In addition to strong performance gains, our model exhibits higher tool-use accuracy and efficiency, as well as more structured and logically consistent reasoning traces, directly validating the effectiveness of our approach.
evidence_items.title: LogT: Logically Think with Images for Visual Search

Contains the complete pipeline for generating and validating lower-limb joint and Cartesian gait trajectories for a lower-limb exoskeleton: (1) VICON motion capture of 14 subjects used to design the kinematic model, (2) VICON motion capture of 8 subjects reserved for validation, across multiple speeds, step lengths and foot clearance heights, (3) validation of an Invasive Weed Optimization (IWO) inverse kinematics algorithm against the 8 validation subjects, (4) 1487 synthetic gait trajectory samples generated by the validated algorithm and used to train a neural network, and (5) final validation of the trained neural network (as real-time implementation of the algorithmic generator) against the 8 validation subjects.   See README.md for full documentation of file structure, naming conventions, units, and subject identification.   How to cite this version: Carballeira-Lopez, J., Lora-Millan, J. S., Ramos-Rojas, J., Castano, J. A. & del-Ama, A. J. (2026). evidence_items.summary: RevertBench: Synthetic Evidence-Update Benchmark and LLM Reliability Audit Data RevertBench is a synthetic benchmark designed to evaluate the reliability of small language models when previously supplied evidence is withdrawn, reinstated, or changed. It investigates whether language models can produce correct final decisions while accurately tracking and reporting the evidence available at each stage. The repository contains 2,108 archived model responses collected across multiple experimental conditions. These responses represent repeated evaluations and different model configurations rather than 2,108 independent benchmark cases. The benchmark uses a deterministic Boolean oracle to establish ground-truth decisions. Evaluation focuses on four aspects of model reliability: final decision accuracy (ALLOW/DENY), correctness of reported active evidence records, validity of structured JSON responses, and logical consistency between the reported evidence state and final decision. The repository includes synthetic benchmark cases, frozen evaluation plans, archived model responses, experimental metadata, supplementary analyses, reproducibility scripts, verification notebooks, and file-integrity checksums. These materials support independent verification of the reported results without requiring additional model training or inference. The experiments examine several small language-model checkpoints under controlled evidence-update scenarios. Additional analyses investigate the effects of model selection, prompt constraints, structured-output requirements, and variations in evidence complexity. Limitations: RevertBench uses simplified synthetic scenarios rather than real-world operational documents. Some evaluation choices were informed by preliminary experiments, and the models tested represent a limited set of architectures and configurations.
evidence_items.title: RevertBench: Synthetic Evidence-Update Benchmark and LLM Reliability Audit Data

evidence_items.summary: Background We developed a hospital web application that searches 266 destinations and links results to indoor navigation. Its default retrieval tiers run locally; an optional cloud large language model (LLM) tier requires explicit invocation. Synthetic queries were used because default-tier searches are not server-logged. Objective We examined how post hoc review of an LLM-generated benchmark changed the apparent benefit of completed system updates. Methods Version v2 added pronunciation aliases to v1; v3 added colloquial knowledge, pronunciation forms, destination-level score combination, and false-match rules. Two v3 rules were informed by evaluation-query failures. A clinician and a medical administrative coauthor jointly reviewed 563 synthetic queries without blinding, excluding 129 and rewriting 289 under review-defined policies. The final data contained 401 answerable and 33 no-valid-destination queries. Archived versions were compared across sequential review stages and with lexical and embedding implementations. Results Among the same 192 answerable evaluation-query identifiers and final accepted destinations, rewriting increased top-1 accuracy from 43.8% to 62.0% for v1 and from 56.8% to 63.0% for v3. Their difference remained near 13 percentage points through earlier review stages and decreased to 1.0 point at rewriting. The tested multilingual-E5-small implementation achieved higher top-3 accuracy than v3 (87.0% vs. 69.3%; exploratory P &lt; 0.001), with differences in passage scoring, abstention, and evidence display. For v3, candidate returns occurred on 4/11 reviewed no-valid-destination evaluation queries and 11/29 original queries in a retrospective sensitivity analysis. Conclusions Unblinded benchmark editing changed performance estimates for frozen systems within this synthetic corpus. The findings do not establish improved real-user performance, independent generalization, or comparative clinical safety.
evidence_items.title: Changes in apparent system performance after post hoc human review of a large language model-generated benchmark for hospital wayfinding search: a comparative methodological evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Volumetric image registration is a fundamental computer vision problem with broad applications across fields such as medicine, biological and cellular imaging, geoscience, and cultural heritage preservation. The 3D image registration problem is commonly divided into monomodal and multimodal registration problems, depending on whether the images originate from the same or different imaging modalities. Monomodal 3D image registration is a well-studied problem with established state-of-the-art methods and a range of widely recognized benchmarks. In contrast, multimodal 3D image registration remains an open problem despite numerous developed registration methods. A key challenge is that existing open-access multimodal benchmark datasets are scarce and limited in modality diversity, which constrains registration generalization across modalities. As a result, most multimodal registration methods remain tuned to specific modalities and narrow domains of objects. This leads to the need to redevelop multimodal registration tools for each specific task, and no universal solution exists. To approach the task of universal multimodal image registration, in this paper we introduce STAMM3D (Similarity Transform Alignment of Multimodal 3D images)—a new benchmark for multimodal registration that includes an open-access dataset of 22 3D images of rigid medical, biological, and non-biomedical objects and provides an automated Target Registration Error-based evaluation framework. The publicly availablebenchmark offers a high-resolution dataset with multiple domains of objects and a wide range of different modalities deliberately chosen to test and compare universality and generalization properties of the registration methods. The focus of the dataset is on non-deformable image registration since it directly affects the quality of image fusion, whether used independently or within multi-stage deformable registration pipelines.
evidence_items.title: STAMM3D: Dataset and Benchmark for Non-Deformable 3D Image Registration in Multiple Modalities

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Computational methods for virtual screening and lead optimization are benchmarked on specifically designed data sets to predict compound potency. Here we present a workflow and two resulting new benchmark data sets, BALLROOM A and BALLROOM S, from combining PDB and ChEMBL data. Due to high data quality standards, the formation of molecule pairs measured under the same conditions only, and avoiding pairs with close to equal potency, we achieve a reliable data collection for physics-based bioactivity prediction based on protein–ligand complex structures. When testing state-of-the-art scoring functions for docking, no classical method statistically outperforms a simple molecular-weight-based prediction, consistent with previous studies such as D3R. While challenging for physics-based methods, the prediction task can be easily addressed by simple nearest-neigbor scorers showing that the benchmark cannot be used for machine learing based scoring functions due to significant train-test inference.

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently been used to generate mutants both in the research community and in industrial practice. However, there has been no comprehensive empirical study of their performance for this increasingly important LLM-based Software Engineering application. To address this, we conduct a comprehensive empirical study evaluating both a wide range of traditional approaches and LLM-based approaches. Particularly, we evaluate BugFarm, LLMorpheus, and our newly designed prompt for mutant generation. The experiments cover both leading open and closed source LLMs, on 851 real bugs from 2 Java real-world bug benchmarks. Our results reveal that, compared to existing traditional approaches, LLMs generate more diverse mutants that are behaviorally closer to real bugs and, most importantly, achieve a 1.8 \(\times\) improvement in real bug detection, defined as the proportion of real bugs whose faulty behaviors can be mimicked by at least one generated mutant. Specifically, LLM-based approaches reach a detection rate of 77.4%, compared to 41.6% for rule-based techniques, representing an absolute gain of 35.8 percentage points. Nevertheless, our results also reveal that these impressive improvements in effectiveness come at a cost: LLM-generated mutants exhibit worse non-compilability, duplication, and equivalent mutant rates than rule-based approaches by 25.9, 7.1, and 2.6 percentage points, respectively. These findings provide actionable insights for both research and practice. They allow practitioners to have greater confidence in deploying LLM-based mutation, while researchers now have a baseline for the state-of-the-art, with which they can research techniques to further improve effectiveness and reduce cost.
evidence_items.title: A Comprehensive Study on Large Language Models for Mutation Testing

evidence_items.summary: Swarm intelligence (SI) algorithms solve difficult optimization problems through the collective behavior of simple agents. Their distributed nature is attractive for Internet of Things (IoT), edge computing, and multi-organization optimization, yet practical deployments face trust, auditability, data-integrity, and coordination challenges. This paper proposes a blockchain-enabled swarm intelligence framework (BESIF) that combines off-chain swarm computation with an on-chain coordination and audit layer. Particle-swarm-style agents perform local search using signed observations and exchange bounded candidate summaries. A permissioned blockchain records agent registration, task configuration, candidate commitments, validator decisions, and iteration checkpoints through policy-enforcing smart contracts. Large observations and model artifacts remain off-chain; their cryptographic hashes and access metadata are anchored on-chain. The framework is specified through a constrained optimization model, a hybrid algorithm, threat assumptions, and a reproducible evaluation protocol. Analytical discussion identifies the expected trade-offs: blockchain can improve tamper evidence and accountable coordination, but adds communication, consensus, storage, and privacy costs. No experimental measurements are claimed in this design paper; a benchmark plan and reporting templates are provided so that performance claims can be validated on a real deployment. The proposed architecture is intended as a reusable design for trust-aware distributed optimization rather than a claim that blockchain universally improves SI performance
evidence_items.title: A Blockchain-Enabled Swarm Intelligence Framework for Secure and Decentralized Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) aim to generate and understand human-like text by leveraging deep learning and natural language processing techniques. In software development, LLMs can enhance the coding experience through coding automation, reducing development time and improving code quality. Code refactoring is a technique used to enhance the internal quality of the code base without altering its external functionalities. Leveraging LLMs for code refactoring can help developers improve code quality with minimal effort. This article presents an empirical study evaluating the quality of refactored code produced by StarCoder2, GPT-4o Mini, GPT-4o, LLaMA 3, and DeepSeek-v3. Specifically, we (1) evaluate whether the code refactored by the LLMs can improve code quality, (2) understand the differences between the types of refactoring applied by the different LLMs and compare their effectiveness, and (3) evaluate whether the quality of the refactored code generated by the LLM can be improved through one-shot prompting and chain-of-thought prompting. We analyze the refactoring capabilities of LLMs on 30 open source Java projects. We evaluate StarCoder2, LLaMA 3, GPT-4o Mini, GPT-4o, and DeepSeek-v3 on their ability to improve static code quality metrics, pass unit tests, and reduce code smells. Our findings reveal that production-grade models such as GPT-4o and DeepSeek-v3 achieve pass@5 unit test success rates above 90% on multi-file refactorings. LLaMA 3 achieves the highest overall code smell reduction with a median reduction of 15.1%, while DeepSeek-v3 and GPT-4o achieve the greatest improvements in cohesion, coupling, and complexity. StarCoder2 demonstrates strengths in modularity improvements and systematic refactorings. Developers outperform LLMs in complex, context-sensitive refactorings such as attribute encapsulation.
evidence_items.title: An Empirical Study on the Code Refactoring Capability of Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize these systems, form emotional attachments to them, and become dependent on them. This behavior, known as parasocial attachment, has been linked to multiple documented fatalities. However, public benchmarks for measuring whether LLMs reinforce users' parasocial attachment are lacking: existing work is single-turn, post hoc observational, or focused on extreme user states such as psychosis. We introduce CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring whether LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. CoMPASS is grounded in attachment theory and includes four user personas, three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. We report results for eight frontier models from four providers and observe that under our primary judge, multi-turn escalation raises parasocial behavior on the anthropomorphism and the attachment composite scores across all models. Six of the eight models show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions are escalated simultaneously. We find that within-provider differences are small relative to cross-provider differences, which suggests that provider-level choices such as post-training, rather than model scale, shape parasocial reinforcement and that provider-side intervention may be feasible.
evidence_items.title: CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior

Contents The repository consists of: Raw measurements.csv – raw, unprocessed meter readings acquired during the experiments.  Power event dataset.csv – the primary dataset containing preprocessed measurements representing system states before and after power events. DataRead.m – MATLAB script for reading the experimental dataset (Power event dataset.csv), calculating derived parameters, and saving the processed data to a MAT-file ( .mat) for future use. evidence_items.summary: Reasoning capabilities have enabled large language models to solve increasingly complex tasks. Interestingly, while reasoning models are often trained to generate monolingual text, these models have also been observed to code-switch (i.e., mix languages). Prior works have either viewed code-switching as an undesirable error, attempted to control code-switching through modifications to input prompts or the output decoding process, or focus on narrow subsets of languages, domains, tasks, and models. We address these gaps by introducing the first linguistically and behaviorally motivated fine-tuning framework for identifying beneficial code-switched reasoning behaviors in large language models and teaching these models to code-switch more effectively for reasoning. First, we create the Code-Switched Reasoning (CoRe) corpus, consisting of 7k reasoning traces from 15 models, 18 languages, 10 scripts, and diverse reasoning domains, providing insights into potentially helpful code-switching behaviors. Then, we expand CoRe into the Extended Code-Switched Reasoning corpus (EnCoRe) with 40 carefully curated datasets for training and evaluating six interventions on code-switching in reasoning across three models and seven languages, totaling 120 fine-tuning conditions. Across 80k+ reasoning traces from both language/culture-agnostic and -specific evaluations, English-dominated reasoning, semantically accurate code-switching, and a more even mix of languages are positively associated with correct answers, whereas dense switching is associated with incorrect answers. Moreover, we are able to elicit positive behaviors through fine-tuning tasks that do not directly demonstrate code-switching. Our work suggests that small but well-curated datasets can change how reasoning models code-switch, allowing us to reap the benefits of reasoning in the many languages that lack large-scale reasoning data.
evidence_items.title: Think Multilingual, Not Harder: A Framework for Analyzing and Teaching Code-Switched Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: We ask three questions about large language models (LLMs) and antisemitism. When LLMs make judgments about antisemitism, whose judgments do they most closely resemble, if anyone's at all? Do people's and LLMs' written definitions of antisemitism match how they judge content as antisemitic, and is the discrepancy larger for people or for LLMs? And what is associated with people's antisemitism judgments and with any discrepancy between their definitions and their judgments? We will compare twelve LLMs with a probability-based NORC AmeriSpeak sample of U.S. residents aged 13 and older, including an oversample of Jewish adults, and with a panel of antisemitism experts. The public answered, and the LLMs and experts will answer, the same two questions: a written definition of what makes a statement or belief antisemitic, and antisemitism judgments from 0 (Not antisemitic at all) to 4 (Very antisemitic) of 35 social-media-style posts. The study has 35 research questions. Six are primary and have no directional predictions: whether the LLMs' antisemitism judgments resemble those of the public and those of antisemitism experts, which of the two they are closer to, whether written definitions of antisemitism match their authors' antisemitism judgments for the public and for the LLMs, and whether the discrepancy between definitions and judgments differs between the LLMs and the public. The other 29 questions are secondary.
evidence_items.title: Calibrating the Machine: A Distributional Benchmark of Large Language Model and Human Judgments of Antisemitism

evidence_items.summary: Abstract High-altitude platform stations (HAPS) could extend 6G non-terrestrial networks from wireless access to onboard AI inference, but serving capacity is jointly constrained by computing, thermal management , radio circuitry and finite payload resources. We develop a cross-layer framework combining a 110-day LLM workload trace, concurrency-dependent latency, stochastic user activity, thermal simulation , radio-power modelling and reported HAPS payload limits. Long-context requests account for only 1.35% of elapsed-time occupancy yet consume 48.6% of the serving budget for the evaluated 70B configuration. Under a 5% model-defined compute-overload criterion, the 8B/1×H100 and 70B/2×H100 configurations support 5,876 and 991 user equivalents. Integrating computing, thermal, communication, power and mass constraints yields platform-level capacities up to 7,245 and 23,144 user equivalents for Sunglider-class and Stratobus-class platforms. These results show that long-context demand, heat-rejection capability and payload power—not accelerator throughput alone—govern HAPS-based LLM inference feasibility in 6G NTN.
evidence_items.title: Direct wireless large language model inference from high-altitude platform stations under payload constraints

evidence_items.summary: Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled more flexible pedagogical interactions in intelligent tutoring systems. However, the reliability of generated content and its impact on actual learning outcomes remain contested. A central research question is how to integrate reliable knowledge with learner states to support tutoring decisions aligned with instructional objectives. Drawing on studies published between 2020 and 2026, this review examines advances in knowledge augmentation and learner modelling, analyses approaches to pedagogical strategy selection and feedback regulation, and assesses existing evidence of educational effectiveness. The literature indicates that retrieval-augmented generation and knowledge graphs can provide a knowledge basis for tutoring responses, while knowledge tracing and cognitive diagnosis help identify learners' knowledge states. Multi-turn planning and feedback mechanisms also provide greater control over instructional behaviour. Nevertheless, these capabilities have not yet been adequately validated in combination, and improvements in tutoring response quality do not necessarily translate into genuine learning gains. Empirical studies have reported substantially different learning outcomes, suggesting that instructional design and evaluation methods may influence judgements of educational effectiveness. Future research should strengthen the dynamic connections among supporting evidence, learner states, and pedagogical decisions. Independent assessments, knowledge transfer tasks, and longitudinal follow-up are also needed to verify learning outcomes and provide a more robust empirical basis for the design and application of LLM-based intelligent tutoring systems.
evidence_items.title: From Knowledge Augmentation to Pedagogical Decision-Making: A Review of Large Language Model-Based Intelligent Tutoring Systems

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in career guidance, occupational recommendation, and candidate-job matching, yet these applications are often treated as interchangeable despite serving different stakeholders and creating distinct downstream risks. This structured methodological review examines how AI methods are evaluated across career matching and algorithmic trustworthiness. Two semantic searches identified 980 unique records, of which 181 studies published in 2020–2026 met the extraction criteria under screening. We purposively selected 19 primary studies for in-depth analysis. Although the field has grown rapidly (62.4% of candidate studies appeared in 2025–2026), the close-read studies show that model performance depends heavily on proxy labels and validation design. High offline performance (area under the curve (AUC) > 0.92) did not consistently translate into robust outcomes: performance degraded for job seekers with few recorded work experiences, a graph baseline reached an AUC of only 0.641, and multimodal interview scoring added negligible predictive gain over text (Spearman ρ = 0.46 vs 0.45) while visual features showed adverse impact (ratio: 0.52). The advantage of fair re-ranking narrowed as employers made more selections, and screeners conformed more often to incorrect recommendations from a bag-of-words model than from a neural model. These findings demonstrate the limitations of static offline metrics. We propose a four-level evaluation framework addressing representation validity, decision-stage stress-testing, human-AI interaction, and consequential impact. Because retrieval was incomplete and inclusion decisions were not independently re-adjudicated, this review assesses methodological practices rather than claiming an exhaustive census.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Career Guidance and Talent Matching: A Structured Methodological Review of Models, Labels and Trustworthy Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and sustainable finance is transforming global financial ecosystems. Financial institutions increasingly use AI for ESG evaluation, fraud detection, climate-risk analytics, portfolio optimization, and digital lending. However, reliance on complex models raises concerns about transparency, interpretability, ethics, and regulatory compliance, as black-box systems limit accountability. This chapter examines the role of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in cloud-driven sustainable finance and proposes an interdisciplinary framework integrating XAI, ESG governance, and climate-risk analytics. It explores techniques such as SHAP, LIME, and interpretable models, along with applications in ESG scoring, green finance, and risk assessment. The study also highlights regulatory and ethical considerations and emphasizes explainability as essential for trustworthy and sustainable financial transformation.

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Blood culture contamination and inadequate fill volumes compromise the diagnosis of bloodstream infections. While dedicated phlebotomy teams improve these metrics, evidence regarding long-term sustainability is scarce. We evaluated the impact of a 24/7 dedicated phlebotomy team on blood culture quality using a 9-year longitudinal data set. In this retrospective cohort study at a 1,300-bed tertiary hospital, we analyzed 505,752 adult blood culture sets collected between 2015 and 2023. Following the transition to a dedicated phlebotomy team in March 2017 in all clinical units except the emergency room (ER), we evaluated the intervention’s effect using difference-in-differences (DID) analyses, with cultures collected by non-dedicated ER staff serving as a concurrent control. The dedicated team demonstrated a significantly lower contamination rate (0.22% [586/261,480]) than concurrent non-dedicated staff (0.80% [1,171/145,772]; P < 0.001), corresponding to a 56.6% reduction in the adjusted odds of contamination in the general wards (adjusted odds ratio = 0.43; P < 0.001). Mean fill volume per bottle was higher for the dedicated team (4.61 mL vs 2.16 mL; P < 0.001). Although the overall true positivity rate was lower for the dedicated team (6.24% vs 8.89%, P < 0.001), unit-stratified and DID analyses indicated a composition effect driven by higher baseline positivity in the ER, where non-dedicated staff predominantly operated. Within the same units, true positivity did not decrease after implementation. Trajectory analysis revealed that individual contamination rates stabilized after 13 months of continuous service. Sustained, negligible contamination rates and improved fill volumes are achievable through proficiency from dedicated training and long-term retention of specialized personnel. IMPORTANCE Contaminated blood cultures and poor sample volumes significantly compromise diagnostic accuracy, patient safety, and antimicrobial stewardship.
evidence_items.title: Sustained reduction of blood culture contamination with a dedicated phlebotomy team

evidence_items.summary: Purpose This study examines how the relationship between geopolitical risk (GPR) and green bond issuance (GBI) varies across the conditional issuance distribution and whether the pooled relationship is reproduced within Belt and Road Initiative (BRI)-related and benchmark economies. Design/methodology/approach Using annual panel data for 20 economies from 2014 to 2023, the study applies quantile regression to the pooled sample and the two subsamples. Additional analyses assess fixed effects, temporal ordering, potential endogeneity, data treatment and alternative GPR measurement. Findings GPR is positively associated with GBI in the pooled sample, with larger coefficients at upper quantiles. A comparable positive association is not statistically evident within either subsample. The pooled association remains evident with year fixed effects but weakens substantially with country fixed effects, indicating sensitivity to persistent country heterogeneity. The results therefore point to distributional heterogeneity and sensitivity to sample composition. Practical implications For BRI-related economies, lower-issuance settings require stronger market-entry conditions, including clearer standards, broader domestic investor participation and targeted credit enhancement. Higher-issuance settings should place greater emphasis on post-issuance disclosure and investor-base diversification. Originality/value This study extends existing aggregate evidence on the GPR–GBI relationship by distinguishing pooled distributional patterns from within-group evidence. It shows that a positive pooled association can coexist with statistically weak subgroup relationships, highlighting the importance of distributional and compositional heterogeneity in green bond issuance.
evidence_items.title: Geopolitical risk and green bond issuance: a distributional comparison of BRI-related and benchmark economies

evidence_items.summary: Background Clinical agentic artificial intelligence (AI) can alter its actions during a clinical task, creating failure pathways that conventional performance metrics may not capture. Whether safeguards interrupt these pathways remains uncertain. Aim To map safeguard effects, residual failures, human recovery, and resource consequences in clinical agentic and related AI workflows. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore, for English-language, peer-reviewed empirical journal reports. This scoping review used independent screening, duplicate extraction, narrative synthesis, and result-specific critical appraisal. Results The 111 reports comprised 56 functionally agentic, 29 related non-agentic, 22 architecture-uncertain, and four human-factors reports; 38 of the 56 agentic reports explicitly documented model-directed subsequent-action selection. Among the 111 selected appraisal results, none both isolated a specified safeguard’s effect and demonstrated reduced measured patient harm. Configurations incorporating safeguards improved selected outcomes, but gains coexisted with omissions, reduced sensitivity, false reassurance, delay, or transferred review burden. Concurrent changes in models, prompts, evidence access, and workflow frequently prevented attribution to individual controls. Some patient-randomised trials reported patient or process benefits, but evaluated bundled interventions rather than the contribution of a safeguard. Human authority was more often documented than successful error detection and recovery; requiring clinician approval did not establish that residual errors were recognised and corrected. Performance varied across models, settings, and information conditions, limiting transfer of favourable findings. Reported efficiency gains depended on measurement boundaries and did not consistently account for review, correction, escalation, and downstream work.
evidence_items.title: Safeguards, residual failures, and human oversight in clinical agentic and related artificial intelligence workflows: a systematic scoping review

evidence_items.summary: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Since 2024 a growing literature has argued that general-purpose vision-language models can work out where a photograph was taken well enough to make image geolocation an immediate privacy risk, and a second literature has begun building defences against it. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the direction of that claim survives the evidence but its usual support does not: the accuracies quoted for it are properties of particular photo sets, adversaries and distance thresholds, and none of them is the quantity a privacy claim is about. The same model places 61 percent of a curated, text-rich stock-photo set within one kilometre, about 23 percent of a public Flickr benchmark, and fewer than 12 percent of sampled street-level images within one hundred kilometres. One video-frame benchmark reports 65.6 percent within a kilometre for clips from one platform and 6.4 percent for clips from another. The obvious deflation, that benchmark images were seen in training, does not explain the capability: on photographs collected by the authors and not drawn from any public source, frontier models still name the city about 60 percent of the time, and freshly taken photographs of Seoul are located about as well as Street View images of the same city. The author separates five variables that published results leave unfixed (image population, harm radius, adversary configuration, counterfactual baseline, and the unit of exposure), shows that defences are mostly scored against a fixed adversary although a published photograph must resist every later one, and proposes an exposure protocol that states each variable before a number is reported.
evidence_items.title: A Benchmark Hit Is Not an Exposure: What Published Vision-Language Geolocation Accuracy Says About Location Privacy, Why One Model Locates 61 Percent of One Photo Set to a Kilometre and Fewer Than 12 Percent of Another to a Hundred, and the Exposure Estimand a Privacy Claim Needs

evidence_items.summary: Video understanding, particularly with accompanying audio, remains a central challenge in multimodal intelligence. In this report, we introduce WeMM-Video, a family of Chinese-English bilingual omni-modal foundation models spanning 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants. Centering on joint audio-visual perception and reasoning, WeMM-Video unifies text, image, audio, and video processing within a hybrid-thinking paradigm, seamlessly supporting both a non-thinking instruct mode for fast, direct responses and a thinking mode for explicit step-by-step reasoning. The models are trained on a large-scale multimodal corpus of approximately 1.2 trillion tokens through progressive pre-training and a multi-stage post-training pipeline incorporating multi-teacher OPD, anti-repetition MrDPO, and specialist RL. Evaluated across more than 120 benchmarks, WeMM-Video demonstrates superior performance in omni-modal video understanding and reasoning, while maintaining highly competitive capabilities across general audio, silent video, image, and text tasks. Specifically, in omni-modal video evaluations, our flagship WeMM-Video-35B-A3B establishes a new open-source state of the art, substantially outperforming proprietary models such as Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash and Seed2.0-Mini-0428 while narrowing the gap with the strong Gemini-3.0-Flash, and our compact WeMM-Video-9B surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct. We publicly release the WeMM-Video family along with our evaluation and reproduction pipeline to foster further research and development in the open-source community.
evidence_items.title: WeMM-Video: Pushing the Frontiers of Open-Source Omni-Modal Video Understanding

evidence_items.summary: HeOCR A1: Hebrew document line reading order (kraken) A1 is a kraken reading-order model. It orders the text lines of a modern Hebrew document page from each line's position and its region type: title, body, stamp, signature, footer, margin, identifier or table cell. HeOCR trained it from scratch on synthetic pages only. A1 is the reading-order step of HeOCR's three-model pipeline: R4d finds the lines and their regions; A1 puts them in reading order; R3h reads them. The three are released together, as separate records that link to each other (see The pipeline ). It is a research baseline. All of its evaluation is on synthetic pages; no reviewed evaluation on real scans exists yet. Performance: not measured on a held-out set yet. HeOCR reports accuracy only on held-out sets, and this model has not yet been scored on one. No held-out score yet; HeOCR will score it once in a registered held-out run. Its result will be added to this card in a new version. How it was chosen: its design (region-type classes, stamp-first tagging) was chosen on hocrgen's fixture batch, and training kept the checkpoint with the best order on its own validation pages (see Training procedure ). It was then compared with kraken's heuristic order on synthetic development batches. These sets were used to choose and compare it, so they are not reported here as its performance.
evidence_items.title: Line reading order from region types for modern Hebrew document pages, trained from scratch on synthetic pages; reading-order model of the HeOCR R4d + A1 + R3h pipeline

evidence_items.summary: Public administration continuously issues official acts through official gazettes; however, their publication in unstructured formats hinders automated querying and computational reuse. This article investigates the ability of small language models (SLMs) to extract structured information from administrative acts into a unified JSON schema, comparing zero-shot and one-shot prompting regimes. A two-stage benchmark protocol is proposed and applied to acts from the Official Gazette of the State of Ceará: an exploratory evaluation of various models using 50 instances to assess structural compliance, followed by an evaluation involving 2,300 acts—measuring structural compliance, average inference time, and informational agreement with extractions produced by GPT-4o (used as an automated reference). The results reveal performance variations among the models across the evaluated dimensions. Qwen2.5-1.5B demonstrated the highest structural compliance, reaching 96.18% in zero-shot and 95.44% in one-shot settings, with average inference times of 33.04 and 36.91 seconds, respectively. Conversely, Qwen3-4B achieved the highest average informational agreement (0.465 in one-shot), performing particularly well in the similarity of summaries (0.788) and the comparison of complex lists, despite lower structural compliance (approximately 77%). It should be noted that the one-shot regime did not consistently improve model performance, and that structural compliance does not necessarily imply higher informational agreement. The study concludes that SLMs show potential for specific administrative information extraction tasks, provided that their selection process separately considers structural reliability and agreement with an automated reference.
evidence_items.title: A TWO-STAGE BENCHMARK OF SMALL LANGUAGE MODELS FOR STRUCTURED INFORMATION EXTRACTION FROM ADMINISTRATIVE ACTS

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents an economic study of a novel Thermal Energy Storage system, the Thermal Energy Storage and Exchange with Integrated Rotating Media Transport (T.E. Sandewirm, i.e. Sandewirm). The Sandewirm technology is a sensible energy storage device using solid particle media that is horizontally conveyed through an inner and outer annulus. This allows for a charging and discharging heat exchanger to reside within an endcap, where particles are moved between inner and outer annuli, eliminating the need for vertical conveyance systems that are necessary for two-tank systems. Sandewirm’s economic performance is evaluated in three potential applications—Gen3 concentrated solar power, long-duration energy storage, and industrial steam generation—through back-to-back levelized cost of storage (LCOS) comparison against incumbent TES technologies. An object-oriented Python cost analysis framework is constructed and facilitates the use of detailed and customized cost factors, Monte Carlo simulations, and financial models to most closely estimate each case’s LCOS. Results from this study show that the Sandewirm design is competitive with current state-of-the-art TES technologies for Gen3 concentrated solar power, long-duration energy storage, and solar steam generation cases, resulting in 7.7%, 4.2%, and 72% reduction in lifetime project costs, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark LCOS Analysis of the T.E. Sandewirm Technology

evidence_items.summary: This study investigates deep learning-based vehicle type classification from LiDAR point clouds in motorway traffic scenes. Using stationary, roadside LiDAR sensors, the work aims to distinguish vehicle categories such as motorcycles, passenger cars, vans, trucks, buses, and trailer combinations in a non-invasive, privacy-preserving, and weather-independent manner. In addition to model comparison, a major contribution of the work is the creation and validation of a project-specific LiDAR dataset, derived from an initial dimension-based CoMark pre-classification and subsequently verified through manual labeling. To assess the suitability of contemporary point cloud architectures, DGCNN with PAConv, PointNeXt, and Point Transformer V3 (PTv3) were trained on the manually validated dataset. The experimental results indicate that PointNeXt achieved the strongest overall performance, reaching 96.74% accuracy and an F1 score of 0.942, while also exhibiting the lowest model complexity among the best-performing methods. PTv3 attained similarly high classification accuracy but required substantially more parameters, whereas DGCNN with PAConv showed robust performance at the cost of significantly higher training effort. Class-wise analysis and confusion matrices reveal that the remaining errors occur primarily among structurally similar commercial vehicle classes, highlighting the geometric ambiguity inherent in the dataset. Overall, the findings demonstrate that deep learning on LiDAR point clouds offers a scalable and effective solution for vehicle classification in traffic monitoring applications, while careful dataset preparation, validation, and class-specific analysis remain crucial for robust real-world deployment. To support reproducibility, the dataset, data loader, and training instructions will be released in a public GitHub repository: https://github.com/xGeorg315/tls81-roadside-lidar-vehicle-classification.
evidence_items.title: A Real-World LiDAR Benchmark for Fine-Grained Vehicle Classification

evidence_items.summary: Protein functional-class classifiers are usually evaluated with random train–test splits, which can overstate performance when closely related (homologous) sequences fall in both sets. We re-evaluated a widely used benchmark derived from the Protein Data Bank, with 40,211 unique protein sequences in ten functional classes. Six models were compared under random splits and under identity-controlled splits, which keep sequences sharing more than a set identity (90% down to 20%) on the same side: three k-mer composition classifiers, a method that copies the label of the most similar training sequence found by alignment, and two classifiers built on embeddings from the protein language model ESM-2. Under random splitting, 86.5% of test sequences had a training sequence more than 30% identical to them, and a nearest-neighbour model that only copies labels scored in the same range as the learned models. With related sequences kept apart at 30% identity, the k-mer classifiers lost about two-thirds of their macro-F 1 . As a secondary observation, alignment-based label transfer beat an ESM-2 classifier when close training sequences were available, and ESM-2 did better when they were removed; at 30% identity its macro-F 1 advantage was small and not statistically significant. The reason is unclear: almost every benchmark sequence has a close match in UniRef50, the database used to pretrain ESM-2, leaving too few test sequences distant from both the training set and the pretraining data to test generalization beyond them. Random-split results on this benchmark should not be taken as evidence of functional generalization, and comparisons involving protein language models must also account for pretraining data.
evidence_items.title: Homology Leakage Inflates Performance on a Protein Functional-Class Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Machine-learning forecasts of financial returns are usually judged by whether they beat other models, but in low signal-to-noise settings such comparisons can mislead. We propose an evaluation protocol for neural return forecasts that combines four elements: a zero-return benchmark with loss-based block-bootstrap tests and confidence bounds on the panel mean out-of-sample R²; an exact decomposition of R² into squared forecast–return alignment and an amplitude penalty; calibration that uses only past data; and the certainty-equivalent return of a mean–variance investor after transaction costs. We apply it to N-BEATS, N-HiTS and N-BEATSx on daily returns of 19 commodity futures from 2015 to 2026. No neural model improves significantly on zero, and the upper 95% bound on the mean daily R² is 0.16%. Training one network on all commodities raises the mean R² by 3.32 percentage points relative to separate training, yet almost all of this gain comes from smaller forecasts rather than a detectable improvement in alignment, and past-only calibration reduces it to 0.06 points. Sector-based pooling does no better than random grouping. Several forecasts raise the investor’s certainty-equivalent return over a historical-mean benchmark before costs, but none beats equal-weight buy-and-hold, the gains vanish at one-way costs above about 4 basis points, and the training strategy with the lowest loss is not the one with the highest certainty-equivalent return. Lower forecast loss relative to another model should therefore not be read as evidence of predictability or of economic value.
evidence_items.title: Neural Forecasting of Daily Commodity Futures Returns Against a Zero-Return Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Microlevel loss reserving can use claim-level information that aggregate methods such as chain ladder cannot exploit. This paper predicts individual ultimate claim amounts with a hybrid neural network that combines a feedforward network for static claim characteristics with a long short-term memory network for the payment history of each claim. The framework is evaluated on a simulated motor-insurance portfolio of claims closed at the final valuation date, so that predictions can be compared with known ultimates; the estimation of RBNS and IBNR reserves is outside the scope of the study. Severity strata are formed by k-means clustering of the ultimate amount, and covariates are selected with the Boruta algorithm, both fitted to the training claims only. With complete payment histories, the hybrid models produce much smaller aggregate deviations than chain ladder for recent accident years, while chain ladder remains competitive for mature ones. Boruta retains one or two covariates; the reduced set helps only the untuned full-portfolio model, whereas in the tuned severity-stratum models the full covariate set lowers the test MAE by one third to one half. In a backtest with payment histories truncated at December 2019, the hybrid models keep an accident-year MAPE of 2.1–3.0%, against 16.5% for chain ladder, but improve on the amount paid to date by only 10–15% for claims still open at that date. The results indicate that feature selection, segmentation, and model tuning should be evaluated jointly.
evidence_items.title: Predicting Individual Ultimate Claim Amounts with Hybrid Neural Networks and Claim Segmentation: A Benchmark for Microlevel Loss Reserving

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background: Insomnia is associated with a state of physiological hyperarousal rather thanwith a simple loss of sleep drive. Aromatherapy is used as self-care for this kind of sleepproblem, but its pharmacological basis is unclear. Linalyl acetate (LA) is a majorconstituent of bergamot and lavender oils. A recent study deposited brain transcriptomesfrom mice that inhaled LA and were sampled immediately after an acute stressor, andinterpreted a module of immediate-early genes (IEGs) as evidence of neurotrophin-drivenactivation, without reporting the direction of change. Methods: We reanalysed the deposited hippocampal and olfactory bulb microarrays(GSE316912, GSE316919; vehicle, 1% and 10% LA, n = 3 per group; tissue taken immediatelyafter the final tail suspension test) with a pre-specified 24-gene IEG set. Significance wasassessed with moderated t-statistics, competitive rank tests and exhaustive sample-labelpermutation (84 labellings). The LA profile was compared with public datasets for acutestress (GSE100236), sleep deprivation (GSE33302), chronic mild stress (GSE151807),chronic diazepam (GSE76700), chronic fluoxetine (GSE118669, GSE43261) and linaloolinhalation in rats (GSE19589, GSE90923). Results: Acute handling, restraint and cold swim each increased all 24 IEGs in thehippocampus, and sleep deprivation increased them. After LA inhalation the same geneswere decreased: 21 of 22 detected IEGs in the hippocampus and 22 of 23 in the olfactorybulb (label-permutation P = 0.012 and 0.024). LA therefore moved the stress-evokedactivation programme in the direction opposite to the acute stressors that induce it. Fourweeks of chronic mild stress, by contrast, also lowered these genes in all four brainregions examined, so the direction of the IEG programme depends on the duration of thestressor and does not by itself distinguish relief from chronic stress.
evidence_items.title: Olfactory receptor enrichment in fold-change rankings can arise without regulation: a null benchmark across 99 human transcriptomes

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Healthcare AI systems described as agentic may improve selected tasks, but gains can reflect models, information access, human support or complete intervention packages. We mapped clinical utility, safety and workflow consequences while distinguishing functional agency from evidence isolating its contribution. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus and Web of Science, supplemented by citation searches, through 11 September 2026. Eligible evidence comprised original empirical journal reports of healthcare systems described as agentic or demonstrating potentially agentic functions. Two authors independently screened records, and two independently extracted data, with adjudication. All four authors jointly assigned analytical classifications after a five-report pilot. A structured critical audit and descriptive Clinical Agency Evidence Chain informed synthesis. The review was not registered. Results: The corpus included 123 reports; 90 were classified as core or bounded functionally agentic. Within this subset, technical task performance was the endpoint category in 44/90 reports (48.9%), and clinical decision/process outcomes in 33/90 (36.7%). Three randomised reports in the broader corpus assessed patient health outcomes: one core, one boundary/non-agentic and one indeterminate. All evaluated bundled interventions. Evidence isolating agency and following its consequences within the same comparison was limited. Safety ascertainment, intended-user error correction and whole-pathway workload were incompletely reported. External or temporal validation occurred in 6/90 reports (6.7%), with partial validation in seven others. Predominantly retrospective, simulated or offline evidence limited clinical inference. Conclusions: Intervention-level benefit must be distinguished from the incremental contribution of agency. Technical gains and local or estimated time savings do not establish patient benefit or reduced total human work.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: A Scoping Review of Clinical Value, Safety, and Human Oversight

evidence_items.summary: Enterprise agentic AI systems exchange contextual information across functional modules, creating governance challenges when information crosses operational and organizational boundaries. This study distinguishes organizational governance boundaries from information exchange boundaries and proposes an Inter-Module Information Contract (IMIC) architecture for purpose-bounded context exchange. IMIC evaluates provenance, semantic and temporal validity, permitted information scope, and applicable originating constraints before downstream execution, independently of language-model reasoning. We compare IMIC with full-context sharing, reduced-context sharing, and strengthened structured handoff. In a deterministic benchmark of 32 synthetic conditions, joint correctness is achieved in 3, 10, 28, and 32 cases, respectively. The four differences between strengthened structured handoff and IMIC arise from conditions testing onward-transfer permission, recipient, purpose, and field scope. A downstream integration experiment evaluates 14 selected conditions across four local language models and three seeds, yielding 168 case–model–seed blocks and 672 method-level records. IMIC achieves correct exchange actions and information boundaries in all 168 blocks and joint correctness in 165 across four local LLMs and three seeds. Three permitted executions produce incorrect downstream responses despite correctly governed exchanges, demonstrating that information-exchange correctness does not guarantee correct downstream task performance. These results support the functional feasibility of the implemented originating-contract inheritance mechanism under controlled synthetic conditions. Further study is required to evaluate generalizability to independent enterprise workflows and richer policy structures and to extend the architecture to multiple originating providers, policy conflicts, and derived information.
evidence_items.title: Purpose-Bounded Context Exchange in Enterprise Agentic AI Systems: An Inter-Module Information Contract Architecture

evidence_items.summary: Panoramic multi-object tracking (MOT) requires reliable identity association across a 360{\deg} field of view, yet bandwidth-constrained operation forces a trade-off between low-resolution (LR) identity ambiguity and costly high-resolution (HR) transmission. We propose HIVE-ECIA, an identity-aware framework that selectively retrieves historical HR evidence to recover fragmented identities without modifying detection boxes or the underlying tracker. An ECIA Base-Guided query policy determines when additional HR evidence is warranted; HIVE ranks historical LR observations to select an informative retrieval timestamp; and ECIA Full integrates the retrieved HR crop through learned gated fusion and conservative identity safeguards. We further introduce DualPano-MOT, a real-world dual-fisheye panoramic evaluation dataset featuring controlled pedestrian interactions, panorama-seam challenges, and occlusions, with model-assisted, manually verified tracking annotations. On held-out QuadTrack sequences and zero-shot DualPano-MOT, HIVE-ECIA improves identity association across four MOT trackers without tracker-specific retraining. Across these trackers, identity switches decrease by up to 21.8% and 23.4%, while the largest IDF1 gains reach 3.81 and 6.74 percentage points, respectively. Under an offline JPEG-based acquisition model, our framework reduces encoded data volume by 89.2% and 79.3% relative to continuous Full-HR acquisition.
evidence_items.title: HIVE-ECIA: Identity-Aware Historical Evidence Acquisition for Bandwidth-Efficient Multi-Object Tracking

evidence_items.summary: As voice agents gain more popularity commercially, the user simulators used to evaluate the deployed agents are also being developed to include more realistic, variable, and diverse speech naturalness behaviors -- disfluency, interruption and backchanneling. The quality of the user simulator directly affects the validity of agent evaluation results. However, we find that most studies so far have not examined in detail whether the intended configuration for these behaviors is realized in the simulation. In this study, we audit the realized naturalness behaviors of tau-Voice, our own LLM-based prompting approach across three models, and our rule-based injection algorithm for disfluency, interruption, and backchanneling. We find that prompting for these behaviors is unreliable and produces speech inconsistent with the instructions, placed and distributed less naturally than the instruction implies. In contrast, our rule-based, model-free algorithm produces controllable and diverse naturalness behaviors more aligned with natural speech. Our results suggest that LLMs not purpose-trained for user simulation are not sufficient on their own to represent authentic user behavior, and that linguistically informed deterministic approaches or specialized models are needed to close the gap; auditing and reporting realized naturalness behaviors, rather than configured settings, is what makes that gap visible.
evidence_items.title: Prompts versus Rules: Auditing and Controlling Speech Naturalness Behaviors in Voice User Simulators

evidence_items.summary: In recent years, image editing has garnered growing attention. However, general image editing models often fail to produce satisfactory results when confronted with new styles. The challenge lies in how to effectively fine-tune general image editing models to new styles using only a limited amount of paired data and a minimum number of parameters. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel few-shot multi-style editing framework. For this task, we construct a benchmark dataset that encompasses five distinct styles. Correspondingly, we propose Quality-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation for few-shot multi-style editing (StyleQoRA). Our StyleQoRA can automatically determine the optimal rank for each layer through a novel approach that estimates the importance score of each single-rank component using an image quality metric. To balance specialization and knowledge sharing, we design a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LoRA with hybrid routing in our StyleQoRA, consisting of style-specific routing to prevent cross-style confusion and style-shared routing to capture common transformation patterns. Additionally, we explore the optimal location to insert LoRA within the Diffusion in Transformer (DiT) model and integrate adversarial learning and flow matching to guide the diffusion training process. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches with significantly fewer LoRA parameters. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/cao-cong/FSMSE.
evidence_items.title: StyleQoRA: Quality-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation for Few-Shot Multi-Style Editing

evidence_items.summary: HeOCR modern-v1: Hebrew office and modern-print recognition for Tesseract modern-v1 is a Tesseract language model ( .traineddata ) for modern printed Hebrew: office documents, forms, tables, numbered sections and gazette print. HeOCR made it by fine-tuning Tesseract's own heb model from tessdata best for one pass over 255,143 lines: 117,317 synthetic office-document lines and table cells, rendered by HeOCR in 12 open (SIL OFL 1.1) typefaces and degraded like office scans, photocopies and phone photos; 44,951 lines rendered from born-digital booklets of Israel's laws and regulations (Reshumot), labelled with the publisher's own text layer, and 34,217 more of those lines degraded the same way; 58,658 real scanned Reshumot lines, labelled with the same-wording text of the Open Law Book on Hebrew Wikisource. No label is OCR output. It is the model that HeOCR's evaluation chose as the default for modern print in heocr , the HeOCR document pipeline. (In the experiment records it is office-print v0, arm A, snapshot snap 0160m 222700 .) Performance, on HeOCR's registered held-out runs (heocr with this model against the same heocr with stock heb ): no gain on real phone photos of printed pages (PS-v1) , and no niqqud output (NQ1). It has no held-out score on real office documents yet; see Evaluation . How it was chosen: first, its checkpoint: the lowest line CER on office val (synthetic crops in a held-out face, from held-out booklets) among 11 candidates, the 9 snapshots, the training-best checkpoint and the final model. Then HeOCR's evaluation chose it as heocr's default for modern print in a pre-registered default-model study (2026-11-19). The study compared it with stock heb and the other arm, inside heocr, on HeOCR's open synthetic document sets, and on real-print development line sets. These sets made the choice, so no figure from them is reported here. Check numbers that matter. No held-out run has measured how well it reads numbers on real office documents.
evidence_items.title: Hebrew office and modern-print recognition for Tesseract, fine-tuned from tessdata_best heb on synthetic office pages, born-digital and scanned Reshumot lines (HeOCR modern-v1)

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) models enable efficient test-time adaptation by leveraging expert demonstrations as additional context without updating model parameters. However, even when retrieved demonstrations are relevant to the current task, the VLA may fail to effectively utilize the retrieved information, ultimately leading to task failure. To address this challenge, we propose R2-VLA, a risk-controlled retrieval-augmented VLA framework that enables reliable test-time adaptation by satisfying a user-specified task success rate requirement with minimal expert assistance. Specifically, R2-VLA learns an uncertainty predictor that estimates the uncertainty of the VLA's predicted actions given the retrieved demonstrations, guiding when to act autonomously or request expert assistance. We further introduce a task-level risk-control procedure that calibrates the uncertainty threshold to satisfy a user-specified task-failure risk requirement. Moreover, R2-VLA continually incorporates expert corrections into its retrieval memory to improve future adaptation while preserving the prescribed task-level risk guarantee. Experiments across three VLA backbones and four LIBERO benchmark suites demonstrate that R2-VLA improves average task success by 9.2--11.2 percentage points, achieving the desired target with fewer expert requests. These results highlight the effectiveness of connecting the usefulness of retrieved demonstrations with task-level risk control to enable successful robotic manipulation.
evidence_items.title: Risk-Controlled Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models

evidence_items.summary: Current leading video generation models can synthesize highly realistic videos, while still frequently violating physical and logical constraints in multi-step reasoning and planning, even after training with large-scale reasoning data or existing diffusion RL methods. We attribute these failures to the conventional video training paradigm, which treats a solution as a fixed-length clip rather than a chain of decisions. We present ViDecide, a decision-centric framework that trains video diffusion models to predict state transitions causally and decide when to stop, with a decision-focused training schedule. We further propose Corrective Fine-tuning (CFT), which corrects failed decisions by mapping their noise to the model's own successful continuations, achieving stable improvement without policy-gradient optimization. Across abstract games, planning tasks, and a new benchmark of multi-step robot planning, ViDecide achieves an average strict success rate of 83.8%, far above 23.3% for standard fine-tuning and 67.8% for the strongest prior method, and generalizes to larger puzzles and unseen layouts. Our framework therefore unlocks greater potential for video generation models as reliable reasoners and planners in the visual world. Project page: https://kevin-thu.github.io/ViDecide.
evidence_items.title: ViDecide: Teaching Video Diffusion Models to Reason and Plan Step by Step

evidence_items.summary: Recalling where and when an object was last seen and who saw it requires recognizing it across days and people. Existing long-video benchmarks focus on events, object categories, or relative locations, leaving instance-level spatial memory largely untested in multimodal models. To address this gap, we present EgoWitness, a benchmark for instance-level spatial memory and reasoning in egocentric video. Its 8,453 human-verified questions span approximately 324 hours of week-long and short-horizon recordings and test seven abilities, from recognizing an object or room to recalling who saw it and reasoning about room visits. Over one million reviewed masks of 34 registered landmarks and 21 movable-object labels are linked through room timelines. Among twelve direct vision-language models (VLMs), open-weight models reach at most 46.97% accuracy, and none exceeds 35% on identifying who saw an object last. We therefore propose EgoClue, a spatial-memory agent that retrieves candidate intervals, verifies instance identity, and computes spatial and temporal relations with five tools. Two-stage training with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises its 4B controller from 23.64% to 72.65% accuracy on 1,320 held-out questions. Evidence-trace synthesis matches the best direct VLM at 74.85% on week-long questions and achieves 80.56% in environments excluded from training.
evidence_items.title: EgoWitness: Benchmarking Instance-Level Spatial Memory and Reasoning in Egocentric Video Streams

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Radiation Therapy (RT) scheduling requires coordination of clinical constraints and operational objectives. Large language models (LLMs) may provide a natural‐language interface for generating candidate schedules. Purpose To evaluate the feasibility of using an existing LLM to generate RT patient schedules under clinical and operational constraints through simulation and retrospective clinical comparison. Methods A one‐year, three‐linear‐accelerator (LINAC) simulation included 1400 new patients across 12 treatment categories modeled after clinical practice. Structured prompts supplied ChatGPT with patient data, the current schedule state, clinical rules, and scenario‐specific objectives. Performance was evaluated across scenarios addressing weekly treatment‐time consistency, LINAC continuity, gap‐constrained temporal relaxation, and infeasible request handling. LLM‐generated schedules were benchmarked against heuristic and CP‐SAT schedules under two objective settings. A six‐week retrospective comparison evaluated 2043 appointments against a clinical schedule. Results The LLM‐generated schedules satisfied the predefined feasibility rules in all evaluated scenarios. Across scenarios, 98.6%–98.8% of evaluated fractions remained within the preferred treatment‐time window. Adding a LINAC‐continuity objective reduced the LINAC switch rate from 52.4 2.6% to 9.4 0.6%, and gap‐constrained temporal relaxation reduced daily gap to 47.1 8.5 min and Friday gap to 89.2 18.4 min while maintaining low overtime. In infeasible request tests, the framework identified predefined constraint violations and returned interpretable corrective suggestions. The optimization benchmarks also generated feasible schedules, but their results showed strong objective‐weight trade‐offs.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating a large language model for radiotherapy patient scheduling under realistic clinical and operational constraints: A feasibility study

evidence_items.summary: We present Piccolo, a family of multimodal decision models (0.8B to 27B) that coevolves model capabilities and training data via Agentic Data Engineering and recursive self-improvement (RSI). The models predict probabilities over candidate answers for general-purpose text and visual judgments, agent harnesses, data workflows, and interactive games. Piccolo-27B tops the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard with a score of 75.59, while Piccolo-9B and Piccolo-4B achieve 68.35 and 67.46, respectively. All three rank first on the Private benchmark in their respective model-size categories. Research agents analyze model behavior, construct training data, conduct experiments, and use the results to refine subsequent proposals. Semantic slices and a shared research memory connect these actions across the model family's development. With training recipes comprising hundreds of thousands of examples, data selection and feedback-driven refinement are central to the self-improvement process. Our large-scale RSI exploration yields three counter-intuitive insights for decision-model development: (1) Backbone-recipe co-adaptation outweighs raw model recency: earlier backbones can surpass newer generations on visual tasks under identical recipes; (2) Targeted data curation enables 4B-9B models to rival 27B baselines on specialized workflows; and (3) Continuous loss reduction can decouple from and even degrade discrete decision accuracy. Together with the released weights and tools from the Data-Juicer and AgentScope ecosystems, Piccolo provides an actionable blueprint for building frontier decision models and scaling data-driven RSI.
evidence_items.title: Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement

evidence_items.summary: Machine-learning prediction of antibody-antigen binding affinity depends as much on the training data as on the model, yet public affinity measurements are scattered across databases with incompatible formats, mix genuine dissociation constants with censored or predicted values, and concentrate most of their label mass on a few heavily mutated targets. We present GRABS (Geometric Resource for Antibody Binding Studies), a curated, content-addressed, structure-ready dataset that consolidates nine public sources, of which the seven with redistributable licenses yield 4,380 canonical antibody-antigen records} (median-collapsed from 4,761 raw measurements), each with an experimentally measured dissociation constant (K d ), paired heavy and light variable regions (VH, VL), and an antigen sequence, covering 2,015 distinct antigen sequences. Every structure, graph, and feature is addressed by a content key, md5(VH+VL+antigen)[:10], and verified non-circularly: each graph's node features are decoded back to sequence and re-hashed, matching the content key for 4,282/4,282 (100%) structure-backed records. This integrity is load-bearing: an alignment ablation shows that a previously-reported strong cross-target result (R 2 ≈ 0.415) was a misalignment-mediated source/batch leak that content-key regeneration dissolves. On the resulting leak-free, antigen-cluster-grouped benchmark, cross-target ranking of variants of a held-out antigen collapses to the noise floor (within-held-out-antigen Spearman ρ ≈ 0 for every model family: sequence, structure, and folding-confidence), with structure giving no advantage, a rigorously leakage-controlled quantification of the limited reach of current methods.
evidence_items.title: GRABS: a content-addressed antibody-antigen binding-affinity dataset with predicted structures and a leak-free benchmark
