evidence_items.summary: Simulated manipulation benchmarks measure policy performance using hand-written success checkers that label each episode as a success or failure. Passing an expert demonstration shows that a checker accepts one way of completing the task. Learned policies, however, may stop after partial progress or complete the task in a different way. A checker may then accept an incomplete execution (phantom success) or reject an execution that satisfies the instruction (silent failure). In this paper, we introduce SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions. SimAudit analyzes the instruction and checker code to identify scenarios where the two may disagree, recreates those scenarios in simulation, and runs the original checker. Multi-view renderings are then used to verify whether the observed behavior satisfies the instruction. Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict. Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures. Most defects in RoboCasa365 accepted incomplete executions, most in RoboDojo rejected valid executions, and both error types were common in RoboTwin 2.0. These findings suggest that validating success checkers requires testing both incomplete executions and valid alternatives to expert demonstrations, and motivate more rigorous evaluation protocols for future benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Phantom Success, Silent Failure: Auditing the Success Checkers of Simulated Manipulation Benchmarks

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.
evidence_items.title: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Video rough-cut is a core stage in media production workflows, organizing raw media materials into an initial video cut. Despite recent advances in large vision-language models (LVLMs) for video-related tasks, automatic rough-cut remains underexplored, without a comprehensive benchmark for evaluation or mature workflows for producing executable cut plans. To address the evaluation gap, we introduce RoughCut-Bench, which covers two practical settings: (1) a visually driven setting over video cases, covering highlight detection and selection, source-video ordering, and adherence to user requirements when provided; and (2) a speech-driven setting over automatic speech recognition (ASR) transcripts, covering filler removal, expression deduplication, and low-value content trimming. Across these settings, the benchmark contains 101 visually driven cases, including 831 raw videos with 1,476 highlight annotations. It also includes 84 speech-driven cases, each consisting of an ASR transcript with annotated cleanup spans. The evaluation compares cut plans with these annotations in both settings and additionally uses a human-aligned agentic evaluator to assess rendered-cut quality in the visual setting. To apply LVLMs to automatic rough-cut, we further propose agentic workflows that guide them to produce structured cut plans from input materials. Experiments show that current LVLMs remain limited in producing expert-aligned cut plans. Our benchmark, code, and prompts are released at https://whalesong-zrs.github.io/RoughCut-Bench-Project-Page.
evidence_items.title: RoughCut-Bench: A Benchmark for Automatic Video Rough-Cut with Large Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Faithfulness Video Score (FVSCORE), a neuro-symbolic framework for specification-driven video generation evaluation. Existing evaluators rely on holistic MLLM judgments or vision-language metrics, yet aligning their scores with human judgments and tracing them to specific temporal violations remain open challenges. FVSCORE addresses these limitations by compiling each video into explicit propositions capturing prompt requirements and implicit propositions capturing unstated physical, temporal, and cross-modal constraints. It grounds each proposition using specialized perceptual tools and evaluates the resulting confidence traces with soft temporal operators inspired by Linear Temporal Logic. A Significance-Aware Calibration step then aligns verification with human perception by retaining only perceptually significant violations before producing a timestamp- and evidence-grounded report. We conduct extensive experiments across public and complex multi-event benchmarks with the strongest video models to date, demonstrating that FVSCORE outperforms holistic and agent-based evaluators in human correlation while providing highly accurate and interpretable feedback.
evidence_items.title: FVScore: Specification-Driven Neuro-Symbolic Video Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Fine-grained questions about long videos ask how many times an action occurs, in what order events unfold, or exactly when a state changes. Answering them can require finding brief moments scattered across hours of footage. Agentic models that decide when and where to look promise to find these moments, yet this ability is hard both to measure and to learn. Sparse supporting evidence may establish that an action occurred without establishing its total count; verifying timeline-wide claims requires checking for missed occurrences and double counting. Answer-only supervision, in turn, does not explicitly supervise the search for evidence. We present NexSight, which builds verifiable tasks to both evaluate and train agentic long-video understanding. Its agentic pipeline, SightForge, accepts a task only if a verifier blind to the draft answer can reconstruct it from evidence densely reacquired from the raw video and counterexample checks fail to refute it. This yields SightLine, 310 evidence-traceable tasks from 108 long videos, evaluated through SightLoop, a shared multiscale harness supporting temporal exploration, local inspection, evidence integration, and revisiting while recording returned observations. On disjoint videos, solver trajectories on verified tasks become step-level supervision for observation decisions. The strongest model reaches only 54.52% on SightLine, yet 79.35% when given the annotated evidence. With under 6K examples, Sight-35B nearly doubles its base model's interactive accuracy (21.29% to 42.26%), outperforms the 397B model of its family, begins using explicit spatial inspection after post-training, which its base model never uses, and gains over 8 points on two external long-video benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: NexSight: Verifiable Tasks for Fine-Grained Agentic Long-Video Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Code-search benchmarks show dense encoders well ahead of BM25, yet coding agents do well with grep. What does this dense advantage measure? Existing benchmarks cannot tell: they use curated queries, old code and a handicapped BM25. To find out, we build Repo-Premium, a realistic repository-level code-search benchmark. It ranks files in real repositories, with curated and raw queries in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust and Java, pull requests from 2022 to 2026, and a preregistered test pool over 91 repositories. Our experiments trace the advantage to two sources: evaluation choices that favor dense retrieval, such as splitting files into chunks for BM25 and counting edited tests as relevant, and queries that lack the code's rare identifiers. Expanding the query with LLM-written identifiers (generate-then-grep) helps BM25 far more than dense retrieval, letting it match dense retrieval in every Python pool, even on pull requests opened after the LLM was released. No method we tried predicts which retriever will win on a given query. From these results we derive three guidelines: measure dense gains against a fair lexical baseline, fuse dense retrieval with BM25, and add the code's words to queries that lack them.
evidence_items.title: Embeddings vs. Grep: Rethinking the Dense Advantage in Code Search

evidence_items.summary: We present CompoundingKernel, a self-improving agent system that writes GPU kernels by search. As of 2026-11-11, its generated kernels rank #1 on the public L1, L2 and Quantization boards of SOL-ExecBench (NVIDIA B200). They have held #1 on L1 since 2026-10-27, albeit a short loss on 2026-11-07. All 235 problems have a site-verified correct kernel; on the 209 public-board problems they are 4.40x faster than the benchmark's reference baseline. The search starts from zero: agents get each problem's PyTorch definition but no reference kernels or official scores. A per-problem archive outside the model holds every correct kernel and its lineage. An LLM controller reads it, picks a parent or a new design, and gives each parallel child agent one direction. Checks outside the model decide correctness. At equal wall time, it beat a coded UCB style tree on 35 of 38 problems by making 2.4x as many correct attempts. Over a thousand agents ran at once, and one warm restart fix raised their evaluation rate 3.6x. We find that the rate of reliable measurements, not the number of agents, limits how far such a search scales. Our code and kernels are available on URL.
evidence_items.title: CompoundingKernel: Self-Improving from Zero to First

evidence_items.summary: AI agents are increasingly equipped with persistence toward task completion to run delegated work autonomously for long periods, under many unstated constraints from internal documents and other people's authority. When completion requires violating a rule, the agent must decide alone, yet benchmarks of instruction-rule conflicts state the rule in the prompt or keep it hidden and do not evaluate persistence. We present Unfinished-Bench, a benchmark that gives models persistence in autonomous runs without a user, in realistic work environments with embedded rules. In each of its 97 scenarios across 7 organizations and 7 risk categories, the goal and the rule cannot both hold. We find that persistence raised violations of a rule in an internal document from 32.2% to 43.6%, five times the 8.5% for the same rule stated by the user. Of the document-rule violations, 98.3% occurred after the rule was displayed, and in 89% of a judged sample the agent first wrote down the rule. Violations of rules placed in the environment without user oversight can lead to serious incidents, so persistence-driven risks need to be evaluated. Benchmark documentation: https://francis21c.github.io/unfinished-bench/
evidence_items.title: Unfinished-Bench: Measuring Rule Violations by Persistent Agents in Realistic Work Environments

evidence_items.summary: Concurrent defects in rotating components produce overlapping vibration components, complicating the recognition of defect combinations absent from training. We formulate this task as compositional multi-label learning and propose a compositional evidence-grounded framework (CEG-LLM). The model uses a frozen large language model as a sequence encoder, with trainable low-rank adapters and four sigmoid defect outputs. Continuous waveform tokens and nominal characteristic-order descriptors represent the signal, while a four-node composition graph conditions label-wise attention. Spectral alignment and compositional regularization guide training, and a fixed template links predictions to structured signal records. On one dataset collected from a rotating component at 1500 rpm, CEG-LLM achieves an observed-state macro-F1 of 0.941. Corresponding values are 0.922 for a one-dimensional vision Transformer (ViT), 0.912 for a signal-to-text language encoder, and 0.900 for a convolutional neural network (CNN). Mean exact match across six withheld defect pairs is 0.767, and macro-F1 at −3 dB is 0.819. A top-token versus random-mask deletion contrast of 0.207 indicates sensitivity to the selected representation under that intervention. These results assess recognition of unseen defect combinations and representation sensitivity within the evaluated operating condition.
evidence_items.title: Evidence-Grounded Multi-Label Learning with a Large Language Model for Compound Defect Detection in Rotating Components

evidence_items.summary: Elevator fault diagnosis is a safety-critical problem that requires capabilities beyond isolated fault classification, including knowledge grounding and structured reasoning for maintenance support. In this work, we present a benchmark for elevator fault diagnosis and organize evaluation into three complementary task groups: (A) sensor-based fault detection and classification, (B) taxonomy-grounded fault classification and cause identification, and (C) reasoning with incomplete or constrained information. To enable reproducible comparison across heterogeneous model families, we standardize task definitions, input/output formats, and scoring protocols and report component-level predictive metrics. Experiments across representative language models show task-dependent performance: higher performance on one task does not necessarily transfer to another. The benchmark is a reproducible testbed for studying diagnostic-assistance methods, not a validation of safe operational deployment.
evidence_items.title: A benchmark for elevator fault diagnosis: Multi-level tasks from perception to diagnostic reasoning

organizations: Department of Computer Engineering, Bitlis Eren University, 13100 Bitlis, Türkiye
evidence_items.summary: Remaining useful life (RUL) models are evaluated mainly on clean sensor data, whereas deployed monitoring systems lose channels and receive plausible but erroneous values when a sensor freezes, drifts, becomes noisy or spikes. Nine model families were evaluated on the four Commercial Modular Aero-Propulsion System Simulation (C-MAPSS) subsets, and five of them on PHM08, under a deterministic protocol of 24 corruption scenarios, one fault family withheld from training and the clean condition. The root mean square error (RMSE) increased on average by up to 24% under single-sensor drift and by 49–121% under unseen spikes. The robustness of a gated recurrent encoder was traced to the training regime. The coverage of conformalised 90% prediction intervals fell to 70–82% under spikes while the mean interval width of the deep models changed by less than 3%. Since missing entries were tolerated far better than spiked or drifting ones, a detect-then-mask repair was developed that masks entries flagged by clean-data statistics. Applied to 360 saved C-MAPSS checkpoints without retraining, it reduced RMSE under unseen spikes by 30% and under strong drift by 26% at a clean-data cost of 0.04 cycles, and with Mondrian recalibration it restored the coverage under spikes to 89%.
evidence_items.title: Silent Sensor Faults in Remaining Useful Life Prediction: A Robustness Benchmark, Uncertainty Audit and Model-Agnostic Input Repair

evidence_items.summary: Convolutional recurrent networks are widely reported as being able to forecast process temperature in machining accurately. Many such evaluations, however, split overlapping sliding windows at random, which lets near-duplicate samples cross the train–test boundary. We re-examine process temperature forecasting and soft sensing on the AI4I 2020 benchmark under a leakage-controlled protocol: a chronological split with a purge gap, training-only scaling, five seeds, block-bootstrap confidence intervals and Diebold–Mariano tests with an autocorrelation-robust variance. LSTM, GRU, CNN-LSTM and an attention-augmented CNN-LSTM are compared with persistence, linear, random forest and multilayer-perceptron baselines that receive the same ten-record window. Under a random split the attention model reaches R2=0.899±0.006; under the chronological split it falls to 0.305±0.089. Rolling-origin cross-validation, a purge-gap sweep, a factorial ablation and sensitivity analyses support this picture. In soft sensing, the error is dominated by a drifting process–air temperature offset that the machine signals in this benchmark do not observe, and refitting on recent data matters more than architecture. When lagged process temperature is available, persistence (MAE 0.054 K) is not beaten at horizons of 1–30 records, and convolutional and attention stages add no benefit while costing up to 2.4 times the training time of a plain LSTM. On this benchmark, the evaluation protocol changed the conclusions more than did the choice of architecture. Claimed gains of deep sequence models for machine monitoring should therefore be reported against persistence and information-matched baselines under a time-ordered split.
evidence_items.title: Leakage-Controlled Evaluation of CNN-LSTM Models for Process Temperature Forecasting and Soft Sensing in Machining: Evidence from the AI4I 2020 Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Machine learning systems are increasingly required to be multi-layered for software engineering validation protocols, and multiple checks are imposed instead of just one. Many important failure modes, such as deep class imbalance, poor probability calibration, ungrounded execution, and ”attributional” issues, come to a head in low-level deployments, such as automated code generation, credit underwriting, and clinical triage, where failures can be devastating. In clinical triage, credit underwriting, and the automated generation of code situations that are of a high stakes regularly show up critical failure modes such as severe class imbalance, poor probability calibration, unfaithful attribution, and ungrounded execution, for which standard k-fold cross-validation and regularized baselines are entirely inadequate. By combining the findings from 41 empirical studies, this review identifies three main levels of architecture: data leakage prevention and baseline benchmarking (Level 1), post-hoc interpretability audits and glass-box comparisons (Level 2), and distribution-free uncertainty quantification (Level 3). It is particularly important to note that a meta-analysis of 297 financial machine learning papers reveals a general disregard for diagnosis; only 7.1% of the papers examined included Remove and Retrain (ROAR) benchmarks for testing the faithfulness of the explanations, whereas 93.9% used TreeSHAP for feature attribution. The existence of multi-tier verification frameworks is especially important in order to prevent silent failure modes in safetycritical software systems, as these findings demonstrate. Class-conditional Mondrian conformal calibration answers the Minority Coverage Collapse Theorem, recovering +61.7 percentage points of minority coverage (p < 10 −80 ), and pairs with conformalized quantile regression and cost-optimal selective human deferral (θ ∗ = ch/CFN).
evidence_items.title: Machine Learning Validation Pipelines: From Tabular Benchmarking to Conformal Calibration and Execution-Grounded Agentic Testing

organizations: Boston Children's Hospital; Harvard Medical School
evidence_items.summary: Background Misdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis of children in pediatric emergency departments lead to complications, and are particularly problematic in settings with limited pediatric expertise. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in diagnostic reasoning for adult emergency department patients, but utility for pediatric cases is largely untested. Methods Retrospective study of patients seen in the emergency department of a major urban pediatric academic medical center and subsequently admitted to the operating room or inpatient service. Records from 100 patients were randomly selected, stratified by age. We compared the accuracy of differential diagnoses (up to five, ranked by likelihood) generated by an LLM agent, Dr CaBot (one configuration with literature search, the other without), with those of four attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians (diagnosticians), all masked to outcome. Encounters were presented to diagnosticians stepwise across four touchpoints: triage, the initial physician evaluation (the a priori primary touchpoint), the full emergency department encounter, and the admission. Ground truth diagnosis was determined by two independent, board-certified pediatric emergency physicians (reviewers) based on the entire clinical encounter. The reviewers, masked to source, then assigned each differential a Bond score (0 to 5; 4 or above was high-scoring). Findings The median patient age was 4 years and 41% had a complex chronic condition. Bond score agreement between the two reviewers had a weighted kappa of 0.64. For the primary comparison at the initial physician evaluation touchpoint, the LLM agent and the diagnosticians both achieved high-scoring differentials in 95% of cases (difference 0%, 95%CI: -5.8, 5.8%). No differences were detected at the other touchpoints.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI versus pediatric emergency physicians for differential diagnosis of acutely ill and injured children

evidence_items.summary: Historical snapshot of the nominal catch datasets compiled by the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission (IOTC) Secretariat and made available to the Working Party on Tropical Tunas (WPTT) in 2020. The datasets cover the period 1950–2019. Two complementary datasets are provided: Best scientific estimates ( IOTC-LATEST-NC-ALL-1950-2019.zip ): Annual catches in live-weight equivalent for the 16 IOTC species, aggregated by year, IOTC statistical area and fishing fleet, and fully disaggregated by species and fishing gear. These estimates incorporate additional information and adjustments made by the Secretariat to address known limitations in the reported data, including the estimation of species and gear composition. Raw nominal catch estimates ( IOTC-LATEST-NC-SCI-1950-2019.zip ): Annual catches in live-weight equivalent for all species for which catch information was available to the Secretariat, aggregated by year, IOTC statistical area and fishing fleet. In addition to data submitted by IOTC Contracting Parties and Cooperating Non-Contracting Parties (CPCs), the dataset may include estimates derived from ancillary sources, such as the FAO global capture production database, or imputed from historical catch records to address gaps in reporting. These procedures aim to improve the completeness of the dataset, although gaps may remain where insufficient information is available. The original ZIP archives are provided together with the accompanying WPTT working paper ( IOTC-2020-WPTT22DP-08 ), documenting the status of IOTC fisheries statistics in 2020. This historical release is archived to support the traceability and reproducibility of scientific analyses using IOTC nominal catch data, including stock assessments and catch limit calculations. The datasets reflect the information available at the time of their release and may differ from subsequent versions following revisions, corrections, or additional data submissions.
evidence_items.title: IOTC nominal catch dataset – WPTT 2020

evidence_items.summary: This thesis examines the linguistic, semantic, and cultural characteristics of English proverbs used to evaluate people's intellectual abilities and inner world. Particular attention is paid to the ways in which traditional proverbial expressions represent intelligence, wisdom, ignorance, emotional maturity, honesty, kindness, and moral values. The study approaches proverbs not merely as fixed linguistic units but as reflections of human experience, social expectations, and cultural attitudes towards personality. It also explores the role of proverbial language in expressing collective judgments about individual behaviour and intellectual potential. The research demonstrates that English proverbs preserve important ethical and cognitive concepts while reflecting the relationship between individual characteristics and social values.
evidence_items.title: ENGLISH PROVERBS EVALUATING PEOPLE'S INTELLECTUAL ABILITIES AND INNER WORLD

The annotations were prepared by Apostolos Vlachos for the session From Traces to Claims: Making Archaeological Inference Explicit in Linked Data Practice , at the 12th Linked Pasts Symposium, University of Porto, November 2026. The original 3D model was produced by Dr Hugo Anderson-Whymark and published on Sketchfab. The annotations contribute to the critical examination of a developing methodological framework addressing evidential constraint, validation tolerance, inferential scope, traceability, and inferential depth.

evidence_items.summary: The fall armyworm, Spodoptera frugiperda, poses a significant threat to global food security, causing substantial damage to maize, rice, sorghum, and sugarcane across 353 plant species. While Telenomus remus shows promise as an egg parasitoid for biological control due to its high fecundity and ability to parasitize multilayered egg masses, its short shelf life limits practical application in mass production systems. This case study explores how researchers developed cold storage protocols to stabilize production and supply of this important biological control agent. Through systematic testing of viable and UV-treated S. frugiperda eggs stored at 4°C, 7°C, and 10°C for varying durations and evaluation of parasitized eggs at different developmental stages under similar storage temperature conditions, the study demonstrates that viable S. frugiperda eggs remained suitable hosts after 7 days of storage at 4°C and 7°C, while parasitized eggs at 7 days post-parasitism could be stored at 10°C for up to 14 days without significant viability loss. These findings provide a foundation for large-scale production systems that can supply parasitoids to regions severely affected by fall armyworm infestations.
evidence_items.title: Cold Storage Optimization for Parasitoid Mass Production: A Telenomus remus Case Study

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are growing increasingly powerful. Yet, fundamental constraints on the reasoning, memory, and performance of individual models has sparked recent interest in scaling abilities using LLM teams. With growing deployment of LLM teams at scale, there is a need for principled guidelines for when teams help, how many agents to use, and how structure impacts performance. Rather than building these teams through trial-and-error, we propose using distributed systems as a formal foundation for designing and evaluating LLM teams. Under this formal framework, we derive predictions about how task structure and team architecture should shape performance. Empirical evidence supports these predictions: LLM team scaling follows classical distributed computing laws based on the structure of a task, and centralized and decentralized architectures exhibit the asymmetric vulnerabilities predicted by distributed systems theory. These results establish distributed computing as a generative framework that yields testable, quantitative predictions about LLM team behavior and informs the construction of more efficient and capable teams.
evidence_items.title: Language model teams as distributed systems

evidence_items.summary: This dataset supports fluorescence lifetime imaging of epithelial metabolism in living intestinal organoids. It includes NAD(P)H intensity and lifetime measurements across the crypt–villus axis, lineage-enriched cultures and metabolic perturbations, together with measurements from fluorescent reporters and probes. Files are organized by figure and panel. The archive contains selected microscope-exported channel images and acquisition metadata, GSLab intensity and phasor exports, segmentation inputs and masks, pixel- and object-level measurements, source tables and statistical outputs. Start with metadata/panel index.csv to find a figure, metadata/file manifest.csv to locate its inputs and metadata/missing inputs.csv to check coverage. The archive uses the figure identifiers recorded when the files were assembled. The companion analysis repository provides Python workflows, MATLAB spatial analysis scripts and figure-specific parameters. The transcriptomic score tables use public mouse organoid datasets GSE164638 and GSE165092. The original sequencing data are available through NCBI GEO.
evidence_items.title: Data for "NAD(P)H-FLIM reveals spatial and temporal epithelial metabolic heterogeneity in live intestinal organoids"

evidence_items.summary: The Institutional Image-Function Attribution Divergence Theory (IIFADT) is a proposed conditional domain-general framework for explaining how the socially established image of a wider institution, system, or recognizable field may influence an observer's interpretation of individuals, representatives, processes, and functional nodes associated with that system. The theory begins with a distinction: the image of a larger system is not necessarily identical to the actual function of every person or component connected with it. An observer may nevertheless use the system's image as a basis for interpreting an associated node. When that image-based interpretation produces an attribution that differs meaningfully from the available evidence of the node's actual function, a divergence may emerge between actual and attributed functional identity. The primary explanatory case concerns a statistical researcher working in a gambling-related field. The researcher collects and analyzes statistical information, but an observer may interpret the researcher's role through the social image of the field rather than through the researcher's actual work. The case is used to distinguish functional misattribution, evaluative spillover, and evidence-based reassessment as separate processes. IIFADT introduces the Institutional Image-to-Node Projection Mechanism (IINPM) as its central process. Its proposed architecture contains twenty layers, seven core propositions, ten research hypotheses, and five outcome classes. The framework separates image availability, observer-level image activation, system-node association, image projection, functional attribution, attribution divergence, and possible downstream outcomes. Mathematical representations are proposed for institutional image, association, image influence, probabilistic functional attribution, attribution divergence, evaluative spillover, decision uncertainty, and feedback.
evidence_items.title: THE INSTITUTIONAL IMAGE-FUNCTION ATTRIBUTION DIVERGENCE THEORY (IIFADT): A CONDITIONAL DOMAIN-GENERAL THEORY OF INSTITUTIONAL IMAGE PROJECTION, FUNCTIONAL ATTRIBUTION, AND INDIVIDUAL-SYSTEMIC DIVERGENCE

evidence_items.summary: Digital tools for language learning are spreading rapidly in primary schools, yet most ready-made resources for Russian were designed for children who already speak Russian and ignore the typical difficulties of learners whose first language is Uzbek. This article presents a system of digital exercises for teaching Russian as a second language in Grades 1–4 of Uzbek-medium schools, built on a contrastive analysis of the two languages. The study followed a design-based research approach that combined theoretical analysis, contrastive analysis of Uzbek and Russian, expert evaluation of digital tools against a ten-criterion checklist, and iterative classroom implementation. The resulting system comprises 28 exercises arranged in three stages (preparatory, conditional-communicative and communicative) and covers phonetics, vocabulary, grammar and the four language skills. Each exercise targets a specific interference point, such as the hard–soft consonant opposition, the vowel [ы], grammatical gender and agreement, prepositions with case forms, and visually confusable Latin and Cyrillic letters. The system is designed to work under three levels of school equipment ("one screen", "group screens" and "one device per pupil") and limits continuous individual screen time to seven minutes. The article argues that the value of digital resources in early second-language teaching depends less on the technology itself than on how precisely the tasks address learners' cross-linguistic difficulties.
evidence_items.title: INTERFERENCE-ORIENTED DIGITAL EXERCISES FOR TEACHING RUSSIAN AS A SECOND LANGUAGE TO UZBEK-SPEAKING PRIMARY SCHOOL PUPILS

evidence_items.summary: Cloud computing has become the default delivery model for enterprise, government and consumer services because of its elasticity, pay-per-use economics and global reach. The same properties, namely multi-tenancy, resource pooling, internet-facing management interfaces and shared responsibility between provider and customer, enlarge the attack surface and blur accountability. This paper presents a structured review of cybersecurity challenges in cloud computing and of the solutions proposed in the literature and in industry guidance. Threats are organised along the three service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) and along five cross-cutting concerns: data security and privacy, identity and access management, virtualization and multi-tenancy, application and interface security, and governance and compliance. Each threat class is mapped to technical and organisational countermeasures, including encryption and searchable or homomorphic schemes, attribute-based access control, multi-factor authentication, Zero Trust architecture, micro-segmentation, remote data auditing, intrusion detection, secure DevOps and continuous compliance monitoring. A layered defence framework with a misconfiguration-focused feedback loop is proposed, together with an evaluation plan for future empirical validation. The paper is a secondary-source, literature-based study; no new experimental measurements are claimed, and no vendor is endorsed. The findings are intended as a reference for students, practitioners and researchers planning secure cloud adoption.
evidence_items.title: Cybersecurity Challenges and Solutions in Cloud Computing

evidence_items.summary: Students ’ ability to demonstrate second-language knowledge in a classroom does not always match what they can retrieve during private study. Speaking tasks are especially sensitive to social evaluation, time pressure, uncertainty, and the learner ’ s interpretation of bodily arousal. Although research has separately examined stress and memory, foreign-language anxiety, working memory, and interoception, these strands are not yet routinely integrated into classroom-level models of moment-to-moment speaking performance. This conceptual article proposes an interoceptive – affective calibration framework: a model in which learners interpret internal bodily signals (such as changes in heart rate, breathing, muscle tension, and visceral sensation), appraise the situation, and allocate attention between communicative goals and self-monitoring. The framework does not assume that bodily arousal is inherently harmful. Instead, it proposes that performance depends partly on whether arousal is interpreted as manageable activation or as evidence of threat, and on whether learners can redirect attention toward meaning and retrieval. The article synthesises relevant work on stress and memory, second-language anxiety, cognitive load, emotion regulation, and interoceptive awareness. It identifies a research opportunity at the intersection of these fields and outlines testable hypotheses, feasible classroom measures, and ethical considerations. The proposed model is intended to guide empirical investigation rather than to present untested mechanisms as established facts.
evidence_items.title: Interoceptive–Affective Calibration in Second-Language Classrooms: A Conceptual Framework for Understanding Speaking Performance

evidence_items.summary: 本書以四言韻文敘述耶穌言行:開篇稱救世耶穌本為神天,因恤世人暫捨本位、代人受難(p005);繼敘五千人隨聽聖理、一時無食,耶穌以五餅二魚飽眾,餘十二筐(p009);稱其講道甚妙(p012);述其至終受死在十字架(p015);再記其教訓門徒、安慰其心,命將其道宣與萬人(p016);末勸未明此理者當求神天光照心性(p018)。依上述頁次,全篇由耶穌的身分與降世,經神蹟、講道、受難,至差遣門徒,終以勸勉讀者作結。館目歸於 David Collie。版次依題封為道光十八年孟冬(1838)新嘉坡堅夏書院藏板。本書可供查考十九世紀華文新教傳教文獻如何以韻文重述福音故事,以及「神天」等譯名用語與四言體例。 本資料集以哈佛燕京藏本 DRS 54467214 為底本,共取 22 幅固定影像,其中 14 幅含正文,提供 JSON、TXT、TEI 和逐項覆核紀錄。此版為 AI 校讀稿,298 項比對中保留 38 項未解。人工全文二校待完成。 This book retells the life and teachings of Jesus in four-character Chinese verse. It opens by declaring that Jesus the Saviour was originally Shentian (God), and that out of compassion for humankind he set aside his place to suffer in their stead (p005). It goes on to the five thousand who followed him to hear the sacred teaching and had nothing to eat, whom he fed with five loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets left over (p009). It praises the excellence of his preaching (p012), recounts his death on the cross (p015), and describes how he taught and comforted his disciples and commanded them to proclaim his way to all people (p016). It closes by urging anyone who does not understand this teaching to pray to Shentian for illumination of heart and mind (p018). Taken in page order, these passages move from Jesus's identity and coming into the world, through miracle, preaching and crucifixion, to the commissioning of the disciples, and end with an exhortation to the reader. The work is attributed to David Collie in the catalog. The title page gives the edition as 道光十八年孟冬(1838)新嘉坡堅夏書院藏板 (early winter of Daoguang 18, 1838; printing blocks held by Jianxia Shuyuan, 新嘉坡 Singapore). The text can be used to study how nineteenth-century Chinese Protestant mission literature retold the gospel story in verse, including its terminology, such as 神天 for God, and its four-character form. The historical work is attributed to David Collie in the catalogue. This dataset uses 22 fixed images, including 14 text-bearing pages, from Harvard-Yenching Library DRS 54467214.

evidence_items.summary: Facial deepfake detectors are usually trained on blending fakes, where a generated face is pasted back into a real frame. Recent generators synthesize the entire face and leave no traces of blending. On a benchmark of 19 datasets released from 2019 to 2026, the best prior facial deepfake detector reaches a mean AUROC of 96.2% on ten blending datasets, but none exceeds 78.1% on five datasets of entire face synthesis (EFS). AI-generated content (AIGC) detectors do not close this gap. We propose TwinD, a detector trained on FaceForensics++ fakes and two kinds of twins: fakes made from a real frame. A reconstruction twin is a real frame reconstructed by an autoencoder, with the real pixels put back in a random region. It targets the neural traces of a decoder. A blob twin blends an altered copy of a real frame with the frame itself, targeting blending artifacts. It needs no generator and no face-shaped mask. Together, these twins provide two complementary forensic cues that generalize to unseen manipulations. TwinDreaches a mean AUROC of 96.3%, 8.9 points above the prior state-of-the-art, with 98.1% on the blending datasets and 95.6% on the EFS datasets. Trained on twins alone, without a deepfake dataset, single models still reach 94.3% on average over three seeds. For reproducibility, the code, trained model, and training data are at: https://github.com/yermandy/TwinD
evidence_items.title: TwinD: Generalizing Deepfake Detection from Blending to Entire Face Synthesis

evidence_items.summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.
evidence_items.title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions

evidence_items.summary: Public brain tumour MRI collections are routinely reported with near-perfect classification accuracy, yet they carry no patient identifiers and their train/test overlap is rarely quantified. We present a duplicate-aware, reproducible frozen-feature benchmark on BRISC 2025 (6000 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted slices; glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumour, no tumour). A perceptual-hash audit found 1352 candidate near-duplicate pairs, with 439 of them crossing the official train/test split, and 104 training images that are pixel-identical to test images; a visual review of sampled pairs showed that most candidates were other slices of the same scan, with an estimated 5–10% false matches. Removing redundant copies and every training image connected to the test set left 5477 images, a split that is duplicate-aware but not patient-independent. Under an identical linear probe, ImageNet-supervised ResNet-18/50 and self-supervised DINOv2 ViT-S/14 were competitive: DINOv2 was numerically ahead (macro-F1 77.3 ± 0.1%, macro-AUROC 93.2%), but no pairwise difference survived Holm correction. In-pool validation overstated official test macro-F1 by 9.7–13.5 points; control experiments showed that this gap is not an artefact of the filtering but mainly reflects a distribution difference between the official partitions. Meningioma recall stayed at 50–53%, and all linear heads were under-confident. We release the splits, audit tables and per-image predictions.
evidence_items.title: Validation Is Not Enough: A Duplicate-Aware, Reproducible Frozen-Feature Benchmark for Brain Tumour MRI Classification on BRISC 2025

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to replace human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statistically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) was introduced for dense settings where all items are annotated by the same annotators. However, in many large-scale annotation settings, items are annotated by different subsets of annotators. We therefore propose the Alternative Annotator Test with Resampled Annotations (AltRA-Test), a statistical test that does not require that all items are annotated by the same annotators. AltRA-Test uses a bootstrap that resamples items, draws k human annotations for each item, and substitutes one of them with an LLM annotation. This produces paired all-human and mixed human-LLM panels. A replacement is supported when the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel is statistically non-inferior to the IAA of the all-human panel, i.e., when the LLM preserves the signal that the human annotators share. We establish that AltRA-Test is a consistent test of asymptotic level alpha. We then evaluate it through simulations and real-world experiments in which we test 18 LLMs and 5 prompting techniques on 20 datasets across text, image, audio, and video. Across these evaluations, about 100 items often suffice for the test. In simulations, where we know whether the LLM is a better or a worse annotator than the humans, AltRA-Test makes more correct replacement decisions than existing baselines. In real-world data experiments, LLMs pass the test in about half of the setups, depending mainly on the task. Since replacement is not always justified, we encourage researchers to test it for their task.
evidence_items.title: AltRA-Test: An Alternative Annotator Test for LLM Judges Without Shared Annotators

evidence_items.summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the stage in which Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) advance their capability to reason over video. However, the VideoLLM also learns to answer from textual regularities of its training data, a shortcut that bypasses the video. The regularities behind the shortcut are hard to define at the data level, and the shortcut forms regardless of training epoch, data size, or backbone. The shortcut is hidden behind a rise in accuracy within the training distribution, yet it is not required for the rise and even costs SFT the gain the video offers under distribution shift. We therefore propose Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO), which intervenes on the fine-tuning update where the shortcut is written rather than on the data. VETO calibrates the subspace that the text alone occupies in the activations of the base model and projects the update onto its orthogonal complement. The VideoLLM is thus left to ground its answer in the full input, with the shortcut suppressed as it forms and never defined. Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves the gain of SFT on the training distribution and suppresses the shortcut. On six benchmarks under shift it gains more than SFT and answers from the full input rather than the shortcut. Code is available at https://github.com/Youngwoo-git/VETO.
evidence_items.title: Suppressing the Shortcut Hidden Behind the Gains of VideoLLM Fine-Tuning

evidence_items.summary: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.
evidence_items.title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience

evidence_items.summary: Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.

evidence_items.summary: Code2Video uses agent-authored 3D proxies to guide video generation, enabling explicit control over structure and dynamics. However, how to construct proxies and prompts for optimal downstream quality remains underexplored, as do the capabilities and limitations of this paradigm. Through controlled experiments and blinded human evaluation, we study proxy granularity, physics simulation, and prompting. The results reveal task-dependent trade-offs: coarse proxies favor natural motion, while medium-grained proxies favor consistency. Physics simulation and proxy-aligned prompting further improve average quality. Guided by these findings, we introduce Coda-DaVinci, a task-adaptive agentic framework for Code2Video generation that selects between proxy-guided and direct generation, adapts modeling granularity to each entity, and coordinates simulation with proxy-grounded prompting. Its multi-agent harness preserves scene assets and guides repairs through visual inspection and independent review. Experiments demonstrate leading instruction following on VTR and scene consistency on R2M, improved physical plausibility over direct generation, and higher visual realism than the compared Code2Video baselines. Long-video evaluations further show gains in event structure and consistency across successive interactions, while revealing limitations in transition stability and adherence to scene settings.
evidence_items.title: Coda-DaVinci: Reimagining Video Generation with Code2Video

evidence_items.summary: Agentic cyber-physical systems rely on perception and state estimation to support autonomous decisions. Degraded, inconsistent, or manipulated sensor observations can therefore propagate through an autonomous pipeline and create security-relevant failures. This work presents a synthetic Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) testbed developed in NVIDIA Isaac Sim for repeatable stress testing of perception and tracking algorithms supporting agentic decision-making. A simplified quadrotor follows scripted trajectories while co-located virtual sensors generate synchronized RGB, RTX LiDAR, and illustrative IR-like observations. The testbed varies target range, motion, clutter, occlusion, and sensor availability, with future stress cases including sensor dropout, temporal misalignment, cross-modal disagreement, and false observations. As an initial exemplar, a nonlinear coordinated-turn Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) is evaluated over a 20-s maneuvering trajectory using LiDAR target-centroid measurements. Position error and uncertainty are compared as LiDAR observations degrade and are lost. The framework provides a reproducible environment for studying how sensing degradation affects downstream autonomous estimation and resilience in agentic C-UAS systems.
evidence_items.title: A Synthetic Multi-Modal Testbed for Security Stress Testing of Agentic Counter-UAS Systems

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Increasingly sophisticated customer needs and regulatory constraints lead to growing complexity in product development. A common solution to manage this complexity is Model‐based Systems Engineering, where activity diagrams contribute to the design of functional architectures. However, their modeling process is time‐consuming and complex, creating the demand for assistance and acceleration. Current methods are limited to basic activity diagrams and overlook architecture definition activities. Moreover, new possibilities through Large Language Models haven't been explored in detail. To address this, a comprehensive three‐part approach using Large Language Models is proposed. The first part defines the use case's behavior with an activity diagram. The second part assigns actions to system functions, starting functional architecture generation. The third part deploys a pipeline to define information exchange between actions across architectural elements. Latter two pipelines use vector databases to reuse existing modeling elements. An preliminary evaluation by expert interviews shows that the proposed approach can offer assistance for manual modeling activities. With that, a step towards a faster and more complete generation of activity diagrams and functional architectures is taken.
evidence_items.title: Leveraging Large Language Models to Model Use Case Behaviors Via Activity Diagrams

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language model (LLM)–powered virtual patient systems are gaining popularity in nursing education but also face persistent challenges, such as hallucinations and role inconsistency. Objective This paper reports the model architecture design, technical considerations, implementation challenges, and evaluation of an LLM-powered AI-assisted simulated-patient system integrated into a nursing triage simulation game. Methods The system integrated a Unity-based game client, with GPT-4o hosted through Microsoft AI Foundry to support real-time simulated-patient dialogue in Traditional Chinese using Cantonese syntax. This developmental study comprised exploratory model selection, formative student feedback–informed enhancement from Version 1 to Version 2, development-stage script-fidelity evaluation, and evaluation of system usability and the Net Promoter Score in 2 tutorial cohorts of nursing students. Results Key technical contributions include a layered hallucination mitigation architecture that combines grounded prompt inclusion, few-shot conversational exemplars, negative role constraints, and calibrated model parameters. In the predefined script-fidelity evaluation, script-inconsistent responses occurred in 78 of 125 (62.4%) Version 1 outputs and 21 of 125 (16.8%) Version 2 outputs—an absolute difference of 45.6 percentage points. The implementation process also addresses stateless API memory management, cloud-based safety filter calibration for domain-specific clinical prompts, and prompt engineering strategies to prevent role drift and hidden scenario information leakage. GPT-4o was selected as the production model through exploratory development testing that considered script consistency, Cantonese-language suitability, response latency, technical reliability, deployment feasibility, cost considerations, and Unity integration compatibility; 45 of 50 (90%) assessed GPT-4o responses were rated fully script-consistent.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model–Powered AI-Assisted Simulated Patient for Nursing Education: Quasi-Experimental Study

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about predictive models, but a fluent answer about a model is not necessarily true of it. We propose a framework in which every answer is checked against a reference that independent software computes from the fitted model. The main finding is simple: the LLM was much more accurate when software had done the calculations than when it had to work them out from the model itself. In a confirmatory study with Gemini 2.5 Flash, the LLM correctly answered 16 of 36 questions whose answer follows exactly from the full model description, such as a prediction or a decision path, but 33 of the same 36 once software had computed the values from which the answer follows. A replication with 50 classifiers, five datasets and three LLM configurations, including a reasoning setting and an open-weight model, reproduced this pattern. Without model information, the LLMs declined to answer or guessed at chance level, and verified answers were reported faithfully once their origin was stated. Model-specific calculations should therefore be left to verified software, while the LLM reports and explains the checked results.
evidence_items.title: From Data to Verified Model Knowledge: How Evidence Access Shapes Large Language Model Answers About Trained Machine-Learning Classifiers

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate other models’ outputs in medicine, an approach known as LLM-as-a-Judge (LaaJ), yet no LaaJ-specific reporting checklist exists. This scoping review included 91 medical LaaJ studies: 69 from 5,571 database records and 22 from a previous review. Judges were mainly used for response evaluation (74.7%), and 76.9% of the studies used at least one proprietary LLM. Agreement with human evaluators was reported in 65.9% of the studies, with widely varying metrics. Based on these findings, this study developed RULE-LLM, a reporting framework of 21 items and eight sub-items across four domains: role and task specification, underlying data and criteria, LLM-Judge design and output, and evaluation of judge performance. Seven experts rated the initial draft (S-CVI/Ave, 0.94), and five independent raters showed substantial agreement when applying the final framework (Fleiss' κ, 0.67; Gwet's AC1, 0.73). RULE-LLM aims to improve the transparency and reproducibility of LaaJ studies.
evidence_items.title: RULE-LLM reporting framework for large language model-as-a-judge evaluation in medicine developed from a scoping review

evidence_items.summary: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Accurate prediction of functional outcomes after acute ischemic stroke can guide clinical decision-making and resource allocation. Prior work has relied predominantly on structured predictors and conventional machine learning, while the ability of large language models (LLMs) to infer modified Rankin Scale (mRS) scores from routine clinical admission notes is largely unexplored. METHODS: We evaluated encoder (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers [BERT], NYUTron) and generative (Llama-3.1-8B, MedGemma-4B) LLMs, in both frozen and fine-tuned settings, for discharge and 90-day mRS prediction. ModernBERT-base was evaluated as a long-context encoder sensitivity analysis. We retrospectively analyzed 9485 admission history and physical notes for discharge prediction and 1898 notes for 90-day prediction from the NYU Langone Get With The Guidelines–Stroke registry (2016-2025). The most recent 12 months were held out for testing. Performance was assessed for binary functional outcome (mRS 0-2 vs 3-6) and compared with structured, hybrid, and clinical risk score baselines. RESULTS: In frozen settings, the clinically pretrained NYUTron encoder outperformed all other models. After fine-tuning, Llama achieved the highest discrimination for discharge (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.84, area under the precision–recall curve 0.81) and 90-day (AUROC 0.87, area under the precision–recall curve 0.84) prediction, while binary accuracy was similar among NYUTron, Llama, and MedGemma. A long-context ModernBERT-base sensitivity analysis did not outperform NYUTron or eliminate differences in exact mRS prediction. For 90-day prediction, fine-tuned Llama outperformed structured (Zhang et al, AUROC 0.82), hybrid (Sung et al, AUROC 0.82), and clinical risk score (Totaled Health Risks in Vascular Events, AUROC 0.80; Stroke Prognostication using Age and NIH Stroke Scale, AUROC 0.79) baselines (all P < .05).
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models Predict Functional Outcomes After Acute Ischemic Stroke

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis (ICI-M) is a rare but often fatal immune-related adverse event. Large language models (LLMs) have provided new opportunities for patient education, yet whether they can effectively support patient education in ICI-M remains unknown. In this study, we submitted 20 standardized ICI-M-related patient questions to five LLMs (ChatGPT-5.5, Gemini-3.5 Flash, DeepSeek-V4, Qwen 3.7, and Doubao), generating 100 responses. Model performance was evaluated using the Global Quality Score (GQS), modified DISCERN (mDISCERN), Quality Analysis of Medical Artificial Intelligence (QAMAI), Ensuring Quality Information for Patients (EQIP), Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool understandability and actionability scores (PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A), and six readability indices. Significant inter-model differences were observed across most quality and readability metrics, and no single model outperformed the others across all dimensions. DeepSeek-V4 achieved the highest mDISCERN score [5.00 (IQR, 4.00–5.00)], whereas ChatGPT-5.5 achieved the highest PEMAT-A score [40.00 (IQR, 35.00–45.00)]. Readability was suboptimal, with a mean FKGL of 16.60 ± 2.64. Correlation analyses demonstrated information quality, usability, and readability represented correlated but distinct evaluation dimensions. While LLMs may serve as adjunctive tools for ICI-M patient education, substantial optimization of content accessibility and actionability is required prior to clinical implementation.
evidence_items.title: Quality, reliability, and readability of large language model responses to questions about immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis: A cross-sectional study

evidence_items.summary: Introduction: What people with kidney concerns or disease and their families struggle with between visits may not surface in clinic. We mapped the needs and burdens they express online by clinical context and author. Methods: A large language model read all 22,170 posts reached by a chronic kidney disease tag or kidney lexicon on a Taiwanese forum and 3 ask-a-physician services (1995-2026), applying a companion friction framework with kidney-specific fields, author (patient or family) and clinical context. A second vendor re-read 11,010 posts; 2 physicians labelled relevance, author and context in 200. Results: Among 6,023 kidney-related posts, the reproducibly measured fields most often voiced on the forum were information needs (79%), emotional burden (48%), system navigation (34%) and worry about progression (24%). After abnormal tests, 54%-56% of posts quoted a laboratory value, nearly always with a question or stated uncertainty; renal-diet burden peaked with diagnosed disease; caregiver burden rose to 29% of dialysis-or-transplantation forum posts. Family-written posts more often voiced navigation difficulty and caregiver burden. Most fields agreed with the second vendor (kappa 0.65-0.98). On the model's labels, family members wrote 25% of forum posts about kidney concerns and 74% about dialysis or transplantation; on a 139-post sample, physicians' labels gave 47%-48% for dialysis or transplantation (model 71%). Conclusion: Kidney-related posts carry context-specific information needs and emotional and practical burdens, many voiced by relatives. They suggest candidate responses (test-result explanation, diet support, family-directed information and support) that need evaluation. Keywords: chronic kidney disease; dialysis; patient experience; caregivers; social media; large language models
evidence_items.title: Patient- and Family-Expressed Needs and Burdens in Kidney-Related Online Discussions in Taiwan: Large Language Model-Based Analysis Across Clinical Contexts

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Reliable preoperative classification and outcome prediction could improve management of locally advanced colorectal cancer. We retrospectively studied 879 participants from two centers, including 741 patients with locally advanced colorectal cancer and 138 with benign colorectal lesions. Clinical, radiomics, deep learning, and early fusion models were trained at center A ( n = 615) and independently tested at center B ( n = 264) using pretreatment contrast-enhanced computed tomography and clinical data. The clinical-radiomics nomogram achieved a test AUC of 0.957 for benign-malignant classification. For 3-year and 5-year overall survival, radiomics achieved test AUCs of 0.874 and 0.898, while fusion achieved 0.870 and 0.899, respectively. These findings identify CT radiomics as a promising digital biomarker for colorectal cancer stratification and show that early deep learning fusion offers limited incremental value over an optimized radiomics baseline.
evidence_items.title: Multicenter evaluation of radiomics and multimodal artificial intelligence for colorectal cancer diagnosis and survival prediction

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping doctoral education, yet few empirically evaluated pedagogical models integrate AI literacy with research and teaching competence. This study examined changes associated with implementing the Dr. I.D.E.A. Model, which positions doctoral candidates who are also university teachers as co-researchers of their own research and teaching practice under an explicit responsible-AI framework. A participatory action research design with convergent triangulation was implemented during the 2025–2026 academic year. Thirty-four doctoral candidates participated in four collaborative virtual workshops organised through cycles of planning, action, observation and critical reflection. Self-report measures administered at three time points were integrated with interviews, focus groups, observation notes, reflective logbooks and independently verified academic products. Self-reported research competence, AI-supported digital competence and creative-pedagogical competence increased significantly between each pair of measurement points (pre–post dₐᵥ = 1.83, 2.10 and 1.69, respectively). All participants integrated generative AI into at least one university course, and 76.5% implemented a sustained course redesign. Because the design lacked a comparison group and relied on perceived competence, maturation, testing effects, response-shift bias and the programme’s ordinary activities may also account for the changes. The findings are therefore associative rather than causal and constitute preliminary evidence that warrants controlled replication in other doctoral contexts.
evidence_items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Doctoral Education: A Participatory Action Research Evaluation of the Dr. I.D.E.A. Model

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The interpretation of neutron scattering data remains a major bottleneck in materials discovery, as it demands an iterative cycle of data reduction, modeling, and refinement. That is too time-consuming for experts and too complex for novices. Here we introduce DrSai-Rongzai, an autonomous agent built on a large language model (LLM) that perfoms joint neutron powder diffraction (NPD) and pair-distribution-function (PDF) analysis without human intervention. Deployed at the China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS), the agent orchestrates established refinement software through a hierarchical “Reasoning + Acting” framework. Its core innovation, Agentic Context Operation (ACO), maintains a coherent ‘working memory’ of file paths, intermediate results, and domain-specific rules across entire processing steps, even when the underlying large language model undergoes context compression. Across reference materials (Si, CsAgTe and Bi2MoO6), the agent refined structural parameters statistically indistinguishable from expert-derived solutions, while requiring markedly fewer iterative cycles. In an exhaustive 18-run factorial ablation study on two high-entropy alloys, we systematically evaluated the MemoWrite and CoreSkillWrite in ACO mechanisms with and without 50k-token context compression, quantifying the necessity of each component. Memo improved both mean composite performance and repeatability even without compression (+ 20.2% and + 11.3%, respectively). Under compression, Memo improved these metrics by + 10.7% and + 17.0%, and retaining CoreSkill provided a further + 12.5% and + 6.6% improvement, yielding a mean composite score of 0.9316 and repeatability stability of 0.9905 for full ACO. The agent is integrated with a permission-controlled CSNS data interface, enabling secure, on-demand analysis of user-proprietary data with automatic archiving.
evidence_items.title: An agentic AI neutron scattering data scientist at the China Spallation Neutron Source

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis relies on computational methods that shape biological conclusions. Developing new methods requires identifying computational operations that address problem constraints to produce intended effects. Here we investigate coordinated agents that extract methodological reasoning from full-text literature and reuse it as prior knowledge for method hypothesis generation. We instantiate this approach as scHypothesizer, a knowledge-grounded agentic framework that uses Mechanism-centered Generation (MCG) to formulate hypotheses from literature-derived Research Primitive Knowledge Graphs (RPKGs) and subjects them to early empirical assessment. We show that coordinated agents recover source-supported reasoning and that full-text RPKGs preserve more complete reasoning than abstract-only representations. In time-filtered retrospective evaluation of 2,429 Problems, MCG achieved the best ranking performance among compared retrieval methods, with a query-macro AUROC of 0.783 and Hit@10 of 69.1%. Finally, scHypothesizer supported early empirical assessment of four researcher-approved hypotheses, providing informative evidence regarding intended Effects, the settings in which they hold, and associated limitations. Together, these results suggest that coordinated agents can make methodological reasoning from prior studies reusable as source-traceable knowledge for generating new method hypotheses and informing their early empirical assessment.
evidence_items.title: A Knowledge-grounded Agentic Framework for Single-cell RNA Sequencing Method Hypothesis Generation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Agentic artificial intelligence transforms self-correction from a localized answer-revision problem into a system-level reliability and recovery challenge. In autonomous, stateful, and long-horizon systems, early errors can propagate through reasoning, planning, retrieval, tool use, external actions, multi-agent interaction, and persistent memory. However, existing research often treats self-correction as either response-level refinement or a capability within broader agent architectures. This study develops an agent-level perspective that connects these fragmented views. It distinguishes reasoning, reflection, verification, correction, and adaptation, emphasizing that reasoning or critique alone does not constitute self-correction unless evaluative information produces a subsequent behavioral change. The study introduces a unified corrective lifecycle covering anomaly detection, error diagnosis and localization, corrective evidence acquisition, repair, validation, commitment or rollback, memory updating, and continuation, termination, or escalation. Existing approaches are organized across five dimensions: correction target, feedback source, temporal scope, persistence, and control architecture. A comparative synthesis shows that self-correction is not uniformly beneficial: repeated reflection can improve performance, stagnate, or degrade initially correct behavior. More reliable gains generally arise when feedback is task-relevant, informative, and at least partially independent of the process that produced the error. The study also identifies key failure modes, including missed errors, unsuccessful repair, over-correction, error amplification, memory contamination, and objective misalignment. These findings motivate research on calibrated intervention, memory integrity, verification, rollback, cost-aware correction, human escalation, and resilience under distribution shift.
evidence_items.title: Self-Reflection and Self-Correction in Agentic AI: A Critical Review of Feedback, Verification, Memory, and Failure Modes

evidence_items.summary: Recent advancements in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have enabled complex reasoning. However, existing remote sensing (RS) benchmarks remain heavily biased toward perception tasks, such as object recognition and scene classification. This limitation hinders the development of MLLMs for cognitively demanding RS applications. To address this, we propose a Vision Language ReaSoning Benchmark (VLRS-Bench), which is the first benchmark exclusively dedicated to complex RS reasoning. Structured across the three core dimensions of Cognition, Decision, and Prediction, VLRS-Bench comprises 2,000 question-answer pairs with an average question length of 129.87 words, spanning 14 tasks and up to eight temporal phases. VLRS-Bench is constructed via a specialized pipeline that integrates RS-specific priors and expert knowledge to ensure geospatial realism and reasoning complexity. Experimental results reveal significant bottlenecks in existing state-of-the-art MLLMs, providing critical insights for advancing multimodal reasoning within the remote sensing community.
evidence_items.title: VLRS-Bench: A Vision-Language Reasoning Benchmark for Remote Sensing

evidence_items.summary: （＊日本語は英文の後に） Sakana AI is launching the Security Research Group, an independent R&D team studying collective, AI-driven cyber defense and the security and safety of AI itself. Our research starts from the idea that intelligence and resilience emerge from collectives, like a school of fish rather than a single swimmer. As a company building frontier AI, we also believe we share responsibility for the security of the society that uses it. Separate from our commercial business, the group’s mission is to serve the public interest: publishing research, reproducible benchmarks, and practical guidelines, and working with government, industry, and academia on research to improve cybersecurity. What We Are Seeing Frontier AI’s ability to find flaws in software is growing, and the number of disclosed flaws is climbing. 1 NIST reports that CVE submissions rose 263% between 2020 and 2025, and that early 2026 ran nearly a third above the same period a year earlier. 2 JVN iPedia, which provides vulnerability information in Japanese, also registered nearly twice as many entries in the latest quarter as a year earlier, most of them from the NVD. 3 AI is widely suspected to play a part, though there is still more to confirm: FIRST points to AI-assisted discovery alongside administrative factors, and NIST staff say AI-based discovery tools have added to their workload. 4 Japan’s government now treats the trend as a national security matter. 1 The strain is already showing. NIST has stopped routine analysis of older records and now prioritizes flaws known to be exploited. 5 Japan’s financial regulators have asked institutions to treat the response as a management issue, with top management directly involved. 6 Flaws are being found at machine speed and fixed at organizational speed, and we suspect the people in between are the ones bearing the cost. The other side is changing too. Attackers are using AI agents, running intrusions against many targets at once.
evidence_items.title: Introducing Sakana AI’s Security Research Group

evidence_items.summary: Interactive video world models turn user commands into the exploration of a generated scene, which requires the scene to keep its 3D structure as the camera moves and each action to keep a stable effect. Existing benchmarks mostly evaluate these properties against references fitted to the video under test, either a scene reconstructed from its own frames or a camera trajectory aligned to the command path with a free scale. Such references can absorb gradual scene deformation and changes in pace and route length, so these errors can pass undetected. We therefore introduce StrideWorld, a benchmark whose references are fixed before the motion they judge. It evaluates scene rigidity against the ground-truth geometry of the start view, and action consistency against the stride of each action, the camera motion of one command. The stride is measured on the model's first steps and then used to test the steps that follow, so each model is judged only against its own steps. Its measurements are validated on rendered videos with known camera motion, and its scores agree with human judgments. Across  videos generated by  open models from 140 start views, all models but one deform their scenes as the camera moves, with offsets up to 7.3 times those of a rigid rendering along the same camera path. Most models keep a steady pace when a single action is held. Along composed routes, several models often stall, and most completed routes end away from the positions predicted by each model's own strides. Only the two models that scale commands by the estimated scene depth bring most routes close to these positions. Fine-tuning two models on a few rendered clips removes most of their mid-route stalls. Code, data, and a leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/chuangwang123/strideworld.
evidence_items.title: StrideWorld: Benchmarking Scene Rigidity and Action Consistency in Interactive Video World Model
