evidence_items.summary: Vision-Language Models increasingly rely on textual reasoning to solve advanced multimodal tasks. Despite its effectiveness, this paradigm faces two fundamental limitations. First, relying on textual reasoning alone can limit perceptual ability in vision-centric questions, where accurate answers depend on interpreting task-relevant visual evidence. Second, applying textual reasoning uniformly across inputs overlooks question-dependent variation in both reasoning modality and depth, often producing verbose and unnecessary traces when little logical inference is required. To this end, we propose Adaptive Visual-Textual Reasoning (AVTR), which introduces visual imagination as a complementary reasoning modality to textual thinking, enabling the model to revisit its visual observations and distill the salient evidence through generative visual reflection. Furthermore, we formulate reasoning-modality selection as a learned routing problem, allowing a single policy to adaptively harness the complementary strengths of visual reflection and textual reasoning in response to the perceptual and inferential demands of the input. Across 16 benchmarks, AVTR improves the average score by 4.5 points over Qwen3.5 baseline, while reducing inference latency by 33\%. It also scales effectively into a smaller size backbone, outperforming the evaluated 2B-scale baselines.
evidence_items.title: AVTR: Adaptive Multimodal Reasoning with Visual Imagination

evidence_items.summary: Dense metric mapping from a single camera and IMU remains challenging: visual-inertial odometry (VIO) provides metric motion but sparse geometry, whereas feed-forward depth models predict dense structure without ensuring metric scale. We present Accord, which constructs an accurate online dense metric map from any camera with an IMU. A VIO filter publishes metric poses, a depth foundation model conditioned on them predicts depth for short keyframe windows, and a factor graph fuses the resulting submaps. Recent work has explored several approaches to this problem. What is essential is the multi-view agreement (Accord), which is considered in SLAM as a source of geometric self-consistency. Accord anchors each keyframe window to metric 3D points triangulated from the filter poses, then exploits bidirectional dense depth agreement between co-visible images to estimate and correct per-image scale errors while preserving the metric scale established by the anchors. Context keyframes further improve depth prediction, and the resulting submaps are fused in a factor graph. We evaluate a single mapping configuration across five public camera-IMU setups and a new Phone-rig/GoPro dataset. With nothing tuned per dataset/setup and every map aligned only by Accord's own trajectory, Accord achieves consistently best/second-best mean F-score at 5 cm on every platform. Accord is open-source along with the phone-rig dataset for the benefit of the research community
evidence_items.title: Accord: Universal Online Metric Localization and Dense Mapping from one Camera and an IMU

evidence_items.summary: Recent work on human-scene interaction (HSI) generation moves from single interactions to long-horizon interaction, where a language-model agent plans and executes a sequence of interactions in a 3D scene under one instruction. However, existing agents struggle in challenging everyday scenarios (e.g., picking up a toy and throwing it into a basket) because they lack spatial control over the motion and quantitative feedback on its execution, and they often fail to complete the interaction sequence. To address these gaps, we present Inhabitant, a training-free agent framework in which the agent specifies each motion through positions, paths and poses, measures how the executed interaction deviates from its intent, and revises the control specification accordingly. For an extensive evaluation in such scenarios, we build Inhabit, a benchmark of 75 household tasks in 31 furniture layouts of an apartment, in which every task chains one to three goals on movable objects and is carried out by the whole body, excluding fingers. On Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 98.7\% of the tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, and 93.3\% and 82.7\% with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, respectively. Ablations confirm that without spatial control the agent fails most tasks, and without quantitative feedback its motion becomes less precise. Code is available on the project page.
evidence_items.title: Inhabitant: An Agent Framework for Long-Horizon Human-Scene Interaction with Spatial Control and Quantitative Feedback

evidence_items.summary: Adapting a film into a game requires selecting source elements and translating them into player actions, rules, and feedback. We introduce Movie2Game-Bench (M2G-bench), a benchmark for evaluating film-to-game adaptation beyond playability. M2G-bench combines general evaluation, movie-specific evaluation, and playtesting by three GUI model players. The protocol connects source content to gameplay steps and implementation evidence, capturing both content preservation and interactive realization. The benchmark comprises 22 films and 658 source-specific reference items. Evaluating 14 models on the same films with their selected primary harnesses reveals complementary strengths in game quality, adaptation, and player experience. A shared weakness concerns playable sequences: this category has the lowest content-presence mean in all 14 models, averaging 37.9 out of 100 compared with 54.8 for iconic elements. Among judgments of retained emotionaldevelopment content, narrative choices account for 60.0% and scenario operation for 7.2%. These findings identify two linked priorities for film-to-game adaptation: preserving source situations that can support gameplay and connecting retained content to player actions and consequences.
evidence_items.title: Movie2Game-Bench: Holistic Evaluation of Film-to-Game Adaptation Beyond Playability

evidence_items.summary: Personalized vision-language assistants use visual observations and personal memories to provide advice tailored to the user. When the observed scene contains a physical hazard, personal context, such as allergies, medical conditions, or mobility constraints, can change what help is appropriate. Responding appropriately therefore requires recognizing the visible hazard and applying the relevant person's information. We introduce PReMind-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates this combination across diverse hazards and personal-memory conditions. It separately measures memory access, grounding, abstention, and hazard response, and assesses joint success on interdependency cases. Existing models often satisfy one requirement while failing the other, and training only for safety or personalization leaves a gap in joint success. We therefore propose PReMind, a two-phase reinforcement learning framework that combines on-demand and forced-call interactions (memory always retrieved) to jointly train grounded memory use and hazard response. At 4B, PReMind raises joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base on the interdependency set and improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention on the main test. Joint-success gains persist under forced-call evaluation and under a second LLM judge across three Phase II seeds; averaged over these seeds, joint success also improves on unseen hazard groups. These findings highlight the need to evaluate and train personal assistants to connect visual evidence with the relevant person's context.
evidence_items.title: PReMind: When Personal Memory Meets Visual Hazards

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries.
evidence_items.title: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.
evidence_items.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements

evidence_items.summary: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.
evidence_items.title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents

evidence_items.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting enables object-level operations on Gaussian primitives, yet existing segmentation methods are largely trained and evaluated through rendered views. This mismatch can produce accurate rendered masks from incomplete 3D selections since alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates learning on dominant contributors while leaving occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised. We propose VODA, a plug-and-play supervision objective that exploits local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervises all Gaussians in selected depth clusters, bypassing contribution-weighted gradient delivery. To evaluate volumetric completeness, we introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and the Removal Depth Error (RDE), a metric comparing predicted and ground-truth depth changes. Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA consistently improves volumetric segmentation on Removal-3D while maintaining or improving performance on LERF and ScanNet. Further analysis shows that VODA recovers lower-contribution Gaussians, while simple gradient reweighting and spatial propagation fail to reproduce comparable gains.
evidence_items.title: The Mask Is Not the Object: Volumetric Supervision for 3D Gaussian Segmentation

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.
evidence_items.title: WeVisForensics: Self-Evolving Agent for Omni AI-Generated Video Detection

evidence_items.summary: Streaming video understanding is becoming increasingly important for real-world interactive systems. Such systems must be proactive for natural and useful human interaction: they should respond as soon as sufficient evidence becomes available while avoiding premature, redundant, or incorrect responses. We present BLIP-Live, a framework unifying data, metrics, harness, and training around a shared formulation of proactivity as effective causal response decisions balancing the two competing objectives of responding vs silence. First, we construct BLIP-Live-780K dataset containing human annotations of proactive response content and timing, which defines this desired behavior. We then propose PAUC-F, a metric to effectively measure our desired proactive behavior. PAUC-F combines existing response timeliness metrics with firing precision to reward early useful responses without rewarding excessive firing. With our desired behavior defined and measurable, we finally investigate model-agnostic inference harnesses that draw out proactive streaming capabilities of offline vision language models (VLMs), together with training pipelines that learn to further improve their proactive responsiveness. Across both settings, we find that combinations of sliding visual windows, online interaction memory, and structured response outputs consistently yield strongest proactive performance. Our experiments result in two models, with our BLIP-Live-Qwen model achieving state-of-the-art performance across four proactive streaming benchmarks, with gains up to 44% over baselines and outperforming multiple closed API models. Our code and data will be released publicly.
evidence_items.title: BLIP-Live: Balancing Timeliness & Firing Precision in Proactive Streaming Video Agents

evidence_items.summary: Streaming video LLMs can continuously observe the world, yet often handle user requests in isolation. We introduce ALIVE, an interactive streaming video model supporting proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction. We construct ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K for two-stage training. Contrastive supervised fine-tuning teaches when and how to respond, while reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA) combines trajectory-level and local advantages to refine decisions, responses, and silence across multi-turn interactions. We also introduce FSI-Bench to evaluate feedback seeking and subsequent task completion. ALIVE achieves the highest overall scores among the compared models on four public benchmarks and FSI-Bench, demonstrating strong streaming understanding and interactive capabilities.
evidence_items.title: ALIVE: Making Streaming Video Models Interactive

evidence_items.summary: Decision-making in humans and AI involves multiple cognitive abilities. System One decision models produce fast, structured choices. Their cognitive strengths and limitations, however, remain poorly understood. We introduce S1CogBench, a benchmark of 24 established cognitive tasks and 27 evaluation modes, evaluating seven open models and the API model Jev. It combines human-response prediction, autonomous execution, and controlled task manipulations to reveal strengths and failures that aggregate scores miss. We find distinct behavioral profiles across the evaluated models. In these models, strong performance on some learning tasks coexists with failures to gather information or adapt to feedback, while high accuracy does not guarantee human-like responses to changing task demands. Shared readout controls show that model rankings depend partly on how choices are extracted. Separate latency comparisons with generative language models show that long responses are much slower than direct decisions, whereas matched one-token generation adds little overhead. To our knowledge, S1CogBench is the first benchmark of System One decision models on established cognitive experiments. It provides a common empirical basis for identifying their capabilities and limitations before integrating them into automated decision systems.
evidence_items.title: S1CogBench: What System One Decision Models Can and Cannot Do on Cognitive Experiments

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal tabular learning involves classification and regression on tables combining structured numerical and categorical features with unstructured text and images. These unstructured fields are commonly represented by pretrained encoder embeddings reduced with principal component analysis (PCA). This reduction prioritizes input variance but may overlook information relevant to predicting the target. We introduce LightTAR, a simple, inexpensive method that adapts dimensionality reduction to the prediction task. LightTAR augments the standard PCA representation with a few target-aware features extracted jointly from the final and an intermediate encoder layer using regularized partial least squares (PLS). We evaluate LightTAR with 21 tabular models, including tree ensembles, neural networks, and tabular foundation models. LightTAR improves average predictive performance for all models and, averaged across models, improves prediction on almost every MulTaBench dataset. These gains come with a small increase in total runtime relative to PCA representations. LightTAR integrates directly into existing encoding pipelines, improving tabular learners' predictive performance without modifying the encoder or the learner.
evidence_items.title: LightTAR: Light and Fast Target-Aware Representations for Multimodal Tabular Learning

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential approach to inferring standardized questionnaire responses from qualitative interviews, but their utility for assessing parenting remains unclear. We evaluated six generative LLMs using zero-shot prompting to infer responses to the Multidimensional Assessment of Parenting Scale (MAPS) from interviews with 43 parents. Models inferred responses to 35 MAPS items from two introductory questions about family, parenting roles, and the meaning of caregiving. Performance was evaluated through exact item-response agreement, correlations between inferred and self-reported parenting scores, systematic score differences, and internal consistency. Across models, Fisher-averaged correlations between inferred and self-reported MAPS subscale scores ranged from .320 to .434, with no consistently superior model. Correlations were strongest and most consistent for Warmth, whereas Physical Control showed little correspondence and substantial floor restriction. Across parent–item pairs, 35.5%–44.7% of inferred responses exactly matched parents’ selected response categories. All models assigned systematically lower response categories than parents and rarely selected the highest category; score underestimation was particularly evident for Positive Parenting. Model-derived subscales generally showed internal consistency, although higher internal consistency did not consistently correspond to stronger correlations with parent-reported scores. Exploratory analyses indicated modest similarity in the associations of inferred and self-reported parenting scores with other psychological constructs. Preliminary comparisons also suggested that shorter interview segments substantially reduced computational requirements without clear evidence of poorer performance.
evidence_items.title: How closely do large language model scores from parent interviews match self-reported parenting?

organizations: The University of Texas at Austin
evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid expansion of data center infrastructure, accelerated by the growing computational demands of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), has led to an unprecedented increase in electricity consumption. As AI developers race to deploy GenAI products, time-to-market pressure drives continuous model training that demands baseload power, often from high-CO 2 emissions sources like natural gas and coal instead of intermittent renewables like wind and solar. Carbon-aware strategies that shift model training in real time to periods or locations with cleaner power on the margin have emerged as a near-term decarbonization lever, but the relative effectiveness of temporal flexibility (pausing model training during high-carbon hours) versus spatial flexibility (migrating workloads to cleaner grid regions) remains poorly understood under real-world constraints. This study evaluates these strategies using 2025 marginal operating CO 2 emissions rate (MOER) data from WattTime across 43 subregions spanning four US grid operators: California Independent System Operator (CAISO), Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), Midcontinent Independent System Operator, and Pennsylvania–Jersey–Maryland (PJM). Using Meta’s LLaMA 3.1 model family as representative workloads, we simulate four scenarios: business-as-usual, reflecting a carbon-informed siting choice with no real-time operational flexibility (S1, BAU); temporal flexibility with varying pause thresholds (S2); ideal spatial flexibility (S3); and spatial flexibility incorporating migration overhead (S4). We find that effective strategies are grid-dependent. In grids with high subregional MOER heterogeneity, spatial flexibility dominates: ERCOT achieves up to 36% emissions reduction via intraday alternation between wind-rich and solar-heavy zones, and the inter-ISO configuration achieves 67.3% reduction, with CAISO and ERCOT absorbing over 80% of training hours.
evidence_items.title: Carbon-aware scheduling of large language model training across multiple US power grid operators: a marginal emissions analysis

organizations: State Key Laboratory of Green Chemical Synthesis and Conversion College of Chemical Engineering Zhejiang University of Technology  Hangzhou P. R. China
Wenzhou‐Kean University  Wenzhou Zhejiang P. R. China
evidence_items.summary: Catalysis is central to energy conversion and green chemistry, but its development is constrained by fragmented literature data, complex reaction systems, difficult mechanistic identification, and reliance on empirical trial and error. Large language models (LLMs), with capabilities in unstructured text understanding, multisource knowledge integration, reasoning, and tool invocation, have been increasingly applied to literature extraction, characterization analysis, mechanistic hypothesis generation, catalyst recommendation, condition optimization, and automated experimentation. However, catalytic tasks are highly specialized, condition‐dependent, and validation‐intensive, making general‐purpose LLMs insufficient for traceable, verifiable, safe, and controllable research. This review summarizes recent progress in applying LLMs to key catalytic tasks and discusses their reliability requirements. We further propose a catalysis‐oriented vertical LLM framework consisting of “task definition–evidence access–constraint control–model adaptation–validation evaluation–feedback updating.” By integrating evidence‐constrained knowledge extraction, constraint‐aware decision‐making, and feedback‐driven closed‐loop optimization, this framework aims to reduce low‐value trial‐and‐error experiments, unnecessary reagent consumption, energy input, and waste generation, thereby supporting reliable and sustainable catalysis research.
evidence_items.title: Construction of Reliable Vertical Large Language Model Systems for Sustainable Catalysis: From Evidence‐Bound Knowledge Extraction to Closed‐Loop Catalyst Discovery

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Formal thought disorder (FTD) is a clinically important feature of psychosis, but its assessment is time-intensive and dependent on trained raters. We hypothesized that a Thought and Language Disorder (TALD)-guided large language model (LLM) framework could identify clinically meaningful FTD features and distinguish healthy controls, clinical high-risk (CHR) non-converters, and CHR converters. Methods: The Story Game transcripts from 74 adolescents and young adults were analyzed, including 15 healthy controls (HC), 40 CHR non-converters (CHR−), and 19 CHR converters (CHR+). A modified 16-domain TALD framework was operationalized using a two-stage LLM agent that screened utterances and assigned domain-specific severity scores. Group differences were examined using sex-adjusted regression models with false discovery rate correction. Ten classifiers and seven feature sets were evaluated using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation and leave-one-out cross-validation. Results: Significant sex-adjusted group effects were observed for Dissociation of Thinking, Poverty of Thought, and Verbigeration, which also ranked highest in the consensus feature-importance analysis. Classification performance was strongest for HC versus CHR (balanced accuracy = 0.881), followed by three-class classification of HC, CHR−, and CHR+ (0.753), and CHR− versus CHR+ classification (0.743). The three-class model exceeded chance performance in permutation testing (p = 0.005). Conclusions: A TALD-guided LLM framework identified a focused set of clinically interpretable FTD features associated with psychosis-risk status and transition. These findings support the feasibility of scale-guided, transcript-based FTD assessment while underscoring the need for validation in larger and more diverse samples.
evidence_items.title: Assessing Formal Thought Disorder in Clinical High-Risk Adolescents and Young Adults: A Scale-Guided Large Language Model Approach to Psychosis Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Aim: Artificial intelligence-based systems are increasingly used for recognizing and assessing skin lesions, yet studies focusing on pregnancy-specific dermatological findings are limited. This study aimed to compare the accuracy of artificial intelligence based large language models in diagnosing pregnancy related dermatological lesions, explaining their etiopathogenesis, and providing clinically appropriate treatment recommendations.Materials and Methods: In this observational study, ten pregnancy-specific dermatological lesions were evaluated using ChatGPT (version 5) and Google Gemini (version 2.5). Each case was presented with an image from Williams Obstetrics, 26th edition, and a standardized patient statement: “I am pregnant. I have a skin lesion like this. What is it, why does it occur, and what should I do for treatment?” Responses were blindly rated by obstetrics and gynecology and dermatology specialists for diagnostic accuracy, etiopathogenesis explanation, and treatment appropriateness, using a five-point Likert scale. Cohen’s kappa was used to assess inter-rater agreement; the Wilcoxon test compared the models; Spearman’s correlation examined score relationships. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.Results: ChatGPT outperformed Gemini in etiopathogenesis explanation (p = 0.002) and treatment recommendations (p = 0.002), with no significant difference in diagnostic accuracy (p = 0.336). ChatGPT generally provided more detailed, applicable responses, whereas Gemini often gave limited or purely directive information. Correlations between criteria were weak and statistically insignificant for both models.Conclusions: ChatGPT was superior to Gemini in etiopathogenesis and treatment recommendations but comparable in diagnostic accuracy. However, no artificial intelligence system can replace clinical evaluation by a physician.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Based Clinical Decision Support in Pregnancy Specific Dermatological Lesions

evidence_items.summary: Cognitive workload models now draw on eye movements, brain activity, cardiovascular variation, electrodermal responses, and patterns of interaction. Their accuracy can be impressive, yet accuracy alone says little about whether the model has captured workload, memorized a participant or task, or produced an explanation that a person can safely use. This critical narrative review examines that problem across cognitive science, neuroergonomics, physiological computing, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Particular attention is given to construct definition, signal-specific confounding, participant-wise validation, and the gap between plausible and faithful explanations. The review develops TRACE-WL: Theoretical alignment, Reliable validation, Attribution fidelity, Cognitive usability, and Ecological robustness. These five requirements link the psychological claim to the validation design and, ultimately, to the conditions of use. The literature indicates that predictive performance and explanation quality must be tested separately. It also cautions against treating feature importance as evidence of a cognitive mechanism without convergent measurements or intervention. TRACE-WL offers a structured way to judge workload systems intended for education, healthcare, transportation, and other human-machine settings.
evidence_items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Cognitive Workload Assessment: Methods, Evidence, and Human-Centered Evaluation

organizations: University of Michigan School of Public Health , , , ,
University of Michigan College of Engineering , , , ,
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for de novo small-molecule design, but the practical and translational utility of generated candidates depends on the configuration of the entire discovery workflow rather than on generative model architecture alone. This review adopts a workflow-based perspective on generative molecular design, tracing the process from existing molecular data sets, preprocessing and representation, to molecule generation, conditioning, candidate prioritization, evaluation, and iterative refinement. It examines how generative AI model families, constraints, and predictive oracles interact within this pipeline, and evaluates generated candidates using intrinsic metrics, computational assessments, and experimental and translational evidence. Active learning, computational and experimental feedback, and human expert input are further discussed as mechanisms for closed-loop refinement. Across these stages, we identify data construction and representation choices, oracle quality, evaluation protocols, and the availability of informative feedback as major determinants of how model performance should be interpreted and whether generated structures progress toward biologically and translationally meaningful candidates, with selected examples. In conclusion, reliable generative drug discovery requires coordinated design across the entire workflow rather than isolated advances in individual components.

Abstract Background To evaluate the clinical performance of a novel artificial intelligence (AI)-based image processing algorithm for two-dimensional angiographic imaging compared with its predecessor across multiple imaging modes, anatomic regions, and endovascular specialties. Materials and methods This retrospective, comparative, randomized, paired, and blinded multicenter reader study included anonymized images acquired during clinically indicated endovascular interventions at 11 institutions in the United States and Europe. A total of 553 image series from 182 patients representing 51 procedure types across interventional radiology, neurointervention, cardiology, and pediatric cardiology were processed using both the AI-based and predecessor image processing algorithms. Thirteen board-certified physicians independently evaluated paired images using five-point Likert scales for overall image quality, contrast of clinically relevant details, noise reduction, and confidence in assessing device and vessel details. The primary endpoint was non-inferiority of overall image quality. Secondary endpoints evaluated superiority across image quality metrics using a predefined hierarchical testing strategy. Results The AI-based image processing algorithm demonstrated non-inferior overall image quality in 98.9% of all evaluations (95% confidence interval [CI], 98%–100%), meeting the primary endpoint across all imaging modes, anatomic regions, and predefined subgroups. Superiority of the AI-based algorithm was demonstrated for overall image quality, contrast of clinically relevant details, noise reduction, and confidence in assessing device and vessel details across fluoroscopy, roadmap, overlay reference, and native acquisition imaging. Overall image quality superiority was not demonstrated for digital subtraction angiography, likely reflecting the intrinsically higher signal-to-noise characteristics of these acquisitions.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate diameter-at-breast-height (DBH) measurement is essential for forest inventory and ecological monitoring. This work evaluates two artificial intelligence-assisted smartphone frameworks: a text-prompt Segment Anything Model 3.1 (SAM3.1) that segments trunks from red–green–blue images, and a depth-guided MobileSAMv2 model that uses depth cues to generate geometry-based prompts. The resulting masks are integrated into a geometric pipeline for accurate and interpretable DBH estimation. Both methods were tested on 202 planted and 285 natural trees. In planted forests, both achieved high accuracy with no failures and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.0 cm. In natural forests, SAM3.1 remained robust (1.5 cm RMSE), while MobileSAMv2 failed in two cases and showed lower accuracy (1.9 cm excluding failures). Using all 487 images, MobileSAMv2 model inference averaged 1.3 s per image on an iPhone 15 Pro. SAM3.1 segmentation averaged 37.2 s per image on an Intel Core i7-1260P CPU, compared with 3.1 s on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU and 0.8 s on an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB GPU through Google Colab. Overall, MobileSAMv2 supports direct on-device deployment, while SAM3.1 offers greater robustness in complex environments and benefits substantially from GPU acceleration.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted tree diameter-at-breast-height measurement

evidence_items.summary: Study on survey of post harvest pathogen, field and storage pests and diseases of three varieties of sugarcane found in Port Harcourt was carried out in the Department of Plant Science and Biotechnology and Rivers State Teaching and Research Farm, all in the Rivers State University. Three sugar cane varieties identified based on stem colour viz: Kasha Cane-B51415 (Dark green), Anancy-BJ6183 (Green) and Kava Rangi-B64.277 (Red stem) were collected from Port Harcourt. The cultural laboratory technique was used for the microbial study while the hand book of South African Sugarcane Research Institute was used for field pests and diseases identification. Microbial shelf-life evaluation further revealed the red variety to contain reduced bacterial (3.8 x106 , 3.5 x106 and 2.2x106 cfu/g) and fungal (0.7 x104 , 1.3 x104 and 1.3 x104 cfu/g) loads for months 1, 2 and 3 respectively than other varieties within the storage months. A total of three bacterial organisms (Bacillus sp, Pseudomonas sp, Staphylococcus sp) and three fungal organisms (Aspergillus niger, A. flavus, Yeast) were isolated within the months of storage. Four field pests were observed viz: locust, aphid, trash caterpillar and fall army worm. However, none was recorded on the red variety. Five field diseases were observed including streak, red rot, rust, leaf spot and smut. The green variety recorded lowest number of prevailing field diseases. Generally, the three varieties of sugar cane performed differently with respect to pest and diseases.
evidence_items.title: Microbial Contamination, Field Diseases and Pests of Three Sugarcane Varieties Found in Port Harcourt

organizations: New York University Grossman School of Medicine;
evidence_items.summary: Nuclear segmentation across patient-derived organoids (PDOs) is complicated by differences in morphology, staining, image scale, and acquisition format. We present ARIPA, an automated human-in-the-loop (HITL) system that coordinates pre-trained segmentation tools through a vision-language model (VLM)-based agentic planning, verification, and refinement loop for hematoxylin and eosin images of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded PDOs. In contrast to existing tools, ARIPA does not require training and achieves good performance. Tissue-aware tiling and image-derived calibration initialize segmentation; optional expert corrections guide configuration search and light-weight object-level rules without retraining or fine-tuning the pre-trained segmentation networks. We evaluated initial ARIPA predictions on more than 50,000 nuclei from 19 images of breast, head and neck, and lung patient-derived cancer PDOs, where nuclear segmentation was challenging due to its 3D structure and variation in imaging layers and malignant cell morphology. Performance was evaluated on agent-selected models before expert feedback, after feedback from the initial runs excluding direct expert edits, and in comparison to a custom-trained HoVer-Net model previously published by our group. At a minimum polygon intersection over union (IoU) of 0.5, image-macro F1 was 0.8380 before feedback, 0.9849 after feedback, and 0.4713 for HoVer-Net. Mean area under the F1 score versus IoU curve was 0.8013, 0.9700, and 0.4317, respectively. The mean paired F1 increase after feedback was 0.1468, with increases in 17 out of the total 19 images and no changes in the remaining two. Ground truth nuclei annotations were created by expert review and editing of ARIPA's post-feedback outputs. In this cohort, ARIPA outperformed the custom-trained HoVer-Net, and its performance was improved further following expert-guided HITL refinement.
evidence_items.title: ARIPA: Agentic Reasoning for Image-based Pathology Analysis

evidence_items.summary: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems evolve toward increasingly autonomous and agentic capabilities, responsibility for decisions becomes distributed across autonomous agents, human stakeholders, and organizations, creating significant accountability challenges. While Agentic AI research has largely focused on technical mechanisms such as alignment, monitoring, explainability, and safety, comparatively little empirical evidence explains how Organizational Accountability is maintained in practice. This study investigates whether Organizational Accountability is explained primarily by technical autonomy, Individual Accountability Avoidance, or organizational governance capabilities. Drawing on a multinational survey of AI practitioners from the United States, Germany, China, and South Africa, the study examines AI projects spanning different levels of automation as a practical proxy for the transition toward Agentic AI. Factor analysis identified the underlying accountability constructs, while correlation and hierarchical regression analyses evaluated the relationships among Automation Level, Moral Disengagement, Responsibility Redirection, Structural Accountability Reinforcement, and Organizational Accountability. The findings indicate that Organizational Accountability is only weakly associated with increasing technical autonomy and is not consistently explained by Individual Accountability Avoidance. Instead, Structural Accountability Reinforcement exhibited the strongest and most consistent relationships with Organizational Accountability, particularly Transparent Compliance and Responsible AI Governance. Additional moderation analyses found no evidence that governance capabilities mitigated the effects of Moral Disengagement or Responsibility Redirection, indicating that governance contributes directly to Organizational Accountability rather than offsetting accountability avoidance behaviors.
evidence_items.title: Organizational Accountability in Agentic AI: A Governance Capability Perspective

evidence_items.summary: Accurate protein complex structure modeling requires knowledge of complex stoichiometry, yet the copy numbers of individual subunits are often unknown. Consequently, predicting protein complex stoichiometry has emerged as a major challenge in recent years. Here, we present StoiAgent, a large language model (LLM)-powered AI agent that automates the retrieval and integration of sequence, structural, and literature evidence to predict stoichiometry while preserving interpretable reasoning traces (chain of thoughts) of its evidence assessment and ranking decision. An open-weight LLM model, Qwen3.6-27B, is used by StoiAgent as the LLM backbone to combine sequences, structural templates, AlphaFold3 structure predictions, and literature evidence, and perform stoichiometry candidate generation and ranking. On 56 CASP17 protein complex targets, it achieves top-1 accuracy of 75.0%, which represents a 23.2 percentage-point improvement over PreStoi with AlphaFold3 ranking (51.8%) and matches the top-1 accuracy of StoPred. Moreover, StoiAgent has a higher top-3 and top-5 accuracy than StoPred (85.7% versus 80.4% and 87.5% versus 85.7%, respectively). Furthermore, it outperforms general-purpose frontier LLMs, including ChatGPT and Gemini, in stoichiometry prediction. Case studies further illustrate how StoiAgent evaluates competing assembly hypotheses by integrating complementary evidence, with recorded reasoning traces documenting its decision-making process. Overall, StoiAgent demonstrates the potential of LLM-powered AI agents to improve protein complex stoichiometry prediction through the automated integration of diverse sources of evidence while providing interpretable explanations to guide downstream structure modeling.
evidence_items.title: Accurate and interpretable protein complex stoichiometry prediction through agentic AI with StoiAgent

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Agentic artificial intelligence (Agentic AI) integrates goal-directed decision-making, state continuity, planning, tool-mediated action, and feedback-driven adaptation into interactive computational systems. Although existing surveys examine agent capabilities, architectures, and applications, cross-paradigm comparisons often conflate functional capabilities with implementation mechanisms and organizational structures. This comprehensive narrative survey synthesizes foundational and contemporary research on symbolic/classical, neural/generative, neuro-symbolic, and multi-agent approaches to clarify conceptual boundaries and examine how agentic capabilities are architecturally realized. It organizes recurring functions into nine groups: goal and context management, perception and state representation, reasoning and decision-making, planning and replanning, memory and knowledge, action and tool use, evaluation and reflection, learning and adaptation, and coordination and orchestration. The principal contribution is an architecture-capability mapping separating functional responsibilities from computational mechanisms and coordination structures. A complementary conceptual reference architecture integrates goal management, environmental interaction, planning, memory, execution, evaluation, and cross-cutting assurance concerns. Representative cases demonstrate how different systems can realize similar functions using different mechanisms. The proposed taxonomy, formal abstraction, and reference architecture are analytical synthesis artifacts rather than experimentally validated models. They support transparent architectural comparison and identify testable research questions.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI: A Comprehensive Survey of Foundations, Architectural Paradigms, Core Capabilities, and a Unified Reference Architecture

evidence_items.summary: World models aim to predict environment dynamics under actions, enabling the prediction of action consequences without executing them in the real world. Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations. This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. To address this, we propose AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective for learning the distribution of visual changes induced by action perturbations. Specifically, we inject temporally correlated noise into the actions of a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation. We then train the world model so that its generated videos respond to this noise as the recorded videos do, without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state. Across OGBench simulation and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 setups, AFFECT makes world-model rollouts more faithful to real outcomes. On DROID, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and on the real robot rises from 0.47 to 0.79, alongside up to 23% lower FVD. These gains carry over to planning, where selecting actions with AFFECT-trained world models improves task success by up to 8.3%.
evidence_items.title: Learning What Actions Change: Action Effect Matching for Dynamics-Faithful World Models

evidence_items.summary: Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow-fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.
evidence_items.title: ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.
evidence_items.title: Posterior Matching Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.
evidence_items.title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher

evidence_items.summary: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.
evidence_items.title: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs

evidence_items.summary: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.
evidence_items.title: WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules
